The two component panels are zero-mean Gaussian, so they look like unsigned anomaly maps. The magnitude panel is positive everywhere and shows the speed maxima at the boundaries between sign changes in either component — the qualitative signature of jet-like and frontal wind structure. A more rigorous prior over wind would use a bivariate Matérn cross-covariance (Gneiting et al. JASA 2010 [^gneiting2010]) so that $u$ and $v$ share lengthscale and a physical correlation; the independent-components shortcut here is the cheapest visual prior that still respects the right marginals.

docs.title: Spectral Kernel Models — A Visual Guide for Earth-System Priors¶
docs.text:
This notebook is a visual survey of stationary spectral kernels — the building blocks behind every Bayesian-spectral layer in pyrox_nn. The companion Kernel Approximation notebook pins down why random Fourier features approximate a kernel; here we step back and ask which kernel we should approximate in the first place, with a particular focus on physically-motivated priors for ocean / land / atmosphere data.

Three things you will see, all by drawing samples from the prior — no inference, no fitting:

  1. The zoo. Side-by-side 1D and 2D realisations of RBF, Matérn-1/2 (Laplace), Matérn-3/2, Matérn-5/2, and the non-stationary ArcCosine [^chosaul2009] kernel. Same lengthscale, same seed family. Differences in regularity, tail content, and stationarity become immediately legible.
  2. A practical decision table. When does each kernel make physical sense, and when does it fail? Five rows, four axes, one paragraph each.
  3. Three earth-system worked examples. A representative kernel choice for each of ocean (SSH-like), land (precipitation-like), and atmosphere (synoptic-temperature-like) signals, with sample paths and 2D fields to ground the recommendation.

Cross-references throughout point to the literature; numbered footnotes collect full citations at the end.

docs.title: 1. The spectral-kernel zoo¶
docs.text: Five kernels, all on the same 1D grid, same lengthscale, same number of features. Three sample paths per kernel.

docs.title: 1.1 Empirical Gram and spectral density¶
docs.text: Two more views of the same five kernels. The Gram matrix shows correlation structure as $\|x - x'\|$ grows. The spectral density $p(\omega)$ — what the random Fourier features actually sample from — is what makes the differences predictable: heavy-tailed densities admit high-frequency content and produce rougher fields; light-tailed densities band-limit the signal.

docs.title: 1.2 The same kernels in 2D¶
docs.text: Same lengthscale, same kernels, samples on a 2D grid. The 2D view is what one usually wants for spatial fields (maps).

docs.title: 2. Why use one over another — a decision table¶
docs.text:
Four practical axes on a single line each.

Kernel Path regularity Spectrum tail Stationary? Use when… RBF $C^\infty$ — analytical super-exponential (Gaussian) yes the field is genuinely smooth and bandlimited (laboratory data, idealised PDEs) Matérn-5/2 2 m.s. derivatives Student-$t_5$ yes "smooth-ish" geophysical fields where you don't trust $C^\infty$ — synoptic atmosphere, large-scale SST [^stein1999][^williamsrasmussen2006] Matérn-3/2 1 m.s. derivative Student-$t_3$ yes the default geostatistics workhorse — mesoscale ocean, soil properties, kriging [^stein1999] Matérn-1/2 (Laplace) continuous, nowhere diff. Cauchy yes rough / mean-reverting fields — turbulence, precipitation, ocean colour patches [^cressiewikle2011] ArcCosine-1 piecewise-affine n/a (non-stationary) no localised abrupt transitions, learned representations, function classes that benefit from ReLU-NN structure [^chosaul2009]

Quick rules of thumb.

  • Don't reach for RBF by default. Stein 1999 [^stein1999] §2.7 makes the now-standard argument: real geophysical fields are almost never $C^\infty$, and Matérn-3/2 or 5/2 is usually a better default. The classic worry is that RBF over-confidently extrapolates because its prior bandwidth is genuinely tiny.
  • Pick $ u$ based on physical regularity. Quasi-geostrophic flows admit two-three derivatives → $ u \in \{1.5, 2.5\}$. Turbulent / intermittent fields → $ u = 0.5$.
  • Heavy spectral tails ⇒ rough samples. If you suspect the data spectrum decays as $|\omega|^{-\alpha}$ for small $\alpha$, choose Matérn-$ u$ with $ u \approx (\alpha - d) / 2$ — that matches the asymptotic spectrum [^stein1999].
  • ArcCosine and friends are for non-stationary structure. If you need amplitude / wavelength to depend on $x$ (e.g., bathymetry-dependent SSH variance, orographic precipitation), a stationary Matérn is wrong; reach for ArcCosine, deep RFFs Cutajar et al. 2017, or the spectral-mixture kernels of Wilson & Adams [^wilsonadams2013].

docs.title: 3. Physics-informed priors for the Earth system¶
docs.text: A pocket reference for kernel choices in three Earth-system tiers. Each table cell is a prior recommendation — what the data tend to look like when you sample from a candidate prior — not a fitted result.

docs.title: Ocean¶
docs.text:
Variable Kernel Why Refs SSH (sea surface height, mesoscale eddies) Matérn-3/2 (anisotropic) known mesoscale length scales (~50–100 km); turbulent cascade slope $\sim k^{-2}$ to $k^{-3}$ in the inertial range [^ubelmann2014][^letraon2003] SST (sea surface temperature) Matérn-3/2 to 5/2 thermal smoothing dominates; submesoscale fronts add roughness [^banzon2016] SSS (sea surface salinity) Matérn-3/2 river-plume / mixing fronts; intermediate regularity [^reul2020] Ocean colour (chl-a, CDOM) Matérn-1/2 + log transform patchy, intermittent, log-normal in amplitude [^doney2007]

Demo: an SSH-flavoured field. A Matérn-3/2 prior on a 2D patch with anisotropic lengthscales (longer in zonal direction) — what mesoscale eddy fields on a satellite altimetry track look like before any data lands.

docs.title: Land¶
docs.text:
Variable Kernel Why Refs Air temperature Matérn-5/2 smooth, large coherence length (~100s of km) [^hengl2018] Soil moisture Matérn-3/2 mixed boundary-layer + subsurface processes [^vereecken2008] Precipitation Matérn-1/2 + log transform intermittent, heavy-tailed, on/off [^cressiewikle2011] [^sun2018] Wind / orographic Matérn-3/2 + nonstationarity direction- and elevation-dependent [^gneiting2002]

Demo: a precipitation-flavoured 1D track. Matérn-1/2 sample paths captures the jagged spatial structure of rain rates along a transect — though for true precipitation one would also need a positivity transform (log or square-root) and possibly a Cox-process zero-inflation [^sun2018].

docs.title: Atmosphere¶
docs.text:
Variable Kernel Why Refs Temperature, pressure (synoptic) Matérn-5/2 quasi-geostrophic ⇒ at least two derivatives [^daley1991][^gaspari1999] Wind bivariate Matérn / divergence-free components share length scale; physical constraint [^gneiting2010] Trace gases (CO₂, CH₄) Matérn-1/2 to 3/2 + non-Gaussian plumes / sources are intermittent [^ganesan2014]

Demo: a synoptic-temperature-flavoured 2D field. A Matérn-5/2 prior with a relatively long lengthscale gives the broad, smooth highs and lows characteristic of synoptic-scale temperature anomaly maps.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• Spectral kernels are priors over functions, parameterised by a spectral density. Choose by reasoning about (a) regularity, (b) spectral tail, (c) stationarity. The decision table in §2 collapses these into a single look-up.
  • For Earth-system data, Matérn-$\nu$ is almost always the right family. $\nu = 5/2$ for synoptic temperature / smooth land variables, $3/2$ for mesoscale ocean / kriging defaults, $1/2$ for turbulent / intermittent / heavy-tailed fields. RBF is rarely the right default [^stein1999].
  • Non-stationary structure needs a different machinery. ArcCosine [^chosaul2009] is the simplest entry point; deep RFFs and spectral-mixture kernels [^wilsonadams2013] go further.
  • Use the prior as a sanity check before fitting. The 2D fields above are what you should expect from your model before any data; if the prior samples don't look like plausible realisations of your domain, the kernel choice is wrong, no matter how good the marginal-likelihood number.

Where to next: with a kernel chosen, the Random Fourier Features regression notebook shows how to do inference (MAP / SSGP / VSSGP) using exactly these spectral layers. The Deep Random Feature Expansions notebook covers the hierarchical / non-stationary extensions.

docs.title: References¶
docs.text:

def dense_log_marginal(K, y, noise_var):
    n = y.shape[0]
    K_y = K + noise_var * jnp.eye(n, dtype=K.dtype)
    L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(K_y)
    alpha = jsl.solve_triangular(L, y, lower=True)
    return (
        -0.5 * (alpha @ alpha)
        - jnp.sum(jnp.log(jnp.diag(L)))
        - 0.5 * n * jnp.log(2.0 * jnp.pi)
    )


def dense_predict(K_train, K_cross, K_test_diag, y, noise_var):
    n = y.shape[0]
    K_y = K_train + noise_var * jnp.eye(n, dtype=K_train.dtype)
    L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(K_y)
    alpha = jsl.cho_solve((L, True), y)
    mean = K_cross @ alpha
    v = jsl.solve_triangular(L, K_cross.T, lower=True)
    var = K_test_diag - jnp.sum(v * v, axis=0)
    return mean, var

def time_kf(N, n_repeats=3):
    times = jnp.linspace(0.0, 1.0, N)
    y = jr.normal(jr.PRNGKey(0), (N,))
    sde = MaternSDE(variance=1.0, lengthscale=0.1, order=1)
    prior = MarkovGPPrior(sde, times)
    f = jax.jit(lambda y: prior.log_marginal(y, jnp.asarray(0.05)))
    f(y).block_until_ready()  # warm jit
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n_repeats):
        f(y).block_until_ready()
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / n_repeats


def time_dense(N, n_repeats=3):
    times = jnp.linspace(0.0, 1.0, N)
    y = jr.normal(jr.PRNGKey(0), (N,))

    def go(y):
        K = matern_kernel(
            times[:, None], times[:, None], jnp.asarray(1.0), jnp.asarray(0.1), nu=1.5
        )
        return dense_log_marginal(K, y, jnp.asarray(0.05))

    f = jax.jit(go)
    f(y).block_until_ready()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n_repeats):
        f(y).block_until_ready()
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / n_repeats

docs.title: Markov Gaussian Processes — Kalman Filtering and RTS Smoothing¶
docs.text:
This notebook is the second installment of pyrox's Markov-GP track. The companion notebook (markov_gp_sde_kernels) introduced the representation layer — MaternSDE, SumSDE, PeriodicSDE, and friends — and verified that the SDE form recovers the same continuous autocovariance as the dense kernel. Here we plug those kernels into a Kalman filter / RTS smoother and turn them into a working temporal-GP model: marginal likelihood via the forward filter, posterior smoothing via the backward pass, and predictions at arbitrary test times by re-running filter+smoother over the merged grid with test points masked out of the update step.

The full pyrox surface is exposed via three names:

  • MarkovGPPrior(sde_kernel, times) — the prior over a sorted 1-D grid.
  • markov_gp_factor(name, prior, y, noise_var) — collapsed Gaussian-likelihood factor for NumPyro models.
  • prior.condition(y, noise_var).predict(t_star) — (mean, var) at arbitrary test times.

We will exercise all three.

docs.title: Background — from SDE kernel to Kalman recursion¶
docs.text:
Given an SDE-form stationary kernel $\big(F, L, H, Q_c, P_\infty\big)$ and a sorted observation grid $t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_N$, the discrete-time linear-Gaussian model is

$$\mathbf{x}_{k} = A_k \mathbf{x}_{k-1} + \mathbf{q}_k, \qquad \mathbf{q}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q_k), \qquad y_k = H \mathbf{x}_k + \varepsilon_k,$$

with $A_k = \exp(F\,\Delta t_k)$ and $Q_k = P_\infty - A_k P_\infty A_k^\top$, and $\varepsilon_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. The initial state is the stationary $(\mathbf{0}, P_\infty)$.

Forward Kalman filter (one pass through the grid):

$$\mathbf{m}_k^- = A_k \mathbf{m}_{k-1}, \quad P_k^- = A_k P_{k-1} A_k^\top + Q_k,$$

$$\mathbf{m}_k = \mathbf{m}_k^- + K_k\big(y_k - H\mathbf{m}_k^-\big), \quad P_k = (I - K_k H) P_k^- (I - K_k H)^\top + \sigma^2 K_k K_k^\top.$$

The marginal log-likelihood drops out as the cumulative innovation contribution

$$\log p(y_{1:N}\mid\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} -\tfrac{1}{2}\Big[\log(2\pi S_k) + \tfrac{(y_k - H\mathbf{m}_k^-)^2}{S_k}\Big], \qquad S_k = H P_k^- H^\top + \sigma^2.$$

Backward RTS smoother uses the filtered sequence to produce $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_k \mid y_{1:N}]$ in a second pass.

Both passes cost $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$ — linear in $N$, where the dense Cholesky path is $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$. Below we verify bit-perfect agreement between the two paths on small grids, then time them on a large grid to see the constant-factor crossover.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Detect Colab and install pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) only when running there.

docs.title: 1. Equivalence with the dense GP — bit-perfect agreement¶
docs.text: The whole story rests on a single equivalence: on the same kernel and the same data, the Kalman / RTS path must produce the same log marginal likelihood and the same posterior marginals as the dense GP. We verify this directly on a small irregular grid for all three Matern orders.

docs.title: 2. End-to-end fit on a noisy time series¶
docs.text: Fit a MarkovGPPrior with a Matern-3/2 kernel to a noisy oscillatory signal and visualize the smoothed posterior.

docs.title: 3. Posterior parity with the dense path¶
docs.text: Side-by-side: the dense GPPrior posterior and the Markov MarkovGPPrior posterior must coincide. We use a smaller dataset so the dense path is tractable.

docs.title: 4. Cost crossover — when does Markov beat dense?¶
docs.text: The Markov path costs $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$ per pass, and the dense Cholesky path costs $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$. The constant factor on the Markov side is non-trivial — each Kalman step involves an $\mathrm{expm}$ (or closed-form transition) plus several $d \times d$ matvecs. We measure the marginal-likelihood evaluation time across a sweep of $N$ values.

docs.title: 5. Composition — SumSDE for trend + roughness¶
docs.text: MarkovGPPrior accepts any SDEKernel. Sums of kernels stay efficient because the state space is the block diagonal of the components — total cost is still linear in $N$, with state dimension $\sum_i d_i$. We fit a SumSDE of a smooth Matern-5/2 (long lengthscale) plus a rough Matern-1/2 (short lengthscale) to a signal that has both components, then read off the individual contributions.

docs.title: 6. Inside a NumPyro model — markov_gp_factor¶
docs.text: The collapsed-Gaussian-likelihood factor drops into a NumPyro model the same way gp_factor does, but uses Kalman filtering for the marginal likelihood. We sketch a tiny model that learns the kernel hyperparameters by MAP — full SVI / MCMC works the same way, but is heavier than this notebook needs.

docs.title: What's next¶
docs.text: This PR ships Gaussian-likelihood temporal regression on a single time axis. Subsequent waves cover non-Gaussian likelihoods on top of the Markov path (CVI / EP), spatio-temporal Markov priors, and natural-gradient inference for the posterior over latent trajectories.

def default_strategies(max_iter: int = 50) -> dict:
    """The four strategies with their default damping and floors."""
    return {
        "Laplace": LaplaceMarkovInference(max_iter=max_iter, tol=1e-6),
        "Gauss-Newton": GaussNewtonMarkovInference(max_iter=max_iter, tol=1e-6),
        "Post. lin.": PosteriorLinearizationMarkov(max_iter=max_iter, tol=1e-6),
        "EP": ExpectationPropagationMarkov(max_iter=max_iter, tol=1e-6),
    }


def fit_all(case: dict, strategies: dict) -> dict:
    """Fit every strategy to one case; return the fits and a summary per strategy."""
    prior = MarkovGPPrior(case["sde"], times)
    results = {}
    for name, strategy in strategies.items():
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        cond = strategy.fit(prior, case["likelihood"], case["y"])
        seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0
        # The eager fit loops compile new code at every iteration and keep it
        # cached; clearing the cache after each fit keeps one kernel's memory
        # bounded across the many fits in this notebook.
        jax.clear_caches()
        rmse = float(jnp.sqrt(jnp.mean((cond.q_mean - case["f"]) ** 2)))
        results[name] = {"cond": cond, "seconds": seconds, "rmse": rmse}
    if "EP" in results:
        ep_mean = results["EP"]["cond"].q_mean
        for res in results.values():
            res["gap_ep"] = float(jnp.max(jnp.abs(res["cond"].q_mean - ep_mean)))
    return results

Laplace               True      6      9.6   0.627          0.0603

Post. lin.            True     20     16.4   0.612          0.0013

The Bernoulli likelihood is log-concave ($h_n < 0$ everywhere), so all four strategies converge. Laplace and Gauss–Newton give identical fits: the Bernoulli curvature $\sigma(f)(1 - \sigma(f))$ stays far above both floors here, so the floors never act. Posterior linearisation and EP agree with each other closely, and both differ from Laplace by a few hundredths in the mean: Laplace centres each site on the mode of the likelihood at one point, while the other two average over the cavity. This is the pattern Kuss & Rasmussen (2005) report for GP classification, where EP's posterior is closer to the MCMC reference than Laplace's. Laplace pays for its bias with speed: it needs the fewest iterations and no quadrature. Past the dotted line (the last observation) every posterior relaxes to the prior mean of zero and the prior variance, because no observation constrains $f$ there.

Here the strategies part ways. The Student-t log-likelihood is not log-concave: for a reading far from the current mean, $h_n > 0$. Laplace and Gauss–Newton then floor the site precision to $\epsilon$, so the site contributes its full gradient $g_n$ to $\lambda_n = \Lambda_n m_n + g_n$ with almost no curvature to balance it. Taking full steps, they overshoot and do not converge in 50 iterations; their means are far from the signal. Posterior linearisation and EP average the curvature over the cavity, where the well-behaved readings dominate, and both track the true signal through the spikes. Posterior linearisation has not met the tolerance after 50 iterations although its mean is already accurate; EP converges.

The standard remedy for Laplace is damping, a shorter step along the same direction. The cell below refits Laplace and Gauss–Newton with damping=0.3 and gives posterior linearisation more iterations.

Robust regression with a Student-t likelihood is a known hard case for every approximation: Jylänki, Vanhatalo & Vehtari (2011) show that EP itself can fail to converge on it and needs damping or a double-loop scheme, which is why pyrox's EP starts damped.

On the log-concave cases Laplace and Gauss–Newton converge in the fewest iterations, because a full Newton step is the right step when the curvature is trustworthy; the damped posterior linearisation and EP take two to three times as many. docs.title: Non-Gaussian Markov GP inference — Laplace, Gauss–Newton, posterior linearisation and EP¶
docs.text:
MarkovGPPrior gives linear-time inference for a GP over one axis, $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$ rather than $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$, through the Kalman filter and RTS smoother. That recursion needs a Gaussian likelihood. Many geoscience variables are not Gaussian: a day is wet or dry, a satellite counts plume detections, a sensor series has spikes. pyrox_ssm ships four strategies that keep the linear-time recursion for such likelihoods by replacing each non-Gaussian likelihood term with a Gaussian site.

This notebook explains how the four strategies differ, fits all four to three likelihoods (Bernoulli, Poisson and Student-t), compares their fits, convergence and cost, and ends with guidance on which strategy suits which kind of geoscience variable.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Detect Colab and install pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm only when running there. The likelihoods come from pyrox_gp; the Markov prior and the strategies come from pyrox_ssm.

docs.title: 1. One loop, four ways to refresh a site¶
docs.text:
Every strategy approximates the likelihood term of observation $n$ by a Gaussian site in the latent $f_n = f(t_n)$,

$$t_n(f_n) \propto \exp\bigl(\lambda_n f_n - \tfrac12 \Lambda_n f_n^2\bigr) \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad \mathcal{N}\bigl(\tilde y_n \mid f_n,\; 1/\Lambda_n\bigr), \qquad \tilde y_n = \lambda_n / \Lambda_n,$$

so that the sites look like Gaussian pseudo-observations $\tilde y_n$ with noise variance $1/\Lambda_n$. One iteration then has two steps:

  1. run the Kalman filter and RTS smoother on the pseudo-observations, which gives the marginal posteriors $q(f_n) = \mathcal{N}(m_n, V_n)$ in $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$;
  2. refresh every site $(\lambda_n, \Lambda_n)$ from the likelihood $p(y_n \mid f_n)$ and the current posterior.

The strategies differ only in step 2. Write $g_n$ and $h_n$ for the first and second derivatives of $\log p(y_n \mid f_n)$ in $f_n$, and $q_{\setminus n}(f_n)$ for the cavity, the posterior marginal with site $n$ divided out.

Strategy Site refresh Literature LaplaceMarkovInference Newton step at the current mean: $\Lambda_n = \max(-h_n(m_n), \epsilon)$, $\lambda_n = \Lambda_n m_n + g_n(m_n)$, with floor $\epsilon = 10^{-6}$ Nickisch, Solin & Grigorievskiy (2018); Rue, Martino & Chopin (2009) GaussNewtonMarkovInference the same Newton step with a strict floor $\epsilon = 10^{-3}$, so every site keeps a usable precision Wilkinson, Särkkä & Solin (2023) PosteriorLinearizationMarkov the Newton step with $g_n$ and $h_n$ averaged over the cavity, $\mathbb{E}_{q_{\setminus n}}[g_n]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{q_{\setminus n}}[h_n]$, by 20-point Gauss–Hermite quadrature García-Fernández et al. (2015); Wilkinson, Särkkä & Solin (2023) ExpectationPropagationMarkov match the mean and variance of the tilted distribution $q_{\setminus n}(f_n)\,p(y_n \mid f_n)$, then divide out the cavity Minka (2001); Wilkinson et al. (2020)

Laplace and Gauss–Newton look at the likelihood at one point, the current mean; posterior linearisation and EP look at it across the cavity's spread, which costs a quadrature per site but sees curvature that a point evaluation misses. In pyrox, GaussNewtonMarkovInference is exactly LaplaceMarkovInference with the larger floor; the Gauss–Newton methods of Wilkinson, Särkkä & Solin (2023) reach the same goal, a positive site precision, by approximating the Hessian instead. Posterior linearisation and EP start damped (damping=0.5); Laplace and Gauss–Newton take full steps (damping=1.0) unless told otherwise.

docs.title: 2. Three likelihoods, three geoscience stand-ins¶
docs.text:
All three data sets share one irregular grid of $N = 80$ times on $[0, 5]$ and a known latent $f(t)$, so every fit can be scored against the truth.

  • Bernoulli, logit link: occurrence data, such as whether a day is wet or dry at a rain gauge. $y_n \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\sigma(f(t_n)))$ with $f(t) = 1.5 \sin 2t + 0.3 \cos 7t$.
  • Poisson, log link: event counts, such as lightning flashes or fire detections per interval. $y_n \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(e^{f(t_n)})$ with $f(t) = 1 + 1.2 \sin 1.5t$.
  • Student-t: a smooth signal measured by a sensor that sometimes spikes, such as a retrieval contaminated by cloud. $y_n = \sin 2t_n + 0.1\,\varepsilon_n$ with 8 of the 80 values shifted by $\pm 2.5$ to $\pm 4$, fitted with a Student-t likelihood ($\nu = 3$, scale 0.1).

docs.title: 3. Fit all four strategies¶
docs.text: The helper below fits each strategy and records whether it converged, how many filter-smoother iterations it used, its wall time, the RMSE of its posterior mean against the true latent, and its largest gap from the EP posterior mean. The strategies run as eager Python loops that compile new code at every iteration, so wall time here is mostly compilation and roughly proportional to the iteration count; read it as relative cost on this machine, not as a benchmark. Every fit also reports log_marginal_approx, but its meaning is strategy-specific, so the tables leave it out.

docs.title: 4. Convergence and cost¶
docs.text: Every strategy costs one filter-smoother pass per iteration, $\mathcal{O}(I\,N\,d^3)$ for $I$ iterations. Posterior linearisation and EP add a 20-node Gauss–Hermite quadrature per site, which is $\mathcal{O}(N)$ and small next to the smoother for this $d$. Iterations therefore drive the cost, and the iteration count depends on the likelihood and on the damping far more than on the strategy's per-step work. In this eager implementation each iteration also pays for compilation, which is why a fit of 80 points takes seconds.

docs.title: 5. Which strategy for which geoscience variable¶
docs.text:
The deciding property is whether the log-likelihood is concave in $f$. If it is, every strategy converges and the choice trades speed (Laplace) against accuracy of the posterior moments (posterior linearisation, EP). If it is not, the point-wise Newton strategies need damping and care, and the cavity-averaging strategies are the safer default.

Variable Likelihood Log-concave in $f$? Suggested strategy Literature Precipitation occurrence (wet or dry day) Bernoulli, logit link yes Laplace for speed; EP or posterior linearisation when the probabilities themselves matter Stern & Coe (1984); Kuss & Rasmussen (2005) Event counts: lightning flashes, fire detections, plume detections per overpass Poisson, log link (a log-Gaussian Cox process in time) yes Laplace, as in INLA; EP for sparse counts with many zeros Møller, Syversveen & Waagepetersen (1998); Rue, Martino & Chopin (2009) Sensor or retrieval series with spikes (cloud contamination, instrument glitches) Student-t no EP; Laplace only with damping Jylänki, Vanhatalo & Vehtari (2011) Any of the above with gaps (cloudy days, outages) any, with mask= — any; a masked site holds zero naturals and the filter skips it —

Where these strategies do well.

  • Long records: each iteration is linear in $N$, so a decade of daily occurrence data or hourly counts is routine.
  • Gaps: every strategy's fit takes mask=, so missing days need no imputation, and a masked fit equals the fit with those days removed.
  • Forecasts: predict extends past the last observation and relaxes to the prior, which is the honest answer for a stationary kernel.

What to look out for.

  1. Undamped Newton steps on a non-log-concave likelihood. Laplace and Gauss–Newton diverged on the Student-t case with their default full steps. Lower damping first; switch to EP if that is not enough.
  2. Laplace bias for binary data. Laplace's posterior mean is shrunk relative to EP's (Kuss & Rasmussen, 2005). If you threshold predicted probabilities, for example to forecast wet days, the difference shows up in calibration.
  3. Gauss–Newton is a floor in pyrox, not a different Hessian. On log-concave likelihoods it is identical to Laplace; its floor only changes sites whose curvature falls below $10^{-3}$.
  4. log_marginal_approx is not comparable across strategies. Each strategy reports its own quantity, so do not use it to choose between them; compare predictions instead.
  5. The latent must be scalar per time. All four strategies take a scalar-latent likelihood, one $f_n$ per observation.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• All four strategies run the same filter-smoother loop and differ only in how they refresh each Gaussian site: at one point (Laplace, Gauss–Newton) or averaged over the cavity (posterior linearisation, EP).
  • On log-concave likelihoods (Bernoulli, Poisson) all four converge; Laplace and Gauss–Newton are fastest, and posterior linearisation and EP agree closely with each other.
  • On the non-log-concave Student-t likelihood, undamped Laplace and Gauss–Newton diverge; damping rescues them, and EP converges with its defaults.

References.

  1. García-Fernández, Á. F., Svensson, L., Morelande, M. R. & Särkkä, S. (2015). Posterior linearization filter: principles and implementation using sigma points. IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing 63(20), 5561–5573.
  2. Jylänki, P., Vanhatalo, J. & Vehtari, A. (2011). Robust Gaussian process regression with a Student-t likelihood. JMLR 12, 3227–3257.
  3. Kuss, M. & Rasmussen, C. E. (2005). Assessing approximate inference for binary Gaussian process classification. JMLR 6, 1679–1704.
  4. Minka, T. P. (2001). Expectation propagation for approximate Bayesian inference. UAI.
  5. Møller, J., Syversveen, A. R. & Waagepetersen, R. P. (1998). Log Gaussian Cox processes. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 25(3), 451–482.
  6. Nickisch, H., Solin, A. & Grigorievskiy, A. (2018). State space Gaussian processes with non-Gaussian likelihood. ICML, PMLR 80, 3789–3798.
  7. Rue, H., Martino, S. & Chopin, N. (2009). Approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models by using integrated nested Laplace approximations. JRSS B 71(2), 319–392.
  8. Stern, R. D. & Coe, R. (1984). A model fitting analysis of daily rainfall data. JRSS A 147(1), 1–34.
  9. Wilkinson, W. J., Chang, P. E., Andersen, M. R. & Solin, A. (2020). State space expectation propagation: efficient inference schemes for temporal Gaussian processes. ICML, PMLR 119, 10270–10281.
  10. Wilkinson, W. J., Särkkä, S. & Solin, A. (2023). Bayes-Newton methods for approximate Bayesian inference with PSD guarantees. JMLR 24(83).

def sde_autocov(sde: MaternSDE, taus: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
    F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params()

    def _k(tau: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
        return (H @ jsl.expm(F * tau) @ P_inf @ H.T).squeeze()

    return jax.vmap(_k)(taus)

def sample_sde_paths(
    sde: MaternSDE,
    times: jnp.ndarray,
    n_paths: int,
    key: jax.Array,
) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Forward-simulate ``n_paths`` realisations of the discrete state-space model."""
    _F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params()
    d = sde.state_dim
    dts = jnp.diff(times)
    A_all, Q_all = sde.discretise_sequence(dts)
    L_inf = jnp.linalg.cholesky(P_inf + 1e-10 * jnp.eye(d))
    L_step = jnp.linalg.cholesky(Q_all + 1e-10 * jnp.eye(d)[None])

    key_init, key_step = jr.split(key)
    x0 = L_inf @ jr.normal(key_init, (d, n_paths))  # (d, n_paths)
    eps = jr.normal(key_step, (dts.shape[0], d, n_paths))

    def step(
        x_prev: jnp.ndarray, inputs: tuple[jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray]
    ) -> tuple[jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray]:
        A_k, L_k, eps_k = inputs
        x_next = A_k @ x_prev + L_k @ eps_k
        return x_next, x_next

    _, xs = jax.lax.scan(step, x0, (A_all, L_step, eps))
    states = jnp.concatenate([x0[None], xs], axis=0)  # (N, d, n_paths)
    f_paths = jnp.einsum("ij,njp->np", H, states)  # (N, n_paths)
    return f_paths


def sample_dense_paths(
    sde: MaternSDE,
    times: jnp.ndarray,
    n_paths: int,
    key: jax.Array,
) -> jnp.ndarray:
    X = times[:, None]
    K = matern_kernel(X, X, sde.variance, sde.lengthscale, nu=sde.order + 0.5)
    K = K + 1e-8 * jnp.eye(X.shape[0])
    L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(K)
    return L @ jr.normal(key, (X.shape[0], n_paths))

Each row pairs the same kernel order; the seeds differ across columns so the realisations are independent draws. Visually the rougher Matern-1/2 paths sit on top, the smoother Matern-5/2 paths at the bottom, with the SDE and dense columns indistinguishable in their statistical character. The variances and correlation lengths match by construction.

def sde_psd(sde, omegas: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Power spectral density of a stationary SDE kernel at angular frequencies ``omegas``."""
    F, L, H, Q_c, _P_inf = sde.sde_params()
    d = F.shape[0]
    LQL = L @ jnp.atleast_2d(Q_c) @ L.T

    def one(w: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
        G = jnp.linalg.solve(1j * w * jnp.eye(d) - F, jnp.eye(d))
        return jnp.real(H @ G @ LQL @ G.conj().T @ H.T).squeeze()

    return jax.vmap(one)(omegas)

Reading the right panel from low to high frequency: the red-noise block is flat at periods longer than its 30-day memory and falls as $\omega^{-2}$ beyond it; the seasonal block puts narrow peaks at one cycle per year and its harmonics, broadened only slightly because its amplitude envelope drifts over five years, plus a hump at periods longer than about five years from the periodic kernel's constant ($j = 0$) term riding on the same envelope; the intraseasonal block is a single hump around 1/45 cycles per day; the tides are exact lines because their frequencies are fixed by astronomy. The SumSDE curve is the sum of the dashed ones to round-off, as printed above.

# TOPEX/Poseidon's exact-repeat period, used by Schlax & Chelton (1994).
repeat_days = 9.9156


def alias_period_days(period_h: float, dt_days: float) -> float:
    """Apparent period of a sinusoid of ``period_h`` hours sampled every ``dt_days`` days."""
    f = 24.0 / period_h  # cycles per day
    cycles_per_sample = f * dt_days
    f_alias = abs(cycles_per_sample - round(cycles_per_sample)) / dt_days
    return 1.0 / f_alias


for name, period_h in tides_h.items():

All the aliases printed above except K1's are shorter than 90 days, as Schlax & Chelton (1994) show for this orbit, so they sit in the same band as real intraseasonal ocean variability. The defence is the one in item 3: put the tide in the model as CosineSDE blocks at the astronomical frequencies and evaluate them at the true observation times.

docs.title: Markov Gaussian Processes — Matern Kernels in State-Space Form¶
docs.text:
This notebook is the first installment of pyrox's Markov-GP track. It introduces MaternSDE — the state-space representation of the Matern-$\nu$ kernel for $\nu \in \{1/2, 3/2, 5/2\}$ — and verifies, end-to-end, that the SDE formulation and the dense kernel describe the same Gaussian process. Once a kernel is in state-space form, GP inference on a 1-D grid drops from $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ Cholesky to $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$ Kalman filtering, where $d \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ is the SDE state dimension.

Subsequent notebooks (issues #37 finish, #38) will compose SDE kernels, run Kalman / RTS smoothing, and expose MarkovGPPrior for NumPyro models. This one stays focused on the representation layer: math, identities, and visual sanity checks.

docs.title: Background — from kernel to SDE¶
docs.text:
Any stationary GP kernel $k(\tau)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ whose spectral density is rational in $\omega^2$ admits an exact, finite-dimensional state-space representation as a linear time-invariant SDE

$$d\mathbf{x}(t) = F\,\mathbf{x}(t)\,dt + L\,dw(t), \qquad f(t) = H\,\mathbf{x}(t),$$

with white-noise driver $w(t)$ of spectral density $Q_c$ and stationary state covariance $P_\infty$ solving the continuous Lyapunov equation

$$F P_\infty + P_\infty F^\top + L Q_c L^\top = 0.$$

Discretising at non-uniform observation times $t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_N$ with $\Delta t_k = t_{k+1} - t_k$ gives the discrete-time linear-Gaussian model

$$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A_k \mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{q}_k, \qquad \mathbf{q}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q_k), \qquad f_k = H\,\mathbf{x}_k,$$

with $A_k = \exp(F\,\Delta t_k)$ and $Q_k = P_\infty - A_k P_\infty A_k^\top$. The recovered continuous autocovariance is $k(\tau) = H \exp(F\tau) P_\infty H^\top$ for $\tau \geq 0$, which we will verify against the dense Matern kernel below.

docs.title: Matern-$\nu$ companion form¶
docs.text:
For Matern-$ u$ with $ u = p + 1/2$ and $\lambda = \sqrt{2 u}/\ell$, the state has dimension $d = p + 1$ and $F$ is the companion matrix of $(\lambda + s)^d$. Concretely:

Order $p$ $ u$ $d$ $\lambda$ Closed-form kernel 0 1/2 1 $1/\ell$ $\sigma^2 \exp(-r/\ell)$ 1 3/2 2 $\sqrt{3}/\ell$ $\sigma^2 (1 + \sqrt{3} r/\ell)\exp(-\sqrt{3} r/\ell)$ 2 5/2 3 $\sqrt{5}/\ell$ $\sigma^2 (1 + \sqrt{5} r/\ell + 5 r^2/(3\ell^2))\exp(-\sqrt{5} r/\ell)$

MaternSDE ships these three orders. Composition rules (sum / product), CosineSDE, PeriodicSDE, and the Kalman-based MarkovGPPrior follow in subsequent PRs.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Detect Colab and install pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) only when running there.

docs.title: 1. Inspecting the SDE parameters¶
docs.text:
A MaternSDE(variance, lengthscale, order) produces a closed-form $(F, L, H, Q_c, P_\infty)$ tuple via sde_params(). We instantiate one kernel per order and print the structural matrices alongside two structural identities:

  1. Variance recovery: $H P_\infty H^\top = \sigma^2$.
  2. Lyapunov closure: $F P_\infty + P_\infty F^\top + L Q_c L^\top = 0$.

docs.title: 2. SDE autocovariance vs. dense Matern kernel¶
docs.text:
The continuous-time stationary autocovariance recovered from the SDE is

$$k_{\text{SDE}}(\tau) \;=\; H\,\exp(F \tau)\,P_\infty\,H^\top, \qquad \tau \geq 0.$$

This must equal the dense Matern Gram value at lag $\tau$. We compute both on a fine grid and overlay them.

docs.title: 3. Discretisation: $A_k$ and $Q_k$ as functions of $\Delta t$¶
docs.text:
Given a time step $\Delta t$, the discrete-time transition is $A(\Delta t) = \exp(F\,\Delta t)$ and the process-noise covariance is $Q(\Delta t) = P_\infty - A(\Delta t) P_\infty A(\Delta t)^\top$. Two endpoints are worth checking:

  • As $\Delta t \to 0$, $A \to I$ and $Q \to 0$ (no time elapsed, no uncertainty added).
  • As $\Delta t \to \infty$, $A P_\infty A^\top \to 0$ (the dynamics decay back to the stationary distribution) and so $Q \to P_\infty$ (the next state is independent of the previous one and has the stationary distribution).

We plot $\|A(\Delta t)\|_2$ and the trace of $Q(\Delta t)$ over a log-spaced range of step sizes.

docs.title: 4. Sample paths via forward simulation of the discrete-time SDE¶
docs.text:
We can draw GP sample paths without ever forming a dense Gram matrix. The recipe is the standard linear-Gaussian forward simulation of the discrete state-space model:

  1. Sample $\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, P_\infty)$.
  2. For $k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1$: sample $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A_k \mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{q}_k$ with $\mathbf{q}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q_k)$.
  3. Read out $f_k = H\,\mathbf{x}_k$.

All work is local in time; no $N \times N$ Cholesky. We compare paths drawn this way against paths drawn from the dense Matern Cholesky for the same time grid.

docs.title: 5. Empirical covariance of SDE samples matches the analytic kernel¶
docs.text: A stronger check than visual matching: estimate the covariance $\hat C_{ij} = \mathrm{Cov}[f(t_i), f(t_j)]$ from many SDE-simulated paths and compare to the closed-form Matern Gram on the same grid.

docs.title: 6. The kernel zoo — primitives and composition rules¶
docs.text:
Matern alone is enough to cover smooth time series, but real signals usually have more structure: a fixed offset, a carrier oscillation, an annual cycle, a quasi-periodic modulation. State-space form scales gracefully here too — every additional kernel is another small block in the state, not another factor of $N$ in inference cost.

This section walks through the four new primitive / composition kernels added on top of MaternSDE:

Class Math State dim ConstantSDE(σ²) $k(\tau) = \sigma^2$ 1 CosineSDE(σ², ω) $k(\tau) = \sigma^2 \cos(\omega\,\tau)$ 2 PeriodicSDE(σ², ℓ, T, J) MacKay periodic, Fourier-truncated to $J$ harmonics $1 + 2J$ SumSDE((k₁, …)) $k(\tau) = \sum_i k_i(\tau)$ $\sum_i d_i$ ProductSDE(k₁, k₂) $k(\tau) = k_1(\tau)\,k_2(\tau)$ $d_1 \cdot d_2$ QuasiPeriodicSDE(matern, periodic) thin wrapper for ProductSDE $d_M (1 + 2J)$

SumSDE is block-diagonal in $F$, $L$, $Q_c$ and $P_\infty$, with the readouts $H$ concatenated. ProductSDE uses Kronecker-sum drift $F = F_1 \otimes I + I \otimes F_2$ and Kronecker-product readout / stationary covariance $H = H_1 \otimes H_2$, $P_\infty = P_{\infty,1} \otimes P_{\infty,2}$. The diffusion is a sum of two Kronecker terms — see the ProductSDE docstring for the full formula.

docs.title: 6.1 Building blocks: ConstantSDE, CosineSDE, PeriodicSDE¶
docs.text: We instantiate one of each, draw a few sample paths via the same forward-simulation recipe used for Matern in §4, and overlay the SDE autocovariance against a dense reference where one is available. PeriodicSDE uses n_harmonics = 7 — enough to match the MacKay periodic kernel to better than 1e-4 in the typical hyperparameter regime.

docs.title: 6.2 Composition: trend + offset via SumSDE¶
docs.text: A common modelling pattern is "smooth trend on top of a fixed offset". With dense kernels this is one line: RBF + Constant. In state-space form it's exactly the same — just SumSDE. The block-diagonal construction keeps each component's state space disjoint, so the cost is purely additive ($\sum_i d_i$).

docs.title: 6.3 Composition: damped oscillation via ProductSDE¶
docs.text: The product of a Matern and a Cosine is the subband Matern kernel — a stationary kernel whose spectral density is centred on a non-zero carrier $\omega_0$. It's the right prior for narrowband oscillatory signals (audio harmonics, geophysical resonances, modulated sensor traces). State dim is $d_M \cdot d_C$ — for Matern-3/2 × Cosine that's $2 \cdot 2 = 4$.

docs.title: 6.4 Quasi-periodic kernels — modulated periodic structure¶
docs.text: The classic "stellar" prior: a periodic signal whose amplitude drifts slowly over time. Mathematically it's $k_{\rm Matern}(\tau) \cdot k_{\rm Periodic}(\tau)$ — a ProductSDE of two stationary kernels. QuasiPeriodicSDE is just a thin convenience wrapper that documents the standard recipe.

docs.title: 7. From the kernel zoo to geoscience signals¶
docs.text: Section 6 showed that every class above is an exact state-space kernel. This section is about when to reach for each one. The useful question is rarely "which kernel is best" but three narrower ones: what does the variable's power spectrum look like, along which axis (time, a transect, a spatial field) is the kernel defined, and how was the variable sampled. We read each class through its spectrum, map it to geophysical signals where the literature motivates that choice, and end with the successes and failures to look out for.

docs.title: 7.1 Every SDE kernel is a statement about a spectrum¶
docs.text:
A stationary SDE $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} = F\,\mathbf{x}\,\mathrm{d}t + L\,\mathrm{d} oldsymbol{ eta}$ with readout $f = H\mathbf{x}$ is a linear filter driven by white noise, so its output has the power spectral density

$$S(\omega) = H\,(i\omega I - F)^{-1}\,L\,Q_c\,L^ op\,(i\omega I - F)^{-\mathsf{H}}\,H^ op,$$

and the Wiener–Khinchin theorem returns the kernel as $k( au) = rac{1}{2\pi}\int S(\omega)\,e^{i\omega au}\,\mathrm{d}\omega$ (Särkkä & Solin, 2019). Three facts follow, and they are most of what you need to choose a kernel.

  • Matern sets a knee and a slope. For Matern-$ u$, $S(\omega) \propto (\lambda^2 + \omega^2)^{-( u + 1/2)}$ with $\lambda = \sqrt{2 u}/\ell$. The spectrum is flat below the knee $\omega \approx \lambda$ and falls as $\omega^{-(2 u+1)}$ above it: slopes of $-2$, $-4$ and $-6$ for orders $p = 0, 1, 2$. The lengthscale places the knee; the order sets how fast high-frequency variance dies, which is the same thing as how many derivatives the paths have.
  • Sums add spectra. SumSDE puts each component's variance in its own band, which is why decompositions such as trend + seasonal cycle + anomaly are natural in this form.
  • Products move spectra. Multiplying a kernel by $\cos(\omega_0 au)$ convolves its spectrum with lines at $\pm\omega_0$, so ProductSDE(MaternSDE, CosineSDE) is a band centred on $\omega_0$ whose width is set by the Matern knee $\lambda$. QuasiPeriodicSDE places one such band at every harmonic $j\omega_0$. CosineSDE, PeriodicSDE and ConstantSDE on their own carry no diffusion ($Q_c = 0$): all their variance sits on exact lines at $\omega_0$, at $j\omega_0$, or at $\omega = 0$.

The helper below evaluates $S(\omega)$ from sde_params() directly and checks two of these facts numerically: that $ rac{1}{2\pi}\int S\,\mathrm{d}\omega$ recovers the Matern variance, and that the spectrum of a SumSDE equals the sum of its components' spectra.

docs.title: 7.2 Which class for which signal¶
docs.text:
Class Spectrum Reach for it when Geoscience example Literature MaternSDE, order 0 (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck) flat, then $\omega^{-2}$ the signal is rough and mean-reverting with one memory time $\ell$ SST anomalies integrating weather noise; the red-noise null hypothesis for climate spectra Hasselmann (1976); Frankignoul & Hasselmann (1977) MaternSDE, orders 1 and 2 flat, then $\omega^{-4}$ or $\omega^{-6}$ the paths should be once or twice differentiable; the default for smooth physical fields a slowly varying trend; interpolating a smooth state between sparse observations Stein (1999); Rasmussen & Williams (2006) ConstantSDE all variance at $\omega = 0$ a level that is unknown but fixed over the record a station, instrument or retrieval offset — SumSDE of CosineSDEs lines at known $\omega_k$ the frequencies are fixed by physics and only amplitude and phase are unknown tidal constituents M2, S2, K1, O1 in a tide-gauge or altimetry record Pawlowicz et al. (2002) PeriodicSDE lines at $j\omega_0$ a cycle repeats with a fixed, non-sinusoidal shape a climatological diurnal or seasonal cycle Solin & Särkkä (2014) QuasiPeriodicSDE bands at $j\omega_0$ the cycle repeats but its amplitude and shape drift the seasonal cycle of atmospheric CO₂ at Mauna Loa Rasmussen & Williams (2006, §5.4.3) ProductSDE(MaternSDE, CosineSDE) one band at $\omega_0$, width $\sim\lambda$ variability is concentrated in one band around a single frequency, with a phase that wanders the 40–50 day Madden–Julian oscillation in tropical winds Madden & Julian (1971); Foreman-Mackey et al. (2017) SumSDE of the above the sum you want the posterior of each component, not only of the total trend + seasonal + anomaly + noise decompositions Rasmussen & Williams (2006, §5.4.3)

Two of these deserve a sentence each. Hasselmann's stochastic climate model treats a slow component (ocean temperature) as integrating fast weather forcing against a restoring feedback, which is exactly the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck SDE, so Matern-1/2 is the physically motivated null model for a mixed-layer anomaly rather than an arbitrary choice. The Mauna Loa CO₂ model in Rasmussen & Williams is a dense-GP sum of a long-term smooth trend, a periodic-times-decay seasonal term, medium-term irregularities and noise; in state-space form the same decomposition is SumSDE((MaternSDE(..., order=2), QuasiPeriodicSDE(...), MaternSDE(..., order=1))) plus a Gaussian likelihood, at linear cost in the record length. Their squared-exponential and rational-quadratic terms have no finite-dimensional SDE, which is why Matern blocks stand in for them here. Foreman-Mackey et al. reach the same band-limited class from the other direction: their celerite kernels are mixtures of stochastically driven damped harmonic oscillators, the stellar-variability analogue of the Matern × Cosine block.

docs.title: 7.3 Time, space and the axis a kernel lives on¶
docs.text:
Every kernel in this notebook is defined on one axis. That axis is usually time, and time is where the state-space form is strongest: it is causal, and irregular time stamps are handled exactly, because discretise_sequence takes each $\Delta t_k$ separately. Satellite overpasses with cloud gaps, or a buoy that drops out for a month, need no gridding or interpolation.

A one-dimensional spatial coordinate works the same way: distance along an altimeter ground track, an aircraft or ship transect, or altitude in a vertical profile. The Markov property then runs along the transect; the filter has a direction, but the smoother uses both sides, so the posterior does not.

For a field over 2-D or 3-D space and time there are two standard routes. The first keeps the SDE in time and puts a spatial kernel across locations, $k\big((\mathbf{s}, t), (\mathbf{s}', t')\big) = k_s(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}')\,k_t(t, t')$, so the Kalman state holds the whole spatial field at each time step (Särkkä, Solin & Hartikainen, 2013; Hamelijnck et al., 2021). The second writes a spatial Matern field as the solution of a stochastic PDE and discretises it into a sparse Gaussian Markov random field (Lindgren, Rue & Lindström, 2011); in pyrox that route belongs to pyrox_lgm. The limitation of the first route is separability: a product kernel cannot represent a signal that propagates, such as the annual-period westward Rossby waves that Schlax & Chelton (1994) found in North Atlantic altimetry. Propagating signals need a non-separable space-time covariance (Gneiting, 2002).

docs.title: 7.4 Successes and failures to look out for¶
docs.text:
Where these kernels do well.

  • Long, irregularly sampled records: the cost is $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$, decades of hourly data are routine, and gaps cost nothing.
  • Decompositions: with a SumSDE, the smoother returns the posterior of each block (trend, season, anomaly) separately, so the components are interpretable without fitting them one after another.
  • Known frequencies: when physics fixes $\omega_k$, as for tides, a CosineSDE block constrains the signal far more tightly than any flexible kernel could.

What to look out for.

  1. Smoothness mismatch. The squared-exponential (RBF) kernel has no finite-dimensional SDE and only an approximate state-space form (Hartikainen & Särkkä, 2010); Stein (1999) argues it is too smooth for most physical processes anyway. Matern is available only for $\nu \in \{1/2, 3/2, 5/2\}$, so check the observed spectral slope before choosing the order: an inertial-range turbulent signal, whose spectrum falls as $\omega^{-5/3}$ (Kolmogorov, 1941), is rougher than even Matern-1/2.
  2. Variance and lengthscale trade off. Under denser sampling of a fixed record, the variance and lengthscale of a Matern kernel cannot both be estimated consistently; only a combination of them can (Zhang, 2004). A short record constrains the slow components poorly, so put priors on $\ell$ and interpret the fitted variance together with it.
  3. Aliasing. A signal sampled less often than twice per period appears at a false, lower frequency. A CosineSDE at the true frequency still fits aliased data correctly, because it is evaluated at the true time stamps; a flexible kernel that lets the data choose the frequency will fit the alias instead. The figure below shows the classic case.
  4. A strictly periodic kernel where the cycle drifts. PeriodicSDE on its own has no diffusion: once its amplitude and phase are drawn, the cycle repeats exactly, so a cycle whose length or phase wanders lies outside its prior. Multiplying by a Matérn envelope removes that constraint: in both QuasiPeriodicSDE and Matern × CosineSDE the envelope broadens the spectral lines and lets phase coherence decay over the envelope's lengthscale (each nonzero harmonic of QuasiPeriodicSDE is itself a Matern × Cosine band). Choose between the two by harmonic content. QuasiPeriodicSDE keeps the periodic kernel's harmonics, for a non-sinusoidal cycle such as a seasonal cycle with a sharp peak; Matern × CosineSDE is a single band, for a near-sinusoidal oscillation such as the Madden–Julian oscillation.
  5. State dimension. Sharp cycle features need more harmonics $J$ (Solin & Särkkä, 2014), and a product multiplies state dimensions: Matern-5/2 × PeriodicSDE with $J = 10$ has $d = 3 \times 21 = 63$, so each filter step costs about $63^3$.
  6. Non-stationary or non-Gaussian variables. All these kernels are stationary. A trend whose rate changes needs a long-lengthscale Matern trend block, not a stationary anomaly kernel. Precipitation, counts and positive concentrations need a non-Gaussian likelihood on a latent Markov GP, which the non-Gaussian Markov notebook covers.

docs.title: What this PR ships and what comes next¶
docs.text:
PR 1 (issue #37 partial, #112 — already merged). The SDEKernel protocol and the MaternSDE family for $\nu \in \{1/2, 3/2, 5/2\}$.

This PR (issue #37 finish). The kernel zoo on top of MaternSDE:

  • Primitives: ConstantSDE, CosineSDE (closed-form rotation discretise), PeriodicSDE (Solin & Sarkka 2014, Fourier-truncated MacKay periodic kernel via a stable log-space Bessel helper).
  • Composition rules: SumSDE (block-diagonal) and ProductSDE (Kronecker-sum drift, Kronecker-product readout / stationary covariance, with the diffusion matrix derived from the Lyapunov identity).
  • Convenience: QuasiPeriodicSDE as a documented ProductSDE(MaternSDE, PeriodicSDE).

Next up — issue #38. MarkovGPPrior plus the Kalman filter / RTS smoother. Once that lands, every kernel above can be plugged directly into a NumPyro model with linear-time temporal inference: f = numpyro.sample("f", MarkovGPPrior(QuasiPeriodicSDE(...), times)).

class MarkovGPModel(eqx.Module):
    log_variance: jax.Array
    log_lengthscale: jax.Array
    log_noise_var: jax.Array
    times: jax.Array

    def __init__(self, times: jax.Array, init: tuple[float, float, float]) -> None:
        self.log_variance = jnp.asarray(jnp.log(init[0]))
        self.log_lengthscale = jnp.asarray(jnp.log(init[1]))
        self.log_noise_var = jnp.asarray(jnp.log(init[2]))
        self.times = times

    def neg_log_marginal(self, y: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
        sde = MaternSDE(
            variance=jnp.exp(self.log_variance),
            lengthscale=jnp.exp(self.log_lengthscale),
            order=1,
        )
        prior = MarkovGPPrior(sde, self.times)
        return -prior.log_marginal(y, jnp.exp(self.log_noise_var))


model = MarkovGPModel(times, init=(0.5, 0.5, 0.1))
print(f"initial NLL: {float(model.neg_log_marginal(y)):.3f}")

@eqx.filter_jit
def loss_and_grad(m: MarkovGPModel, y: jax.Array) -> tuple[jax.Array, MarkovGPModel]:
    return eqx.filter_value_and_grad(lambda mm: mm.neg_log_marginal(y))(m)


opt = optax.lbfgs()
params, static = eqx.partition(model, eqx.is_array)
opt_state = opt.init(params)


@eqx.filter_jit
def step(params, static, opt_state, y):
    m = eqx.combine(params, static)
    val, grads = loss_and_grad(m, y)
    grad_params, _ = eqx.partition(grads, eqx.is_array)
    updates, opt_state = opt.update(
        grad_params,
        opt_state,
        params,
        value=val,
        grad=grad_params,
        value_fn=lambda p: eqx.combine(p, static).neg_log_marginal(y),
    )
    params = optax.apply_updates(params, updates)
    return params, opt_state, val


losses = []
hyper_traces = {"variance": [], "lengthscale": [], "noise_var": []}
for it in range(40):
    params, opt_state, val = step(params, static, opt_state, y)
    losses.append(float(val))
    m_now = eqx.combine(params, static)
    hyper_traces["variance"].append(float(jnp.exp(m_now.log_variance)))
    hyper_traces["lengthscale"].append(float(jnp.exp(m_now.log_lengthscale)))
    hyper_traces["noise_var"].append(float(jnp.exp(m_now.log_noise_var)))

def gp_model(times: jax.Array, y: jax.Array | None = None) -> None:
    variance = numpyro.sample("variance", dist.LogNormal(0.0, 1.0))
    lengthscale = numpyro.sample("lengthscale", dist.InverseGamma(3.0, 3.0))
    noise_var = numpyro.sample("noise_var", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.05), 1.0))
    prior = MarkovGPPrior(
        MaternSDE(variance=variance, lengthscale=lengthscale, order=1), times
    )
    markov_gp_factor("y", prior, y, noise_var)

The NUTS posterior is a tilted ridge: larger variances go with longer lengthscales. Full-rank SVI reproduces both the tilt and the spread. Mean-field SVI cannot represent the correlation, so it fits an axis-aligned ellipse and understates the spread of $\log \sigma^2$ and $\log \ell$, the known behaviour of mean-field variational inference (Blei, Kucukelbir & McAuliffe, 2017). The noise variance is nearly uncorrelated with the other two, so all three methods agree on it. The L-BFGS estimate sits below the low-variance edge of the posterior cloud: it maximises the likelihood alone, while the posterior adds the priors and averages along the ridge, where larger variances paired with longer lengthscales fit almost as well.

Hyperparameter uncertainty propagates into predictions. Below, the NUTS posterior predictive averages the Kalman posterior over 200 posterior draws of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ (one jax.vmap over condition and predict), and is compared with the plug-in band from the L-BFGS estimate.

def simulate_gp(sde, t: jax.Array, key: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
    """Draw f(t) from the SDE prior by forward simulation of its discrete-time model."""
    _F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params()
    A_seq, Q_seq = sde.discretise_sequence(jnp.diff(t))
    d = sde.state_dim
    k0, k1 = jr.split(key)

    def chol(cov):
        # Lower Cholesky factor through gaussx on a PSD-tagged operator.
        return gaussx.cholesky(
            lx.MatrixLinearOperator(cov, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
        )

    x0 = chol(P_inf).mv(jr.normal(k0, (d,)))
    eps = jr.normal(k1, (t.shape[0] - 1, d))

    def step(x, inputs):
        A_k, Q_k, e_k = inputs
        x = A_k @ x + chol(Q_k + 1e-12 * jnp.eye(d)).mv(e_k)
        return x, x

    _, xs = jax.lax.scan(step, x0, (A_seq, Q_seq, eps))
    return jnp.concatenate([x0[None], xs]) @ H[0]


truth = MaternSDE(variance=1.0, lengthscale=1.0, order=1)
true_noise = 0.01


def make_record(T: float, n: int, key: jax.Array, gaps: bool = False):
    t = jnp.linspace(0.0, T, n)
    yy = simulate_gp(truth, t, key) + jnp.sqrt(true_noise) * jr.normal(
        jr.fold_in(key, 1), (n,)
    )
    mask = (t % 20.0) < 10.0 if gaps else jnp.ones(n, dtype=bool)
    return t, yy, mask

    return jax.vmap(lambda a: jax.vmap(lambda b: one(a, b))(log_ell_grid))(log_var_grid)

Three things stand out.

  • Every surface is a ridge along $\sigma^2 / \ell^3 = \text{const}$, the red line through the truth, as Zhang's result predicts. Along the ridge the likelihood barely changes, so $\sigma^2$ and $\ell$ separately are poorly determined even when their combination is sharp.
  • Infill helps, but far less than record length. On the same stretch of the same realisation, ten times more observations thin the ridge and trim it: the range of $\ell$ within two log-units of the maximum goes from 1.00–2.76 to 0.91–2.00. It stays a long ridge spanning a factor of two, because denser samples of the same ten decorrelation times mostly add information about short-lag behaviour, which pins down $\sigma^2 / \ell^3$ rather than $\ell$ itself.
  • Record length does. The ten-times longer record shrinks the ridge to a small ellipse around the truth. Even with half of it missing, its 501 observations constrain $\ell$ far better than the 1000 observations packed into the short record, because what informs $\ell$ is the number of decorrelation times observed, not the number of points. Masking the gaps keeps every observed step and adds no imputed ones.

docs.title: Training a Markov GP — maximum likelihood, NUTS, variational inference, and what the data can tell you¶
docs.text:
MarkovGPPrior.log_marginal(y, noise_var) is the Kalman-filter marginal likelihood of a GP with a Gaussian likelihood. It is differentiable in every kernel hyperparameter through the SDE construction and the lax.scan-based filter, and it costs $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$ per evaluation. That makes three ways of setting the hyperparameters $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\sigma^2, \ell, \sigma_n^2)$ cheap:

  1. a point estimate: maximise $\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})$ with L-BFGS (type-II maximum likelihood);
  2. the full posterior $p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{y})$ with NUTS, through markov_gp_factor in a NumPyro model;
  3. an approximate posterior with stochastic variational inference, mean-field and full-rank.

The last section asks what any of them can recover: which hyperparameters a record actually constrains, and how record length, sampling density and gaps change that, framed for geoscience time series.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Detect Colab and install pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm only when running there.

docs.title: 1. Synthetic data¶
docs.text: A noisy mixture of two sinusoids on an irregular time grid of $N = 60$ points over $t \in [0, 8]$, fitted below with a Matern-3/2 SDE prior. The signal is not a draw from that prior, so no hyperparameter value is "true" here; section 4 uses data drawn from a known Matern-3/2 GP for that.

docs.title: 2. A point estimate: type-II maximum likelihood with L-BFGS¶
docs.text: We optimise in log-space so that $\sigma^2, \ell, \sigma_n^2 > 0$ holds automatically. The model lives in a small equinox.Module so it composes with optax.

docs.title: 3.1 The model¶
docs.text:
markov_gp_factor adds the Kalman marginal likelihood $\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})$ to a NumPyro model as a factor site, with the latent function integrated out. The model therefore has only three sample sites, one per hyperparameter, and every log-density evaluation is one $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$ filter pass.

The priors encode what a record can and cannot inform:

  • $\sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(0, 1)$: weakly informative around the data's own scale.
  • $\ell \sim \mathrm{InverseGamma}(3, 3)$: mean 1.5, with almost no mass below the sampling interval (about 0.13) or above the record length (8). A lengthscale below the sampling interval is indistinguishable from noise, and one beyond the record shows no decorrelation inside it, so the likelihood is flat in both directions; the prior keeps the posterior away from those regions. The inverse-gamma's light left tail is what does this.
  • $\sigma_n^2 \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 0.05, 1)$.

docs.title: 3.2 MCMC with NUTS¶
docs.text: NUTS (Hoffman & Gelman, 2014) is the right sampler here: three continuous parameters, a smooth log-density with exact gradients, and no latent function in the state because the factor has integrated it out, so there is no funnel between $\mathbf{f}$ and its hyperparameters to trap the sampler. Two chains of 1000 draws after 500 warm-up steps are plenty for three parameters.

docs.title: 3.3 Stochastic variational inference: mean-field and full-rank¶
docs.text: SVI fits a Gaussian $q(\boldsymbol{\theta}; \boldsymbol{\nu})$ in the unconstrained (log) space by maximising the ELBO. With three parameters the choice of guide is easy: AutoMultivariateNormal learns a full $3 \times 3$ covariance at negligible cost, which matters because the posterior is correlated; AutoNormal (mean-field) is shown for contrast, because it is the default people reach for on larger models.

docs.title: 3.4 Comparing the posteriors¶
docs.text: The scatter plots show $(\log \sigma^2, \log \ell)$ samples from each method, with the L-BFGS estimate marked; the table gives each method's posterior standard deviation of the three log-hyperparameters.

docs.title: 4. What a record can tell you about its hyperparameters¶
4.1 The variance–lengthscale ridge¶
docs.text:
The tilted ridge in §3.4 is not an accident of this data set. For a Matérn-$\nu$ process observed more and more densely on a fixed interval (infill sampling), $\sigma^2$ and $\ell$ cannot both be estimated consistently: only the combination $\sigma^2 / \ell^{2\nu}$ can (Zhang, 2004), which for Matern-3/2 is $\sigma^2 / \ell^3$. Sampling the same stretch more often sharpens that combination and nothing else. Only a longer record, more decorrelation lengths, separates $\sigma^2$ from $\ell$.

For a geoscience series the lengthscale is a decorrelation time: the memory of a sea-surface temperature anomaly, the persistence of a soil-moisture anomaly, the duration of a drought spell. Estimating it needs a record that spans many such times, which is often what a geophysical record does not have.

docs.title: 4.2 Record length, sampling density and gaps¶
docs.text:
To make this concrete we draw data from a known Matern-3/2 GP ($\sigma^2 = 1$, $\ell = 1$, noise variance $0.01$) and map the log marginal likelihood over $(\ell, \sigma^2)$ with the noise variance held at its true value, for four records:

  1. a short record: $T = 10$ (ten decorrelation times), $N = 100$, every tenth point of record 2;
  2. the same stretch of the same realisation sampled ten times more densely: $T = 10$, $N = 1000$ (infill, like moving from daily to hourly sampling), so records 1 and 2 differ only in sampling density;
  3. a ten-times longer record at the original density: $T = 100$, $N = 1000$;
  4. the long record with every other block of 10 time units missing, passed to the filter through mask= (like a sensor that is down every other season): $T = 100$, 501 observed.

The surfaces use jax.vmap over a grid and one jax.jit, so each costs a second or two.

docs.title: 4.3 Practical guidance for geoscience records¶
docs.text:
1. Count decorrelation times, not points. Compare the record length with the plausible range of $\ell$ before trusting a fitted lengthscale. In the experiment above, ten decorrelation times left every $\ell$ from 1.0 to 2.8 within two log-units of the maximum with 100 points, and from 0.9 to 2.0 with 1000.
  2. Report what is identified. For a Matérn-$\nu$ fit, $\sigma^2 / \ell^{2\nu}$ is well determined and $\sigma^2$ and $\ell$ separately may not be; interpret them together, and prefer predictions and their uncertainty over individual hyperparameter values.
  3. Use priors that encode the record. Keep $\ell$ between the sampling interval and the record length, as the inverse-gamma prior in §3.1 does. Penalised-complexity priors for the Matérn range and variance (Fuglstad et al., 2019) are a principled default; pyrox-lgm implements them for its latent Gaussian models.
  4. Propagate hyperparameter uncertainty where it matters. Plug-in estimates are fine for interpolation inside a dense record and overconfident for forecasts and long gaps. Use NUTS when the posterior is small, as here; use full-rank rather than mean-field VI when it is not.
  5. Handle gaps with mask=. Missing seasons or outages need no imputation, and as §4.2 shows, a long record with gaps can be worth more than a short complete one.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• MarkovGPPrior.log_marginal is differentiable and linear in $N$, so type-II maximum likelihood (L-BFGS), NUTS and SVI over the kernel hyperparameters are all cheap; markov_gp_factor puts it in a NumPyro model with the latent function integrated out.
  • The hyperparameter posterior is a correlated ridge in $(\log \sigma^2, \log \ell)$. NUTS and full-rank SVI capture it; mean-field SVI understates its spread.
  • Only $\sigma^2 / \ell^{2\nu}$ is fixed by dense sampling of a fixed record; separating $\sigma^2$ from $\ell$ takes a record many decorrelation times long, and a long record with gaps beats a short dense one.

For non-Gaussian likelihoods, plug a MarkovGPPrior into one of the strategies in the companion non-Gaussian Markov GP notebook; LaplaceMarkovInference's log_marginal_approx approximates the evidence and can play the role of the loss.

References.

  1. Blei, D. M., Kucukelbir, A. & McAuliffe, J. D. (2017). Variational inference: a review for statisticians. JASA 112(518), 859–877.
  2. Fuglstad, G.-A., Simpson, D., Lindgren, F. & Rue, H. (2019). Constructing priors that penalize the complexity of Gaussian random fields. JASA 114(525), 445–452.
  3. Hoffman, M. D. & Gelman, A. (2014). The No-U-Turn sampler: adaptively setting path lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. JMLR 15, 1593–1623.
  4. Zhang, H. (2004). Inconsistent estimation and asymptotically equal interpolations in model-based geostatistics. JASA 99(465), 250–261.

def psd(matrix: jax.Array) -> lx.MatrixLinearOperator:
    """Tag a symmetric positive semi-definite matrix for gaussx."""
    return lx.MatrixLinearOperator(matrix, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)


def optimal_q(
    prior_: SparseMarkovGPPrior, t_: jax.Array, y_: jax.Array, noise_var: float
) -> tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array]:
    """Optimal Gaussian q(u) for a Gaussian likelihood (Titsias, 2009), via gaussx."""
    K_zz_op_, K_xz_, _ = prior_.predictive_blocks(t_)
    K_zz_ = K_zz_op_.as_matrix()
    B = psd(K_zz_ + K_xz_.T @ K_xz_ / noise_var)
    m_q_ = K_zz_ @ gaussx.solve(B, K_xz_.T @ (y_ - prior_.mean(t_))) / noise_var
    S_q_ = K_zz_ @ gaussx.solve_columns(B, K_zz_)
    return m_q_, 0.5 * (S_q_ + S_q_.T)


def cholesky_matrix(cov: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
    """Lower Cholesky factor of a covariance as a dense array, via gaussx."""
    return gaussx.cholesky(psd(cov)).as_matrix()

def fit_sparse(M_: int) -> SparseConditionedMarkovGP:
    Z_ = jnp.linspace(times[0], times[-1], M_)
    prior_ = SparseMarkovGPPrior(sde, Z_, jitter=1e-6)
    m_, S_ = optimal_q(prior_, times, y, sigma2)
    L_ = cholesky_matrix(S_ + 1e-9 * jnp.eye(M_))
    g_ = eqx.tree_at(
        lambda g: (g.mean, g.scale_tril),
        FullRankGuide.init(M_, scale=0.3),
        replace=(m_, L_),
    )
    return SparseConditionedMarkovGP(prior=prior_, guide=g_)

class SparseCountFit(eqx.Module):
    """Whitened guide parameters and log-hyperparameters, optimised together."""

    q_mean: jax.Array
    q_tril: jax.Array
    log_variance: jax.Array
    log_lengthscale: jax.Array

    def build(self) -> tuple[SparseMarkovGPPrior, WhitenedGuide]:
        sde = MaternSDE(
            jnp.exp(self.log_variance), jnp.exp(self.log_lengthscale), order=1
        )
        prior = SparseMarkovGPPrior(sde, Z_c, jitter=1e-6)
        diag = jax.nn.softplus(jnp.diag(self.q_tril))
        scale_tril = jnp.tril(self.q_tril, k=-1) + jnp.diag(diag)
        return prior, WhitenedGuide(self.q_mean, scale_tril)


def negative_elbo(fit: SparseCountFit) -> jax.Array:
    prior, guide = fit.build()
    return -sparse_markov_elbo(prior, guide, poisson, t_c, y_c, integrator=quadrature)

    log_variance=jnp.asarray(0.0),

)

def adam_step(fit, state):
    value, grads = eqx.filter_value_and_grad(negative_elbo)(fit)
    updates, state = adam.update(grads, state, fit)
    return eqx.apply_updates(fit, updates), state, value

def sparse_count_model(t: jax.Array, y: jax.Array) -> None:
    variance = numpyro.sample("variance", dist.LogNormal(0.0, 1.0))
    lengthscale = numpyro.sample("lengthscale", dist.InverseGamma(3.0, 6.0))
    q_mean = numpyro.param("q_mean", jnp.zeros(M_c))
    q_tril = numpyro.param(
        "q_scale_tril", 0.5 * jnp.eye(M_c), constraint=dist.constraints.lower_cholesky

    prior = SparseMarkovGPPrior(
        MaternSDE(variance, lengthscale, order=1), Z_c, jitter=1e-6
    )
    sparse_markov_factor(
        "elbo",
        prior,
        WhitenedGuide(q_mean, q_tril),
        poisson,
        t,
        y,
        integrator=quadrature,
    )

The NumPyro posterior sits at a smaller variance and a shorter lengthscale than the Adam point estimate, which falls outside both 90% intervals. The two are fits to different objectives: the NumPyro model adds priors (the inverse-gamma on $\ell$ has mean 3) and averages over $q(\boldsymbol{\theta})$, and the shift runs along the variance–lengthscale ridge of the training notebook, since $\sigma^2/\ell^3$ is similar for both (about 0.029 against 0.024). Treat the intervals as approximate: one $q(\mathbf{u})$ is shared by every value of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ the guide proposes, and the variational bound adds its own bias, so they are typically narrower than an exact posterior would be. NumPyro's AutoMultivariateNormal.sample_posterior does not handle the model's constrained numpyro.param site here, which is why the draws come from Predictive over the guide.

def simulate_gp(sde, t: jax.Array, key: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
    """Draw f(t) from the SDE prior by forward simulation of its discrete-time model."""
    _F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params()
    A_seq, Q_seq = sde.discretise_sequence(jnp.diff(t))
    d = sde.state_dim
    k0, k1 = jr.split(key)
    x0 = gaussx.cholesky(psd(P_inf)).mv(jr.normal(k0, (d,)))
    eps = jr.normal(k1, (t.shape[0] - 1, d))

    def step(x, inputs):
        A_k, Q_k, e_k = inputs
        x = A_k @ x + gaussx.cholesky(psd(Q_k + 1e-12 * jnp.eye(d))).mv(e_k)
        return x, x

    _, xs = jax.lax.scan(step, x0, (A_seq, Q_seq, eps))
    return jnp.concatenate([x0[None], xs]) @ H[0]

t_s = jnp.sort(jr.uniform(jr.PRNGKey(20), (N_s,), maxval=T_s))
t_eval = jnp.linspace(0.0, T_s, 1000)


def closed_form_sparse_mean(sde, M_: int, y_s: jax.Array) -> jax.Array:
    """Posterior mean at t_eval from the optimal Gaussian q(u) on an even grid of M_ times."""
    Z_ = jnp.linspace(0.0, T_s, M_)
    prior_ = SparseMarkovGPPrior(sde, Z_, jitter=1e-6)
    K_zz_op_, K_xz_, _ = prior_.predictive_blocks(t_s)
    # Mean at t_eval: K_ez K_zz^{-1} m_q = sigma^{-2} K_ez B^{-1} K_zx y, as in optimal_q.
    B = psd(K_zz_op_.as_matrix() + K_xz_.T @ K_xz_ / noise_s)
    K_ez_ = prior_.predictive_blocks(t_eval)[1]
    return K_ez_ @ gaussx.solve(B, K_xz_.T @ y_s) / noise_s
