docs.title: Sparse variational Markov GP — inducing times, non-Gaussian likelihoods and NumPyro¶
docs.text:
SparseMarkovGPPrior is the inducing-time-grid analogue of MarkovGPPrior. It wraps any SDEKernel and a sorted inducing grid $\mathbf{z}$ of length $M$, exposing the standard SVGP building blocks $(K_{ZZ}, K_{XZ}, \mathrm{diag}\,K_{XX})$ derived from the SDE autocovariance $k(\tau) = H \exp(F\tau) P_\infty H^\top$.

Because the predictive-block contract matches the dense SparseGPPrior, the variational guides of pyrox_gp (FullRankGuide, MeanFieldGuide, WhitenedGuide) plug straight in. sparse_markov_elbo gives the ELBO in closed form for a Gaussian likelihood and by quadrature (a gaussx integrator) for any other, and sparse_markov_factor registers it in a NumPyro model.

Cost: $\mathcal{O}(M^3 + N M)$ per ELBO evaluation. This is the SVGP construction (Titsias, 2009; Hensman, Fusi & Lawrence, 2013) applied to an SDE kernel; it does not yet exploit the Markov structure of $q(\mathbf{u})$, which the sparse Markovian algorithms of Adam et al. (2020) and Wilkinson, Solin & Adam (2021) do to make the cost linear in $M$.

The notebook covers the Gaussian case with a closed-form $q(\mathbf{u})$, a Poisson likelihood fitted by optimising the ELBO, the same model in NumPyro, and, last, how to choose the inducing grid and when the dense Markov path is the better tool.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Detect Colab and install pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm only when running there. The guides and the Poisson likelihood come from pyrox_gp; the Gaussian likelihood from the pyrox core.

docs.title: 1. Gaussian likelihood: synthetic regression data¶
docs.text: Noisy mixture of two sinusoids on an irregular time grid.

docs.title: 2. Sparse Markov GP setup¶
docs.text: Pick M = 12 evenly-spaced inducing times and a Matern-3/2 SDE prior. The variational guide is a FullRankGuide over the inducing function values $u = f(Z)$.

docs.title: 3. Conjugate update — closed-form q(u) for a Gaussian likelihood¶
docs.text:
For Gaussian observations the optimal $q(u) = \mathcal{N}(m_q, S_q)$ is closed-form (Titsias 2009):

$$S_q = (\sigma^{-2} K_{ZZ}^{-1} K_{ZX} K_{XZ} K_{ZZ}^{-1} + K_{ZZ}^{-1})^{-1},\qquad m_q = \sigma^{-2} S_q K_{ZZ}^{-1} K_{ZX}\,(y - \mu).$$

With $B = K_{ZZ} + \sigma^{-2} K_{ZX} K_{XZ}$ the same solution is $S_q = K_{ZZ} B^{-1} K_{ZZ}$ and $m_q = \sigma^{-2} K_{ZZ} B^{-1} K_{ZX}(y - \mu)$, which the cell below computes with gaussx solves on a PSD-tagged operator and no explicit inverse. This sidesteps the need to optimise the ELBO and gives the optimal $q(u)$ at the prescribed inducing locations directly. We use it here to demonstrate the sparse_markov_elbo / SparseConditionedMarkovGP API on a fitted guide.

docs.title: 4. Posterior at the fitted guide¶
docs.text: SparseConditionedMarkovGP.predict(t_star) produces the mean / variance at arbitrary test times via the standard SVGP predictive (cost $O(M^3 + |t_*|\,M)$).

docs.title: 5. Comparison: sparse vs dense Markov GP¶
docs.text: At the closed-form $q(u)$ and well-spaced inducing points, the SVGP posterior should approximate the dense-Markov posterior. The remaining difference is the inducing-set bias from working with $M = 12$ pseudo-points instead of all $N = 80$ data points.

docs.title: 6. Sweep: how many inducing points do we need?¶
docs.text: Increase M and re-fit the closed-form $q(u)$. Past a kernel-dependent threshold, the sparse posterior is indistinguishable from the dense one.

docs.title: 7. A non-Gaussian likelihood: counts¶
docs.text:
For a non-Gaussian likelihood there is no closed-form $q(\mathbf{u})$, so we maximise the ELBO directly. The data are event counts on an irregular grid, $y_n \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(e^{f(t_n)})$, the kind of series a detection product produces (fire detections, lightning flashes or plume detections per overpass). sparse_markov_elbo evaluates the expected log-likelihood $\mathbb{E}_{q(f_n)}[\log p(y_n \mid f_n)]$ by 20-point Gauss–Hermite quadrature.

The guide is a WhitenedGuide, which parameterises $q(\mathbf{v}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}_v, L_v L_v^\top)$ in whitened coordinates $\mathbf{u} = L_{ZZ}\mathbf{v}$; that keeps the optimisation well conditioned as the kernel hyperparameters move (Hensman, Matthews & Ghahramani, 2015). We optimise the guide and the log-variance and log-lengthscale jointly with Adam.

docs.title: 8. The same model in NumPyro¶
docs.text:
sparse_markov_factor adds the sparse ELBO to a NumPyro model as a factor. Putting priors on the kernel hyperparameters and registering the whitened guide's parameters as numpyro.param sites in the model gives a nested bound: SVI with an automatic guide over $(\sigma^2, \ell)$ maximises

$$\mathbb{E}_{q(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{u}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \log p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) - \log q(\boldsymbol{\theta})\bigr] \le \log p(\mathbf{y}),$$

where $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{u}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ is the sparse ELBO. Variational inference is the appropriate choice here, and MCMC is not: the factor is a lower bound on $\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})$, not the likelihood, so NUTS over $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ with this factor would sample the wrong distribution. For MCMC over the hyperparameters of a Gaussian-likelihood model, use the exact markov_gp_factor as in the training notebook. Two hyperparameters make a full-rank guide (AutoMultivariateNormal) cheap.

docs.title: 9. Choosing the inducing grid, and when not to go sparse¶
9.1 How dense must the inducing grid be?¶
docs.text: The inducing times must resolve the posterior, so their spacing $\Delta z$ has to be small relative to the lengthscale $\ell$, and how small depends on the kernel's roughness. The cell below draws 1000 noisy observations over 50 lengthscales from Matern GPs of each order and compares the closed-form sparse posterior mean on an evenly spaced grid with the exact dense Markov posterior mean, for spacings from $2\ell$ down to $\ell/8$. The error is the RMSE between the two means, relative to the standard deviation of the dense mean.

docs.title: 9.2 Sparse or dense Markov, for geoscience records?¶
docs.text:
For a GP over time, the dense Markov path is already linear in $N$. Going sparse pays off only in specific situations, and the $\mathcal{O}(M^3)$ cost of this SVGP construction sets a hard limit:

Situation Better path Why Long record with many decorrelation times, e.g. a decade of daily data with a week-long memory dense Markov $M$ must grow like $T/\Delta z$; at $\Delta z = \ell/4$ and $T = 500\ell$ that is $M = 2000$ and about $10^{10}$ operations per ELBO, against $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$ for the filter Many observations per decorrelation time, e.g. a 1 Hz sensor whose signal of interest varies over hours sparse a few inducing times per $\ell$ summarise thousands of points, and the $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ term stays cheap Rough signals (Matern-1/2) dense Markov the inducing grid converges slowly (§9.1) Non-Gaussian likelihood inside a larger NumPyro model fitted by SVI sparse sparse_markov_factor is a variational objective that composes with other SVI components; the dense strategies are fixed-point loops Hyperparameter posterior by MCMC dense Markov markov_gp_factor is the exact marginal likelihood; the sparse factor is a bound

The sparse Markovian algorithms of Adam et al. (2020) and Wilkinson, Solin & Adam (2021) remove the $\mathcal{O}(M^3)$ limit by running Kalman recursions over the inducing times, which would make the first row a case for going sparse as well.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• SparseMarkovGPPrior(sde_kernel, Z) exposes the SVGP predictive blocks for any state-space kernel, so pyrox_gp's variational guides apply unchanged.
  • For a Gaussian likelihood, the optimal $q(\mathbf{u})$ is closed-form; for any other, sparse_markov_elbo with a gaussx integrator is optimised directly, and on Poisson counts 30 inducing times match a dense Laplace fit on 200 points closely.
  • sparse_markov_factor puts the sparse ELBO in a NumPyro model; SVI is the right inference there, because the factor is a bound, not a likelihood.
  • The inducing spacing must be a fraction of the lengthscale: about $\ell/4$ for smooth kernels (errors of 0.1% to 2% against the dense posterior), and finer than $\ell/8$ for Matern-1/2. With the current $\mathcal{O}(M^3)$ cost, long records with many decorrelation times are better served by the dense Markov path.

References.

  1. Adam, V., Eleftheriadis, S., Artemev, A., Durrande, N. & Hensman, J. (2020). Doubly sparse variational Gaussian processes. AISTATS, PMLR 108, 2874–2884.
  2. Hensman, J., Fusi, N. & Lawrence, N. D. (2013). Gaussian processes for big data. UAI.
  3. Hensman, J., Matthews, A. G. de G. & Ghahramani, Z. (2015). Scalable variational Gaussian process classification. AISTATS, PMLR 38, 351–360.
  4. Titsias, M. (2009). Variational learning of inducing variables in sparse Gaussian processes. AISTATS, PMLR 5, 567–574.
  5. Wilkinson, W. J., Solin, A. & Adam, V. (2021). Sparse algorithms for Markovian Gaussian processes. AISTATS, PMLR 130, 1747–1755.

# Shapes: D_x = N_Ωx = 64 cells; D_y = N_Ωy = 8 sensors; T = 16 hourly steps

N_CELLS = 64
N_SENSORS = 8
N_STEPS = 16
# Δs = 1 km, so the channel is L = 64 km long
cell_km = jnp.arange(N_CELLS, dtype=jnp.float64)  # → (D_x,)
# κ ∈ 𝒲_s,x, the wavenumbers the grid resolves [rad km⁻¹]
wavenumber = 2.0 * jnp.pi * jnp.fft.rfftfreq(N_CELLS, d=1.0)  # → (D_x / 2 + 1,)
# every eighth cell, from cell 3
sensor_cells = jnp.arange(3, N_CELLS, N_CELLS // N_SENSORS)  # → (D_y,)
# t_k = k hours, k = 1, …, T
obs_times = jnp.arange(1.0, N_STEPS + 1.0)  # → (T,)


# today (filterax): the base class of a deterministic dynamics module
class AdvectionDiffusion(flx.AbstractDynamics):
    """f(x; θ): the exact step of ∂x/∂t = −u ∂x/∂s + K ∂²x/∂s² on the periodic grid."""

    speed: Float[Array, ""]
    diffusivity: Float[Array, ""]

    def __call__(self, state, t_prev, t_next):
        dt = t_next - t_prev
        # x̂(κ, t) for every resolved wavenumber
        modes = jnp.fft.rfft(state)  # (D_x,) → (D_x / 2 + 1,)
        # exp((−i u κ − K κ²) Δt)
        growth = jnp.exp(
            (-1j * self.speed * wavenumber - self.diffusivity * wavenumber**2) * dt
        )  # → (D_x / 2 + 1,)
        # x(s, t + Δt) = 𝔉⁻¹[exp((−i u κ − K κ²) Δt) x̂(κ, t)]
        return jnp.fft.irfft(growth * modes, n=N_CELLS)  # → (D_x,)


def observe(state):
    """h(x) = H x: the tracer at the sensor cells."""
    return state[sensor_cells]  # (D_x,) → (D_y,)


# the spectrum of Σ_x,0: Gaussian in κ, lengthscale ℓ = 4 km, variance σ_x² = 1
LENGTHSCALE = 4.0
all_wavenumbers = 2.0 * jnp.pi * jnp.fft.fftfreq(N_CELLS, d=1.0)  # → (D_x,)
spectrum = jnp.exp(-(all_wavenumbers**2) * LENGTHSCALE**2 / 2.0)  # → (D_x,)
spectrum = N_CELLS * spectrum / jnp.sum(spectrum)  # → (D_x,)


def colour(white):
    """x₀ = Σ_x,0^(1/2) z, with z ~ 𝒩(0, I), through the FFT of the periodic grid."""
    modes = jnp.sqrt(spectrum) * jnp.fft.fft(white)  # (D_x,) → (D_x,)
    return jnp.real(jnp.fft.ifft(modes))  # → (D_x,)


truth = {"speed": 2.0, "diffusivity": 0.3}  # u [km h⁻¹], K [km² h⁻¹]
NOISE_STD = 0.1  # σ_ε, tracer units
key_x0, key_eps, key_ens = jr.split(jr.PRNGKey(5), 3)

# x₀ ~ 𝒩(0, Σ_x,0)
x0_true = colour(jr.normal(key_x0, (N_CELLS,)))  # → (D_x,)
dynamics_true = AdvectionDiffusion(
    jnp.asarray(truth["speed"]), jnp.asarray(truth["diffusivity"])
)
states, state, t_prev = [], x0_true, 0.0
for t_next in obs_times:
    # x_k = f(x_k−1; θ)
    state = dynamics_true(state, t_prev, t_next)  # → (D_x,)
    states.append(state)
    t_prev = t_next
x_true = jnp.stack(states)  # → (T, D_x)
# H x_k for every k
y_clean = jax.vmap(observe)(x_true)  # (T, D_x) → (T, D_y)
# y_k = H x_k + ε_k, ε_k ~ 𝒩(0, σ_ε² I)
y = y_clean + NOISE_STD * jr.normal(key_eps, y_clean.shape)  # → (T, D_y)
# Σ_ε = σ_ε² I_D_y
obs_noise = NOISE_STD**2 * jnp.eye(N_SENSORS)  # → (D_y, D_y)
print(
    f"D_x = {N_CELLS} cells, D_y = {N_SENSORS} sensors, T = {N_STEPS} hours, "
    f"{y.size} observations"
)
print(f"the tracer moves {truth['speed'] * N_STEPS:.0f} km over the record")

θ) state = dynamics_true(state, t_prev, t_next) # → (D_x,) states.append(state) t_prev = t_next x_true = jnp.stack(states) # → (T, D_x) # H x_k for every k y_clean = jax.vmap(observe)(x_true) # (T, D_x) → (T, D_y) # y_k = H x_k + ε_k, ε_k ~ 𝒩(0, σ_ε² I) y = y_clean + NOISE_STD * jr.normal(key_eps, y_clean.shape) # → (T, D_y) # Σ_ε = σ_ε² I_D_y obs_noise = NOISE_STD**2 * jnp.eye(N_SENSORS) # → (D_y, D_y) print( f"D_x = {N_CELLS} cells, D_y = {N_SENSORS} sensors, T = {N_STEPS} hours, " f"{y.size} observations" ) print(f"the tracer moves {truth['speed'] * N_STEPS:.0f} km over the record")

The left panel shows the true field as a space-time (Hovmöller) diagram, with the sensor cells dotted. The bands of positive and negative anomaly slope to the right at the advection speed. The right panel shows four of the eight sensor records, where a feature seen at one sensor turns up at the next one about 4 hours later (8 km at 2 km h⁻¹).

# Shapes: N_Ex = 32 members; D_x = 64 cells; D_y = 8 sensors; T = 16 steps

N_MEMBERS = 32
# x₀⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ 𝒩(0, Σ_x,0), e ∈ ℰ_x, drawn once and passed in as data
init_ensemble = jax.vmap(colour)(  # (N_Ex, D_x) → (N_Ex, D_x)
    jr.normal(key_ens, (N_MEMBERS, N_CELLS))
)


def tracer_model(init_ensemble, y):
    # Shapes: D_θ = 2 parameters; N_Ex members; T steps; D_y sensors

    # today (numpyro): the two sample sites of θ
    # u ~ 𝒩(1.5, 1²)
    speed = numpyro.sample("speed", dist.Normal(1.5, 1.0))
    # K ~ LogNormal(log 0.5, 1)
    diffusivity = numpyro.sample("diffusivity", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.5), 1.0))
    # user
    dynamics = AdvectionDiffusion(speed, diffusivity)
    # today (pyrox_ssm), calling filterax
    # log p(y_1:T ∣ θ) ≈ ∑ₖ log 𝒩(r̄ₖ; 0, H̃ₖ H̃ₖᵀ + Σ_ε)
    return ensemble_factor(
        "y",
        # today (filterax)
        flx.filters.ETKF(),
        dynamics,
        observe,
        init_ensemble,
        y,
        obs_times,
        obs_noise,
    )


# today (numpyro)
seeded_model = handlers.seed(tracer_model, rng_seed=0)
# today (numpyro)
trace = handlers.trace(seeded_model).get_trace(init_ensemble, y)
for name, site in trace.items():
    kind = "factor" if isinstance(site["fn"], dist.Unit) else type(site["fn"]).__name__
    print(f"site {name!r:14} {kind:<10} value shape={tuple(jnp.shape(site['value']))}")
# Shapes: N_Ex = 32 members; D_x = 64 cells; D_y = 8 sensors; T = 16 steps N_MEMBERS = 32 # x₀⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ 𝒩(0, Σ_x,0), e ∈ ℰ_x, drawn once and passed in as data init_ensemble = jax.vmap(colour)( # (N_Ex, D_x) → (N_Ex, D_x) jr.normal(key_ens, (N_MEMBERS, N_CELLS)) ) def tracer_model(init_ensemble, y): # Shapes: D_θ = 2 parameters; N_Ex members; T steps; D_y sensors # today (numpyro): the two sample sites of θ # u ~ 𝒩(1.5, 1²) speed = numpyro.sample("speed", dist.Normal(1.5, 1.0)) # K ~ LogNormal(log 0.5, 1) diffusivity = numpyro.sample("diffusivity", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.5), 1.0)) # user dynamics = AdvectionDiffusion(speed, diffusivity) # today (pyrox_ssm), calling filterax # log p(y_1:T ∣ θ) ≈ ∑ₖ log 𝒩(r̄ₖ; 0, H̃ₖ H̃ₖᵀ + Σ_ε) return ensemble_factor( "y", # today (filterax) flx.filters.ETKF(), dynamics, observe, init_ensemble, y, obs_times, obs_noise, ) # today (numpyro) seeded_model = handlers.seed(tracer_model, rng_seed=0) # today (numpyro) trace = handlers.trace(seeded_model).get_trace(init_ensemble, y) for name, site in trace.items(): kind = "factor" if isinstance(site["fn"], dist.Unit) else type(site["fn"]).__name__ print(f"site {name!r:14} {kind:<10} value shape={tuple(jnp.shape(site['value']))}") 
site 'speed'        Normal     value shape=()
site 'diffusivity'  LogNormal  value shape=()
site 'y'            factor     value shape=(0,)

So the trace holds two scalar sample sites and one factor, as in Example 1. However, here the factor is an estimate: the 64-cell field is carried by the 32 members inside the filter, and NUTS never sees it.

# Shapes: D_θ = 2 parameters; 2 chains × 200 = 400 posterior draws

# today (numpyro)
nuts_kernel = NUTS(tracer_model, dense_mass=True, init_strategy=init_to_median)
# today (numpyro)
nuts = MCMC(
    nuts_kernel,
    num_warmup=100,
    num_samples=200,
    num_chains=2,
    chain_method="sequential",
    progress_bar=False,
)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
# today (numpyro)
# 400 draws θ ~ p(θ ∣ y_1:T), each leapfrog step one assimilation run and its gradient
nuts.run(jr.PRNGKey(1), init_ensemble, y, extra_fields=("num_steps",))
jax.block_until_ready(nuts.get_samples())
nuts_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0
nuts.print_summary()
nuts_samples = nuts.get_samples()  # → {name: (400,)}
extra_fields = nuts.get_extra_fields()
n_div = int(extra_fields["diverging"].sum())  # → ()
n_grad = int(extra_fields["num_steps"].sum())  # → ()
print(
    f"NUTS wall-clock: {nuts_seconds:.1f} s for 2 chains x 300 iterations, "
    f"{n_div} divergences"
)
print(f"leapfrog steps after warm-up: {n_grad}, {n_grad / 400:.1f} per draw")

def ensemble_log_lik(theta, members):
    """log p(y_1:T ∣ θ) by the ETKF, from the initial ensemble ``members``."""

    def model():
        # today (pyrox_ssm), calling filterax

            AdvectionDiffusion(theta[0], theta[1]),
            observe,
            members,

            obs_times,

    # today (numpyro)
    site = handlers.trace(model).get_trace()["y"]
    return site["fn"].log_factor

def kalman_log_lik(theta):
    """The exact log p(y_1:T ∣ θ) by the Kalman filter, with no model noise."""
    dynamics = AdvectionDiffusion(theta[0], theta[1])
    # F(θ), column n is f(e_n; θ)
    columns = jax.vmap(lambda e: dynamics(e, 0.0, 1.0))(jnp.eye(N_CELLS))
    transition = einx.id("col row -> row col", columns)  # → (D_x, D_x)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    prior = LinearGaussianSSMPrior(
        jnp.broadcast_to(transition, (N_STEPS, N_CELLS, N_CELLS)),
        obs_matrix,
        jnp.zeros((N_STEPS, N_CELLS, N_CELLS)),
        obs_noise,
        jnp.zeros(N_CELLS),
        init_cov,
    )
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # log p(y_1:T ∣ θ) = ∑ₖ log 𝒩(r_k; 0, H Σ_x,k∣k−1 Hᵀ + Σ_ε)
    model = lambda: lgssm_factor("y", prior, y)
    # today (numpyro)
    site = handlers.trace(model).get_trace()["y"]
    return site["fn"].log_factor


def time_grad(log_lik, repeats=3):
    """One jitted log likelihood and its gradient at the truth, in ms."""
    # today (jax)
    value_and_grad = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(log_lik))
    theta = jnp.array([truth["speed"], truth["diffusivity"]])  # → (2,)
    jax.block_until_ready(value_and_grad(theta))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        jax.block_until_ready(value_and_grad(theta))
    return 1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / repeats

def grid_posterior(log_lik):
    """Posterior mean and sd of θ on the grid, from a log likelihood of θ."""
    # today (jax): one θ at a time, so the memory stays that of one run
    log_liks = jax.jit(lambda grid: jax.lax.map(log_lik, grid))(theta_grid)
    # p(θ ∣ y_1:T) ∝ p(y_1:T ∣ θ) p(θ), normalised over the grid
    weights = jax.nn.softmax(log_liks + log_prior)  # → (N_grid,)
    mean = einx.dot("grid, grid param -> param", weights, theta_grid)  # → (2,)
    deviation = theta_grid - mean  # → (N_grid, 2)
    var = einx.dot("grid, grid param -> param", weights, deviation**2)  # → (2,)
    return mean, jnp.sqrt(var)

1.5, 1²) + log LogNormal(K; log 0.5, 1) log_prior = dist.Normal(1.5, 1.0).log_prob(theta_grid[:, 0]) + dist.LogNormal( jnp.log(0.5), 1.0 ).log_prob(theta_grid[:, 1]) # → (N_grid,) def grid_posterior(log_lik): """Posterior mean and sd of θ on the grid, from a log likelihood of θ.""" # today (jax): one θ at a time, so the memory stays that of one run log_liks = jax.jit(lambda grid: jax.lax.map(log_lik, grid))(theta_grid) # p(θ ∣ y_1:T) ∝ p(y_1:T ∣ θ) p(θ), normalised over the grid weights = jax.nn.softmax(log_liks + log_prior) # → (N_grid,) mean = einx.dot("grid, grid param -> param", weights, theta_grid) # → (2,) deviation = theta_grid - mean # → (N_grid, 2) var = einx.dot("grid, grid param -> param", weights, deviation**2) # → (2,) return mean, jnp.sqrt(var) theta_true = jnp.array([truth["speed"], truth["diffusivity"]]) # → (2,) exact = float(kalman_log_lik(theta_true)) # → () key_16, key_128 = jr.split(jr.PRNGKey(11)) size_ensembles = { 16: jax.vmap(colour)(jr.normal(key_16, (16, N_CELLS))), 32: init_ensemble, # the X₀ that NUTS used 128: jax.vmap(colour)(jr.normal(key_128, (128, N_CELLS))), } t0 = time.perf_counter() rows = {"Kalman": (exact, *grid_posterior(kalman_log_lik), time_grad(kalman_log_lik))} for n_members, members in size_ensembles.items(): log_lik = lambda th, m=members: ensemble_log_lik(th, m) rows[f"N_Ex = {n_members}"] = ( float(log_lik(theta_true)), *grid_posterior(log_lik), time_grad(log_lik), ) grid_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0 print( f"{'':<12}{'log p(y | theta_true)':>22}{'u mean ± sd':>18}" f"{'K mean ± sd':>18}{'grad, ms':>10}" ) for label, (log_p, mean, sd, ms) in rows.items(): print( f"{label:<12}{log_p:>22.2f}{float(mean[0]):>10.4f} ± {float(sd[0]):.4f}" f"{float(mean[1]):>10.4f} ± {float(sd[1]):.4f}{ms:>10.1f}" ) print(f"(4 grid posteriors and gradient timings: {grid_seconds:.1f} s)")

Kalman                       77.34    1.9696 ± 0.0182    0.3295 ± 0.0561       7.2
N_Ex = 16                    67.74    1.9864 ± 0.0171    0.3306 ± 0.0543       6.6
N_Ex = 32                    74.36    1.9670 ± 0.0182    0.3046 ± 0.0550       8.6
N_Ex = 128                   77.62    1.9696 ± 0.0182    0.3313 ± 0.0560      18.8
(4 grid posteriors and gradient timings: 28.8 s)

At the true $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ the ensemble log likelihood is 9.60 below the exact 77.34 with 16 members, 2.98 below with 32 and 0.28 above with 128. Each row uses one $\mathbf{X}_0$, so the size of the error is itself random, but it shrinks with $N_{\mathcal{E}_x}$. On the posterior the effect is smaller than these gaps suggest. What moves the posterior is how the error changes with $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, not its level. With 16 members the speed shifts by 0.017 km h⁻¹, about one posterior standard deviation. With 32 the speed is within 0.003 km h⁻¹ of the exact posterior mean and the diffusivity is 0.025 km² h⁻¹ low, under half a standard deviation. With 128 both are within 0.002 of the exact values. The grid posterior at 32 members also matches the NUTS one (1.967 against 1.966 km h⁻¹ for $u$, 0.305 against 0.306 km² h⁻¹ for $K$). So NUTS sampled the ensemble posterior well, and the miss of the true speed in section 4 is in the data.

One gradient costs 6.6 ms with 16 members, 8.6 ms with 32 and 18.8 ms with 128, against 7.2 ms for the Kalman filter. At $D_x = 64$ the Kalman filter is as cheap as a small ensemble, because $D_x^3$ is small. The ensemble pays off when the state is too large for a $D_x \times D_x$ covariance: its cost grows with the number of members and model runs, not with $D_x^3$, and it never stores $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x$.

docs.title: Ensembles: a tracer channel with an ensemble Kalman likelihood, and an ensemble of variational fits¶
docs.text:
In Examples 1 to 4 the state was small, a few values per station, so the Kalman filter carried its full covariance and integrated the path out. Here the state is a gridded field: the anomaly of a tracer in every cell of a channel, moved along by a transport model. On a real grid of thousands of cells the $D_x \times D_x$ covariance of a Kalman filter cannot be stored, let alone propagated. An ensemble Kalman filter carries $N_{\mathcal{E}_x}$ copies of the state instead and runs the transport model on each. Its innovations give an estimate of the log likelihood, which we add to a NumPyro model as a factor. In Example 5a we infer the advection speed and the diffusivity of the channel from that factor with NUTS. We keep the channel small and the dynamics linear on purpose, so that the exact Kalman log likelihood still exists and we can measure what the ensemble costs us in bias. In Example 5b we run a different kind of ensemble on the same model, the ensemble of variational fits of pyrox.inference.ensemble_vi. Its members mean something else.

pyrox-ssm capability shown: pyrox_ssm.ensemble.ensemble_factor (behind the [ensemble] extra), which runs filterax.differentiable_assimilate with a deterministic square-root filter (filterax.filters.ETKF here) from an initial ensemble passed in as data. It adds the sum of the per-step log likelihoods as a NumPyro factor and returns the filterax AssimilationResult, whose analysis ensembles give us the filtered field. For 5b, pyrox.inference.ensemble_vi from the core package. Cost: every log-density evaluation is one assimilation run. Per step that is $N_{\mathcal{E}_x}$ runs of the transport model plus an analysis in the space of the members, $\mathcal{O}(N_{\mathcal{E}_x}^2 (D_x + D_y) + N_{\mathcal{E}_x}^3)$, against $\mathcal{O}(D_x^3)$ for the Kalman filter. The gradient adds a backward pass that recomputes the forecasts (filterax's RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint, the default). We time one gradient at three ensemble sizes and for the Kalman filter in section 6.

What you'll learn:

  1. How to write a transport model as a filterax dynamics module and infer its parameters with ensemble_factor in a plain NumPyro model, with the initial ensemble drawn once outside the model.
  2. How the NUTS posterior compares with the truth, and how to get the filtered field with bands from the analysis members.
  3. How large the bias of the ensemble log likelihood is at 16, 32 and 128 members, against the exact Kalman filter, and what each costs per gradient.
  4. What ensemble_vi puts in its ensemble (fits from different starts), and when that helps.

The NUTS workflow and the posterior predictive over draws are explained in Example 1, and the Kalman recursions in Kalman filtering and RTS smoothing. We reuse them here without deriving them again.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
The physical symbols of this page are below. Everything else follows the notation of the earlier examples, with the state $\mathbf{x}$, the observations $\mathbf{y}$ and the parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

Symbol Meaning Shape, units $x(s, t)$ tracer anomaly (concentration minus its background) $\mathbb{R}$, tracer units $s$ position along the channel $[0, L)$, km $u$ advection speed $\mathbb{R}$, km h⁻¹ $K$ eddy diffusivity $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, km² h⁻¹ $\kappa$ wavenumber $\mathcal{W}_{s,x}$, rad km⁻¹

The tracer anomaly lives on a periodic channel of length $L = 64$ km. It is carried along at the speed $u$ and spread by the diffusivity $K$,

$$\frac{\partial x}{\partial t} = -u \frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + K \frac{\partial^2 x}{\partial s^2}$$

We split the channel into $D_x = N_{\Omega_x} = 64$ cells of 1 km, so the state $\mathbf{x}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ is the field in every cell at the time $t_k = k$ hours, $k = 1, \ldots, T$, with $T = 16$ and $t_0 = 0$. On a periodic grid each Fourier mode evolves on its own, so we can step the equation exactly. With $\hat{x}(\kappa, t)$ the discrete Fourier transform of the field at the wavenumber $\kappa \in \mathcal{W}_{s,x}$ (the $D_x$ wavenumbers $2 \pi n / L$ that the grid resolves) and $\mathrm{i}$ the imaginary unit,

$$\hat{x}(\kappa, t_k) = \exp((-\mathrm{i} u \kappa - K \kappa^2)(t_k - t_{k-1})) \hat{x}(\kappa, t_{k-1})$$

This is the dynamics $\mathbf{x}_k = f(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta})$, with the parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (u, K) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$. It has no model noise. It is also linear, $f(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{F}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{F}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$, which a real transport model would not be. We keep it linear so that the exact Kalman log likelihood is there as a reference. The initial field is a draw from a stationary Gaussian, and $D_y = N_{\Omega_y} = 8$ sensors, one every 8 km, measure the field with noise every hour,

$$\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,0})$$

$$\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{x}_k + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_k$$

$$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon)$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,0} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ has unit variance and a Gaussian spectrum with a 4 km lengthscale, $\mathbf{H} \in \{0, 1\}^{D_y \times D_x}$ picks the sensor cells, so the observation operator is $h(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{x}$, and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I}_{D_y}$ with $\sigma_\varepsilon = 0.1$.

The ensemble Kalman log likelihood. The ETKF (ensemble transform Kalman filter) carries $N_{\mathcal{E}_x}$ members $\mathbf{x}_{k \mid k}^{(e)} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$, $e \in \mathcal{E}_x$, in place of a mean and a covariance. It starts from the initial ensemble $\mathbf{X}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathcal{E}_x} \times D_x}$, whose rows $\mathbf{x}_{0 \mid 0}^{(e)} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,0})$ we draw once. At every step it runs the transport model on each member, $\mathbf{x}_{k \mid k-1}^{(e)} = f(\mathbf{x}_{k-1 \mid k-1}^{(e)}; \boldsymbol{\theta})$, and scores $\mathbf{y}_k$ under the Gaussian that the forecast members imply,

$$\log p(\mathbf{y}_{1:T} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{T} \log \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y}_k; \bar{\mathbf{h}}_k, \tilde{\mathbf{H}}_k \tilde{\mathbf{H}}_k^\top + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon)$$

$$\bar{\mathbf{h}}_k = \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}_x}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}_x} h(\mathbf{x}_{k \mid k-1}^{(e)})$$

where column $e$ of $\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times N_{\mathcal{E}_x}}$ is the anomaly $(h(\mathbf{x}_{k \mid k-1}^{(e)}) - \bar{\mathbf{h}}_k) / \sqrt{N_{\mathcal{E}_x} - 1}$. Then a square-root analysis moves the members to $\mathbf{x}_{k \mid k}^{(e)}$ without drawing random numbers. The Kalman filter computes the same sum exactly, with $\mathbf{H} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid k-1}$ and $\mathbf{H} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid k-1} \mathbf{H}^\top + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon$ in place of $\bar{\mathbf{h}}_k$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_k \tilde{\mathbf{H}}_k^\top + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon$, where $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ are the forecast mean and covariance.

Two properties decide how we can use this in NUTS or SVI. First, $\mathbf{X}_0$ is data and the filter draws no random numbers. So the log likelihood is a deterministic and smooth function of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, as every evaluation sees the same members (common random numbers). Second, it is biased, not exact. The mean and covariance of the members are Monte Carlo estimates from $N_{\mathcal{E}_x}$ draws, and the covariance has rank at most $N_{\mathcal{E}_x} - 1$. The bias shrinks as $N_{\mathcal{E}_x}$ grows. For linear-Gaussian dynamics like ours the log likelihood converges to the Kalman log marginal of lgssm_factor, and that is the check we run in section 6.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: We detect Colab and install pyrox, pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm[ensemble] (which pulls in filterax) only when the notebook runs there.

docs.title: 1. A tracer moved along a periodic channel¶
docs.text: We simulate one record from the model, so that we know the truth: an advection speed $u = 2$ km h⁻¹ and a diffusivity $K = 0.3$ km² h⁻¹. Over the 16 hours the field moves 32 km, so every feature passes four sensors. The AdvectionDiffusion module below is the exact Fourier step of the Background section, written as a filterax.AbstractDynamics whose fields are $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, and observe is $h$. We draw $\mathbf{x}_0$ by colouring white noise with the square root of the spectrum, through the FFT.

docs.title: 2. The model as a plain NumPyro function¶
docs.text: We draw the initial ensemble of $N_{\mathcal{E}_x} = 32$ members here, once, outside the model, and pass it in as data. Drawing it inside the model would give every evaluation of the log density new random numbers, so NUTS would see a noisy log density. A wind measurement puts the advection speed near 1.5 km h⁻¹, give or take 1 km h⁻¹, so we take $u \sim \mathcal{N}(1.5, 1^2)$, and the diffusivity gets $K \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 0.5, 1)$. Then ensemble_factor takes the filter, the dynamics built from the two sample sites, $h$, $\mathbf{X}_0$, the record, the observation times and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon$, and registers the factor "y".

docs.title: 3. NUTS¶
docs.text: We run two chains of 200 draws after 100 warm-up steps with a dense mass matrix. Both chains start at the prior medians (init_to_median). The log likelihood in $u$ has a second local mode near $u = -0.6$ km h⁻¹, and section 7 shows fits from random starts (NumPyro's default) ending there. Each leapfrog step is one assimilation run and its gradient. The wall-clock time includes JIT compilation.

docs.title: 4. The transport parameters against the truth¶
5. The filtered field¶
docs.text:
The AssimilationResult that ensemble_factor returns holds the analysis members $\mathbf{x}_{k \mid k}^{(e)}$ at every step (analysis_history, shaped $(T, N_{\mathcal{E}_x}, D_x)$). So for one $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ the filtered field is their mean $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k \mid k}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$, and its uncertainty is their variance (with $1 / (N_{\mathcal{E}_x} - 1)$, as in the filter). We run the filter at $N_{\mathcal{E}_\theta} = 50$ NUTS draws, the set $\mathcal{E}_\theta$, with jax.vmap, and combine them as in Example 1, so the bands carry the uncertainty of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ too,

$$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_k \mid \mathbf{y}_{1:k}] \approx \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}_\theta}} \sum_{\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathcal{E}_\theta} \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k \mid k}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$$

and the variance in each cell is the mean of the member variances over $\mathcal{E}_\theta$ plus the variance of $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{k \mid k}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ over $\mathcal{E}_\theta$. These are filtered estimates, so step $k$ uses the observations up to $\mathbf{y}_k$ only (the draws of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ come from the whole record). We score them against the true field, at the sensor cells and in the cells between them.

docs.title: 6. The bias in $N_{\mathcal{E}_x}$, and the cost¶
docs.text: We now measure the bias of the ensemble log likelihood, and what it does to the posterior, at $N_{\mathcal{E}_x} = 16$, 32 (the $\mathbf{X}_0$ that NUTS used) and 128 members. The reference is the exact Kalman filter. The dynamics are linear, so we build $\mathbf{F}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ by applying $f$ to the columns of $\mathbf{I}_{D_x}$, and give it to LinearGaussianSSMPrior with zero model noise and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,0}$ as the initial covariance. Then lgssm_factor gives the exact log likelihood. With two parameters we can also compute each posterior on a 25 × 15 grid of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ around the mode, with no sampling error: the weights are $p(\mathbf{y}_{1:T} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) p(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ normalised over the grid. We also time one jitted evaluation and its gradient, the price of every NUTS leapfrog step and SVI step.

docs.title: 7. Example 5b: an ensemble of variational fits with ensemble_vi¶
docs.text:
pyrox.inference.ensemble_vi uses the word ensemble for a different object. It runs $N_{\mathcal{E}_ u}$ independent SVI fits of one guide $q( oldsymbol{ heta}; oldsymbol{ u})$, each from its own random start, vmapped into one computation. It returns the stacked variational parameters $ oldsymbol{ u}^{(e)}$, $e \in \mathcal{E}_ u$, and the loss history of every fit. So a member in 5a is a state $\mathbf{x}_k^{(e)}$ inside one evaluation of the log likelihood, and the members together estimate the distribution of the state for one $ oldsymbol{ heta}$. A member in 5b is a whole approximate posterior $q( oldsymbol{ heta}; oldsymbol{ u}^{(e)})$. The spread over these members says where the optimiser can end up, not how uncertain $ oldsymbol{ heta}$ is. That is useful when the loss has several local optima, as this one has in $u$.

ensemble_vi takes any NumPyro model whose two arguments are the data, so we pass tracer_model unchanged, with data=(init_ensemble, y), and an AutoNormal guide. Its default starts each fit at a uniform point in $[-2, 2]$ on the unconstrained scale. Each of the $N_{\mathcal{E}_ u} = 8$ fits minimises $\mathcal{L}_ ext{ELBO}( oldsymbol{ u}) = -\mathrm{ELBO}$ with Adam for 200 steps. Every step of every fit is one assimilation run with the same 32-member $\mathbf{X}_0$. ensemble_vi does not return where each fit started, so we rebuild the starts with EnsembleVI.init and the same seed.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• A transport model with an ensemble Kalman likelihood is a plain NumPyro function: priors on $u$ and $K$, a filterax.AbstractDynamics built from them, and ensemble_factor("y", flx.filters.ETKF(), dynamics, observe, init_ensemble, y, obs_times, obs_noise). The initial ensemble is drawn once, outside the model, so the factor is deterministic and smooth in $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.
  • NUTS on the two parameters, with 32 members, took 52.5 s with 3.6 leapfrog steps per draw. The diffusivity's 90 % interval holds the truth, and the speed's misses it by 0.004 km h⁻¹, as the exact Kalman posterior does too.
  • The analysis members in the returned AssimilationResult, averaged over 50 NUTS draws, give the filtered field with bands. Between the sensors the RMSE is 0.114 and 98.8 % of the cell-hours fall within $\pm 2\sigma$.
  • The ensemble log likelihood is biased: 9.60 below the exact value at the truth with 16 members, 2.98 with 32 and 0.28 above with 128. Its posterior is within 0.003 km h⁻¹ of the exact one in $u$ from 32 members on, and with 16 members it is off by about one posterior standard deviation. Report $N_{\mathcal{E}_x}$ with any result.
  • One gradient costs 8.6 ms with 32 members and 7.2 ms with the Kalman filter at $D_x = 64$. The ensemble is for states too large for a $D_x \times D_x$ covariance, where the Kalman filter is not an option.
  • ensemble_vi is an ensemble of fits, not of states. On this model four of eight fits from random starts ended at a second mode of $u$, about 500 nats worse in $\mathcal{L}_\text{ELBO}$, so it is a way to find the modes before fitting the posterior in the right one.

For nonlinear dynamics or observations with a moment-matched filter, see Example 6. For the exact Kalman filter on a small state, see Example 1.

# Shapes: N_Ω = 6 stations; N_n days at station n; D_x = 2 (the Matérn-3/2 state)

# ω = 2π / 365.25 days⁻¹, the annual angular frequency
OMEGA = 2.0 * jnp.pi / 365.25


def seasonal(t, a, b):
    """Shared seasonal cycle μ(t) = a cos(ωt) + b sin(ωt)."""
    return a * jnp.cos(OMEGA * t) + b * jnp.sin(OMEGA * t)


truth_shared = {
    "cos_amp": -8.0,  # coldest near day 0 (1 January)
    "sin_amp": -1.5,
    "noise_var": 0.25,  # (0.5 °C)^2
}
# μ_θ = (log σ_f², log ℓ) of the population
truth_loc = jnp.log(jnp.array([4.0, 4.0]))  # → (2,)
# τ_θ, the population spread in log units
truth_scale = jnp.array([0.3, 0.3])  # → (2,)
# c_n, station offsets set by elevation and siting
truth_offset = jnp.array([10.0, 8.5, 11.5, 9.0, 12.0, 7.5])  # → (N_Ω,)

# (first day, last day + 1, outage or None, extra dropout rate)
schedule = [
    (0, 120, None, 0.0),
    (60, 190, (110, 135), 0.0),
    (150, 290, None, 0.3),
    (240, 365, (290, 305), 0.0),
    (170, 205, None, 0.0),
    (320, 350, None, 0.0),
]
n_stations = len(schedule)

key_theta, *station_keys = jr.split(jr.PRNGKey(2025), n_stations + 1)
# z_n ~ 𝒩(0, I₂)
z_true = jr.normal(key_theta, (n_stations, 2))  # → (N_Ω, 2)
# τ_θ ⊙ z_n
scaled_offsets = einx.multiply("p, n p -> n p", truth_scale, z_true)  # → (N_Ω, 2)
# θ_n = μ_θ + τ_θ ⊙ z_n
theta_true = einx.add("p, n p -> n p", truth_loc, scaled_offsets)  # → (N_Ω, 2)
# (σ_f,n², ℓ_n) = exp(θ_n)
kernel_true = jnp.exp(theta_true)  # → (N_Ω, 2)

times_per_station, y_per_station, latent_per_station = [], [], []
withheld_per_station = []
for n, (first, end, outage, extra) in enumerate(schedule):
    key_f, key_eps, key_gap = jr.split(station_keys[n], 3)
    # every day the station existed, t = first, …, end − 1
    days = jnp.arange(first, end, dtype=jnp.float64)  # → (n_days,)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_f,n², ℓ_n) as a linear SDE
    sde_n = MaternSDE(kernel_true[n, 0], kernel_true[n, 1], order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    prior_n = MarkovGPPrior(sde_n, days)
    innovations = jr.normal(key_f, (days.shape[0], prior_n.state_dim))
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # f_n(t), the SDE run forward from the innovations
    f_n = markov_gp_from_innovations(prior_n, innovations)  # (n_days, D_x) → (n_days,)
    # c_n + μ(t)
    climatology_n = truth_offset[n] + seasonal(  # (n_days,) → (n_days,)
        days, truth_shared["cos_amp"], truth_shared["sin_amp"]
    )
    noise_std = jnp.sqrt(truth_shared["noise_var"])  # → ()
    # ε_n,k ~ 𝒩(0, σ_ε²)
    obs_noise = noise_std * jr.normal(key_eps, days.shape)  # → (n_days,)
    # y_n,k = c_n + μ(t_n,k) + f_n(t_n,k) + ε_n,k
    y_n = climatology_n + f_n + obs_noise  # → (n_days,)
    # a day is reported unless it drops out or falls in the outage
    reported = jr.uniform(key_gap, days.shape) >= 0.08 + extra  # → (n_days,) bool
    in_outage = jnp.zeros(days.shape, dtype=bool)  # → (n_days,) bool
    if outage is not None:
        in_outage = (days >= outage[0]) & (days < outage[1])  # → (n_days,) bool
    reported = reported & ~in_outage
    times_per_station.append(days[reported])
    y_per_station.append(y_n[reported])
    latent_per_station.append((days, climatology_n + f_n))
    # the days the station missed, with the values it would have reported
    withheld_per_station.append((days[~reported], y_n[~reported], in_outage[~reported]))

record_lengths = [int(t_n.shape[0]) for t_n in times_per_station]
print(f"{'station':<9}{'first day':>10}{'last day':>10}{'N_n':>6}{'σ_f²':>8}{'ℓ':>7}")
for n, t_n in enumerate(times_per_station):
    print(
        f"{n + 1:<9}{int(t_n[0]):>10}{int(t_n[-1]):>10}{record_lengths[n]:>6}"
        f"{float(kernel_true[n, 0]):>8.2f}{float(kernel_true[n, 1]):>7.2f}"
    )

Each row is filled from the left, and every station keeps its own calendar. Step $k$ is a different day at each station, and a gap inside a record is a longer step, not a masked entry. Padding happens only after the last observation, so the padded steps are pure forecasts that the mask leaves out of the likelihood.

The per-station prior below is the one the model uses. station_prior builds the summed SDE of the background section, with the prior mean $10 + \mu(t)$ as mean_fn, and station_log_marginal calls its log_marginal with the station's mask row. We check the padding claim on station 6 with its true parameters, comparing the padded and masked log marginal with the one on its own unpadded record.

# c_n ~ 𝒩(10, 10²), folded into the GP prior
OFFSET_MEAN = 10.0
OFFSET_VAR = 100.0


def station_prior(t_n, variance_n, lengthscale_n, a, b):
    # Shapes: N padded steps; D_x = 3 (constant + Matérn-3/2 state)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # k(t, t') = 10², the offset c_n as a state that never changes
    offset_sde = ConstantSDE(variance=jnp.asarray(OFFSET_VAR))
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_f,n², ℓ_n) as a linear SDE
    anomaly_sde = MaternSDE(variance=variance_n, lengthscale=lengthscale_n, order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # 10² + k_Matérn-3/2, the two states stacked block-diagonally
    sde = SumSDE(kernels=(offset_sde, anomaly_sde))
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # c_n + μ + f_n ~ 𝒢𝒫(10 + μ, 10² + k_Matérn-3/2) on station n's padded days
    return MarkovGPPrior(sde, t_n, mean_fn=lambda t: OFFSET_MEAN + seasonal(t, a, b))


def station_log_marginal(t_n, y_n, o_n, variance_n, lengthscale_n, a, b, noise_var):
    # Shapes: N padded steps
    # user
    prior = station_prior(t_n, variance_n, lengthscale_n, a, b)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # log p(y_n ∣ ·) = ∑ₖ o_n,k log 𝒩(y_n,k; 10 + μ(t_n,k) + H μ_x,n,k∣k−1, H Σ_x,n,k∣k−1 Hᵀ + σ_ε²)
    return prior.log_marginal(y_n, noise_var, mask=o_n)  # (N,) → ()

def noncentred_log_normal(name, loc, scale):
    """Positive per-station parameter exp(θ_n,d) with θ_n,d = μ_θ,d + τ_θ,d z_n,d."""
    # today (numpyro)
    # z_n,d ~ 𝒩(0, 1), one per station under the enclosing plate
    z = numpyro.sample(f"{name}_z", dist.Normal(0.0, 1.0))  # → (N_Ω,)
    # θ_n,d = μ_θ,d + τ_θ,d z_n,d
    log_value = loc + scale * z  # → (N_Ω,)
    # today (numpyro)
    # exp(θ_n,d), recorded in the trace
    return numpyro.deterministic(name, jnp.exp(log_value))  # → (N_Ω,)


def network_model(times, y, mask):
    # Shapes: N_Ω = 6 stations; N padded steps; D_θ = 7 + 2 N_Ω = 19 sampled values

    # today (numpyro): the global sample sites
    # a ~ 𝒩(0, 10²)
    a = numpyro.sample("cos_amp", dist.Normal(0.0, 10.0))
    # b ~ 𝒩(0, 10²)
    b = numpyro.sample("sin_amp", dist.Normal(0.0, 10.0))
    # σ_ε² ~ LogNormal(log 0.1, 1)
    noise_var = numpyro.sample("noise_var", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.1), 1.0))
    # μ_θ,1 ~ 𝒩(log 2, 1), the population log-variance
    variance_loc = numpyro.sample("variance_loc", dist.Normal(jnp.log(2.0), 1.0))
    # τ_θ,1 ~ HalfNormal(0.5)
    variance_scale = numpyro.sample("variance_scale", dist.HalfNormal(0.5))
    # μ_θ,2 ~ 𝒩(log 7, 1), the population log-lengthscale
    lengthscale_loc = numpyro.sample("lengthscale_loc", dist.Normal(jnp.log(7.0), 1.0))
    # τ_θ,2 ~ HalfNormal(0.5)
    lengthscale_scale = numpyro.sample("lengthscale_scale", dist.HalfNormal(0.5))

    # today (numpyro): one value per station from here on
    with numpyro.plate("station", times.shape[0]):
        # user
        # σ_f,n² = exp(μ_θ,1 + τ_θ,1 z_n,1)
        variance = noncentred_log_normal(  # → (N_Ω,)
            "variance", variance_loc, variance_scale
        )
        # user
        # ℓ_n = exp(μ_θ,2 + τ_θ,2 z_n,2)
        lengthscale = noncentred_log_normal(  # → (N_Ω,)
            "lengthscale", lengthscale_loc, lengthscale_scale
        )
        # today (jax)
        # one Kalman filter per station, batched over the station axis
        per_station = jax.vmap(
            station_log_marginal, in_axes=(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, None, None, None)
        )
        # log p(y_n ∣ a, b, θ_n, σ_ε²) for n = 1, …, N_Ω
        log_marginals = per_station(  # (N_Ω, N) → (N_Ω,)
            times, y, mask, variance, lengthscale, a, b, noise_var
        )
        # today (numpyro)
        # log p(Y ∣ ·) = ∑ₙ log p(y_n ∣ ·), one factor term per station
        numpyro.factor("y", log_marginals)


def site_kind(site):
    """A short label for a trace site: plate, deterministic, factor or its family."""
    if site["type"] != "sample":
        return site["type"]
    fn = site["fn"]
    if isinstance(fn, dist.ExpandedDistribution):
        fn = fn.base_dist
    return "factor" if isinstance(fn, dist.Unit) else type(fn).__name__

So the trace holds seven global sample sites, two sample sites with one value per station, the two deterministic per-station hyperparameters and one factor with one term per station. The latent paths and the offsets are integrated out by the Kalman filters, so NUTS sees $7 + 2 N_\Omega = 19$ unconstrained values whatever the record lengths.

All seven shared and population parameters have the truth inside their 90 % intervals. We recover the noise variance (0.27 ± 0.04 against 0.25) and the population lengthscale (4.30 ± 0.62 days against 4) well, because every station contributes to them. The population spreads are the weakest part. Both have a posterior mean of 0.16, about half the true 0.3, and their intervals run from almost zero to about 0.4. Six stations with three to four months of data each cannot tell how different the stations really are, so the model pools more strongly than the truth would justify.

We see the effect in the per-station rows. Eight of the twelve intervals contain the true value. All four misses are stations whose truth lies far from the population and whose estimate is pulled towards it: the variances of stations 1 and 3 (true 5.48 and 6.79 °C², posterior means 3.95 and 3.83), the variance of station 5 (true 2.54 °C², posterior mean 3.84) and the lengthscale of station 4 (true 2.97 days, posterior mean 4.01).

def predict_station(theta, t_n, y_n, o_n, t_star):
    # Shapes: N padded steps; M test times; D_x = 3
    # user
    prior = station_prior(
        t_n, theta["variance"], theta["lengthscale"], theta["cos_amp"], theta["sin_amp"]
    )
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # p(x_n,1:N ∣ y_n; draw e) by the Kalman filter and RTS smoother
    cond = prior.condition(y_n, theta["noise_var"], mask=o_n)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # μ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾, (σ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾)² of c_n + μ(t_*) + f_n(t_*)
    mean, var = cond.predict(t_star)  # (M,) → (M,), (M,)
    # (σ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + (σ_ε⁽ᵉ⁾)² for a new observation y_n,*
    obs_var = var + theta["noise_var"]  # → (M,)
    return mean, var, obs_var


def station_draws(samples, n_rows):
    """N_E evenly spaced draws per station, with the shared parameters broadcast."""
    num_samples = samples["noise_var"].shape[0]
    # N_E draws, evenly spaced through the chains
    idx = jnp.linspace(0, num_samples - 1, N_DRAWS).astype(int)  # → (N_E,)
    draws = {}
    for name in ("variance", "lengthscale", "cos_amp", "sin_amp", "noise_var"):
        values = samples[name][idx]  # → (N_E,) shared or (N_E, n_rows) per station
        if values.ndim == 1:
            # the same draw of a shared parameter at every station
            draws[name] = einx.id("member -> n member", values, n=n_rows)
        else:
            draws[name] = einx.id("member n -> n member", values)
    return draws  # → {name: (n_rows, N_E)}


def posterior_predict(draws, t, y, o, t_star):
    # Shapes: n_rows stations; N padded steps; M test times; N_E draws
    # today (jax)
    over_draws = jax.vmap(predict_station, in_axes=(0, None, None, None, None))
    # today (jax)
    over_stations = jax.vmap(over_draws, in_axes=(0, 0, 0, 0, None))
    # today (jax)
    over_stations = jax.jit(over_stations)
    # μ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾, (σ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾)², (σ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + (σ_ε⁽ᵉ⁾)²
    means, f_vars, y_vars = over_stations(
        draws, t, y, o, t_star
    )  # → 3 × (n_rows, N_E, M)
    # μ̄_n,* = (1/N_E) ∑ₑ μ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾
    mean = einx.mean("n member m -> n m", means)  # (n_rows, N_E, M) → (n_rows, M)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (μ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾ − μ̄_n,*)²
    spread = einx.var("n member m -> n m", means)  # (n_rows, N_E, M) → (n_rows, M)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾)²
    f_var_mean = einx.mean("n member m -> n m", f_vars)  # → (n_rows, M)
    # 𝕍[c_n + μ(t_*) + f_n(t_*) ∣ Y] ≈ (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + spread
    f_var = f_var_mean + spread  # → (n_rows, M)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ ((σ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + (σ_ε⁽ᵉ⁾)²)
    y_var_mean = einx.mean("n member m -> n m", y_vars)  # → (n_rows, M)
    # the same for a new observation y_n,*
    y_var = y_var_mean + spread  # → (n_rows, M)
    return mean, f_var, y_var

Inside each record the band is narrow and follows the observations, and it widens over the two outages (stations 2 and 4) and over the days a station missed. Before a station starts and after it stops, the posterior mean relaxes to the station's climatology $c_n + \mu(t)$, with the seasonal cycle that the network learned from all six stations. Within a few lengthscales the band widens to the stationary anomaly spread plus the uncertainty of $c_n$. Station 1, for instance, stopped on day 119, and its prediction for the rest of the year is the shared annual cycle shifted by its own offset.

Because the data are simulated, we know the values the stations would have reported on the days they missed. Below we compute, for each station, the fraction of its missed days whose value falls inside the $\pm 2\sigma$ band for $y_{n,*}$, which should be close to 95 %, and the RMSE of the posterior mean on those days.

On their own, the short stations constrain their kernels only loosely, and we see this in the width of every orange interval. Station 6's variance has a 90 % interval of [2.35, 13.50] °C² on its own and [2.85, 5.88] °C² in the network, and station 5's lengthscale [1.37, 8.31] days on its own and [2.88, 5.75] days in the network. Over the four hyperparameters of the two short stations, the network's 90 % intervals are 1.7 to 3.7 times narrower. Station 6's estimates also move closer to the truth, as on its own a month of data puts the posterior mean of its variance at 6.09 °C² (true 4.16) and in the network at 4.12.

The price is the bias of shrinkage. Station 5 has the smallest true variance in the network (2.54 °C²). The network pulls its estimate up to 3.84, so its interval misses the truth, whereas the fit on its own has a posterior mean of 2.56 and an interval 1.8 times wider that contains it. Partial pooling trades this bias at the unusual stations for much tighter estimates at the typical ones.

The hyperparameters matter because of what they do to the predictions. Below we predict stations 5 and 6 from their fits on their own, with the same posterior_predict, where each draw now carries the station's own $a$, $b$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$. We compare with the network's prediction over each record and the 30 days on either side. The true latent was never simulated outside a station's record, so there we draw the true climatology $c_n + \mu(t)$ as a dashed line instead.

Inside the two records the predictions agree. The posterior mean is 0.39 °C RMSE from the true latent for both fits at both stations. The mean half-widths of the bands differ by about 10 % (0.75 against 0.84 °C at station 5, 0.76 against 0.69 °C at station 6), because a month of daily data pins the path down wherever there are data. The difference is away from the data. On its own, a station learns its seasonal cycle from one month, so its band keeps widening with the distance from the record. Over the 30 days on either side its mean half-width is 4.81 to 7.52 °C. The network knows the seasonal cycle from the other stations, so its band stops growing once the anomaly has forgotten the last observation, at a mean half-width of 4.07 to 4.27 °C. Its posterior mean is also closer to the true climatology in three of the four windows, for example 0.58 against 1.37 °C RMSE in the 30 days before station 6. In the fourth it is slightly further (0.46 against 0.35 °C after station 5).

def time_grad(n_rows, repeats=20):
    # Shapes: n_rows stations (1 or N_Ω); N padded steps; 3 log parameters each
    t_rows = times[:n_rows]  # → (n_rows, N)
    y_rows = y[:n_rows]  # → (n_rows, N)
    o_rows = mask[:n_rows]  # → (n_rows, N) bool

    def neg_log_likelihood(log_params):
        params = jnp.exp(log_params)  # → (n_rows, 3)
        # today (jax)
        per_station = jax.vmap(
            station_log_marginal, in_axes=(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, None, None, 0)
        )
        # log p(y_n ∣ ·) for each row
        log_marginals = per_station(  # (n_rows, N) → (n_rows,)
            t_rows,
            y_rows,
            o_rows,
            params[:, 0],
            params[:, 1],
            truth_shared["cos_amp"],
            truth_shared["sin_amp"],
            params[:, 2],
        )
        # ℒ_NLL = −∑ₙ log p(y_n ∣ ·)
        return -einx.sum("n ->", log_marginals)

    # today (jax)
    # ℒ_NLL and its gradient, jitted once
    loss_and_grad = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(neg_log_likelihood))
    log_params = jnp.log(jnp.tile(jnp.array([4.0, 4.0, 0.25]), (n_rows, 1)))
    jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(log_params))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(log_params))
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / repeats

        f"({ms / grad_ms[1]:.1f}x one station)"

One log likelihood and its gradient cost 2.87 ms for one station and 4.29 ms for all six, so six times the records cost 1.5 times as much. This is because the vmapped filters share the sequential scan over the $N$ padded steps. Most of the cost of the network fit is in the number of gradients that NUTS needs for the hierarchical posterior (22.2 leapfrog steps per draw after warm-up), not in the extra stations. The network fit took 97.5 s with the two chains on two cores, and the two short stations on their own took 20.5 s. docs.title: Many sites, one model: pooled hyperparameters over ragged station records¶
docs.text:
Example 1 fitted one station. Here we fit a small network of stations whose records start and end on different days, have different lengths and have their own gaps. This is what a real station archive looks like. Two of the stations have only a month of data. That is too little to learn a kernel from, so on their own their hyperparameters are barely constrained. We pad the records to one shape with pad_sites and run one Markov-GP marginal likelihood per station under jax.vmap. The stations share what they have in common through population-level priors on the kernel hyperparameters, so the short stations borrow strength from the long ones.

pyrox-ssm capability shown: pad_sites, which pads ragged per-station series to one (N_Ω, N) grid and returns the observation mask, and MarkovGPPrior.log_marginal(..., mask=...) vmapped over stations inside a numpyro.plate, so one NumPyro model holds every station with its own hyperparameters, and MarkovGPPrior.condition(..., mask=...).predict(...) vmapped over posterior draws and stations, which gives every station's posterior predictive on a dense grid. Cost: every log-density evaluation is one Kalman filter pass per station, $\mathcal{O}(N_\Omega N D_x^3)$ in the number of stations $N_\Omega$, the padded record length $N$ and the state dimension $D_x$. The vmapped stations run as one batched filter, so they share the sequential scan over the $N$ steps. We measure the wall-clock times of every fit, of the predictions and of one gradient in section 8.

What you'll learn:

  1. How to turn ragged station records into padded arrays and a mask with pad_sites, and why the padding changes no station's likelihood.
  2. How to write a hierarchical Markov-GP model as a plain NumPyro function, with per-station kernel hyperparameters drawn around population values in a non-centred form.
  3. How to predict every station through its gaps, before its record starts and after it ends, averaged over the posterior draws.
  4. How partial pooling pulls the estimates and the predictions of a short record towards the population, compared with fitting that record on its own.

The single-station model, its priors and the Kalman marginal likelihood are explained in Example 1, and we reuse them here without deriving them again.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
The network is a set $\Omega_y$ of $N_\Omega \equiv N_{\Omega_y} = 6$ stations, indexed by $n = 1, \ldots, N_\Omega$. Station $n$ reported on the days $\mathcal{T}_{y,n}$, and it has $N_n \equiv \vert \mathcal{T}_{y,n} \vert$ daily mean temperatures $y_{n,k}$ (°C) on the days $t_{n,k} \in \mathcal{T}_{y,n}$, $k = 1, \ldots, N_n$. The days are strictly increasing within a station, and a gap is simply a day that is not in $\mathcal{T}_{y,n}$. Each station follows the model of Example 1,

$$y_{n,k} = c_n + \mu(t_{n,k}) + f_n(t_{n,k}) + \varepsilon_{n,k}$$

$$\mu(t) = a \cos(\omega t) + b \sin(\omega t)$$

$$f_n \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(t, t'; \sigma_{f,n}^2, \ell_n))$$

$$\varepsilon_{n,k} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$$

with $\omega = 2\pi / 365.25 \text{ days}^{-1}$ as before, where we have moved the mean temperature $c_n \in \mathbb{R}$ (°C) out of the seasonal cycle $\mu(t)$. We pool the parameters at three levels, each for a physical reason:

  1. The offset $c_n$ is not pooled at all, as it depends on the station's elevation and siting.
  2. The seasonal amplitudes $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ (°C) are shared by every station (complete pooling), because the stations sit in one region and see the same annual cycle. So is the noise variance $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$, because every station has the same type of sensor.
  3. The weather anomaly differs from station to station, but not by much, so its kernel variance $\sigma_{f,n}^2$ and lengthscale $\ell_n$ (days) are partially pooled.

For the partial pooling we write the two hyperparameters in log form, $\boldsymbol{\theta}_n = (\log \sigma_{f,n}^2, \log \ell_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$, and draw them around a population mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ with a population spread $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{2}_{>0}$,

$$\boldsymbol{\theta}_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta, \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\tau}_\theta^2))$$

If $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\theta$ is small the stations share one kernel, and if it is large each station is on its own, so the data decide how much the stations pool. With six stations $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\theta$ is poorly known. In this centred form the posterior of each $\boldsymbol{\theta}_n$ narrows as $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\theta$ shrinks, which makes a funnel that NUTS cannot step through. So we sample the equivalent non-centred form, in which the standardised offsets $\mathbf{z}_n \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ are a priori independent of the population,

$$\boldsymbol{\theta}_n = \boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta + \boldsymbol{\tau}_\theta \odot \mathbf{z}_n$$

$$\mathbf{z}_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_2)$$

The offset $c_n$ gets Example 1's prior $\mathcal{N}(10, 10^2)$. A Gaussian constant plus a GP is again a GP, so we do not sample $c_n$ at all and fold it into the anomaly's prior instead,

$$c_n + f_n \sim \mathcal{GP}(10, 10^2 + k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(t, t'; \sigma_{f,n}^2, \ell_n))$$

In state-space form the constant kernel is a one-dimensional state that never changes (ConstantSDE), which SumSDE stacks with the two-dimensional Matérn-3/2 state, so $D_x = 3$ and the Kalman filter integrates $c_n$ out together with the path. This removes six sampled values that would be strongly correlated with $a$ and $b$, which matters for NUTS (section 4).

To vmap one Kalman filter over the stations, every station needs a record of the same length. pad_sites extends station $n$ after its last day to $N = \max_n N_n$ steps at its median spacing $\delta_n$, so $t_{n,N_n+j} = t_{n,N_n} + j \delta_n$ for $j = 1, \ldots, N - N_n$. It also returns the mask $o_{n,k} \in \{0, 1\}$, which is 1 on the $N_n$ real days. A masked step runs only the filter's predict step, so the padding adds exactly zero to the log marginal. The model's log likelihood is then a sum of Example 1's masked log marginals over the stations,

$$\log p(\mathbf{Y} \mid a, b, \boldsymbol{\Theta}, \sigma_\varepsilon^2) = \sum_{n=1}^{N_\Omega} \sum_{k=1}^{N} o_{n,k} \log \mathcal{N}(y_{n,k}; 10 + \mu(t_{n,k}) + \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,n,k \mid k-1}, \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,n,k \mid k-1} \mathbf{H}^\top + \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$$

where $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\Omega \times N}$ stacks the padded records as rows and $\boldsymbol{\Theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\Omega \times 2}$ the $\boldsymbol{\theta}_n$. Here $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,n,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,n,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ are station $n$'s one-step-ahead state mean and covariance, and the measurement row $\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times D_x}$ adds the constant to the Matérn-3/2 value.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: We detect Colab and install pyrox, pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm only when the notebook runs there.

docs.title: 1. A network of ragged station records¶
docs.text:
We simulate one year of a six-station network from the model itself, so that we know every true parameter. The seasonal cycle is Example 1's (an 8 °C annual cycle with its coldest point near 1 January). The sensor noise is again 0.5 °C, and the station offsets range from 7.5 to 12 °C. The population of anomaly kernels is centred on Example 1's values, a variance of $(2 \text{ °C})^2$ and a four-day lengthscale. Its spread is 0.3 in log units (about ±35 %), and each station's $\boldsymbol{\theta}_n$ is one draw from it.

The stations then report on their own schedules. Stations 1 to 4 each cover about four months, starting and ending in different seasons. Station 2 has a 25-day logger outage, station 3 misses another 30 % of its days at random, and station 4 has a 15-day outage. Stations 5 and 6 span only 35 and 30 days. As in Example 1, every station also misses each day with probability 0.08. We keep only the days a station reported. So each record is a pair of arrays (days and values) of its own length, and the records cannot be stacked into one array.

docs.title: 2. Padding the records with pad_sites¶
docs.text: pad_sites takes one array of days and one array of values per station. It returns three (N_Ω, N) arrays: the padded days $\mathbf{T}$, the padded values $\mathbf{Y}$ (zero after each record ends) and the mask $\mathbf{O}$. We print the mask's row sums, which must equal the record lengths. We also look at the end of a short station's row, where the padded days continue at its median spacing.

docs.title: 3. The hierarchical model as a plain NumPyro function¶
docs.text:
The global parameters are ordinary sample sites with Example 1's priors, $a, b \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10^2)$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 0.1, 1)$. The population mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta$ gets a normal prior centred on Example 1's prior medians for $\sigma_f^2$ and $\ell$ (2 °C² and 7 days) with unit standard deviation. So before any data a station's $\boldsymbol{\theta}_n$ is at least as uncertain as it was in Example 1. The spread gets $\tau_{\theta,d} \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(0.5)$ for $d = 1, 2$, which says that stations in one region rarely differ by more than a factor of three. Inside numpyro.plate("station", N_Ω), every sample site has one value per station.

pyrox-ssm has no helper for the non-centred step yet, so we write it inline in noncentred_log_normal. It samples $z_{n,d}$ from a standard normal, shifts and scales it, and records $\exp(\theta_{n,d})$ as a deterministic site, so the posterior of $\sigma_{f,n}^2$ and $\ell_n$ ends up in the trace. (NumPyro's LocScaleReparam(centered=0) does the same rewrite on a centred Normal site.) Then jax.vmap runs station_log_marginal over the station axis of the padded arrays, with the shared $a$, $b$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ broadcast. Finally, numpyro.factor adds the $N_\Omega$ log marginals as one factor site under the plate.

We do not call markov_gp_factor here. It registers its own factor site for one prior, so it cannot run under jax.vmap. The vmapped log_marginal with one factor is the pattern its docstring shows for ragged sites.

docs.title: 4. NUTS¶
docs.text: We run two chains of 150 draws after 250 warm-up steps, with a dense mass matrix as in Example 1. So warm-up adapts to the correlations between the seasonal amplitudes and the kernel hyperparameters. We start the chains at the prior medians (init_to_median). The warm-up is longer than Example 1's, because the dense mass matrix now has $19 \times 19$ entries to adapt. We split the CPU into two XLA devices at import (numpyro.set_host_device_count(2)), so chain_method="parallel" runs the two chains on two cores at once. The wall-clock time includes JIT compilation.

docs.title: 5. Pooled estimates against the truth¶
docs.text: For every station we compare the posterior of $\sigma_{f,n}^2$ and $\ell_n$ with the value we simulated it with. For the shared parameters and the population we do the same with $a$, $b$, $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$, $\exp(\boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta)$ and $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\theta$. Each row gives the posterior mean, the standard deviation and the 90 % interval.

docs.title: 6. Prediction at every station¶
docs.text:
A posterior draw $e$ gives $a^{(e)}$, $b^{(e)}$, $(\sigma_\varepsilon^{(e)})^2$ and every station's $\boldsymbol{\theta}_n^{(e)}$. For one draw and one station, station_prior(...).condition(y_n, noise_var, mask=o_n) runs the Kalman filter and RTS smoother over the station's padded record. Then predict(t_star) gives the posterior mean and variance of the latent $c_n + \mu(t_*) + f_n(t_*)$ at any test times $t_*$, as in Example 1. The constant state is smoothed together with the path, so the offset stays integrated out and the bands include the uncertainty of $c_n$. We do this for $N_{\mathcal{E}} = 100$ NUTS draws, $e \in \mathcal{E}$, and for all stations at once, with one jax.vmap over the draws inside another over the stations. With $\mu_{n,*}^{(e)} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $(\sigma_{n,*}^{(e)})^2 \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ the posterior mean and variance at station $n$ under draw $e$, we average as in Example 1,

$$\mathbb{E}[c_n + \mu(t_*) + f_n(t_*) \mid \mathbf{Y}] \approx \bar{\mu}_{n,*} = \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} \mu_{n,*}^{(e)}$$

$$\mathbb{V}[c_n + \mu(t_*) + f_n(t_*) \mid \mathbf{Y}] \approx \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} (\sigma_{n,*}^{(e)})^2 + \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} (\mu_{n,*}^{(e)} - \bar{\mu}_{n,*})^2$$

and a new observation $y_{n,*}$ adds $(\sigma_\varepsilon^{(e)})^2$ to each $(\sigma_{n,*}^{(e)})^2$. The test grid has a point every 12 hours from day 0 to day 380. So it covers each station's record and its gaps, the days before the station started and after it stopped (when other stations were reporting), and 15 days past the end of the year. A station's prediction conditions on its own record only. The other stations reach it through the shared $a$, $b$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ and through the pooled kernel hyperparameters, because in this model the anomalies of different stations are independent.

docs.title: 7. The short stations on their own¶
docs.text:
To see what pooling buys, we fit stations 5 and 6 without the network, with Example 1's model. Each station gets its own $a$, $b$, $\sigma_f^2$, $\ell$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ with Example 1's priors, and its offset is integrated out as above, so nothing is shared. The two fits then have independent posteriors. So we run them as one pair of NUTS chains on a plate of two stations (padded with pad_sites again), which costs one batched filter per gradient rather than two.

Note that the fit on its own has to learn the seasonal cycle and the noise from a month of data as well as the kernel. The network model gets $a$, $b$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ from all six stations, so this comparison shows everything a short record gains from the network, not only what it gains from pooling $\boldsymbol{\theta}_n$.

docs.title: 8. Cost¶
docs.text: Each NUTS leapfrog step costs one Kalman filter pass per station over the $N$ padded steps, plus its reverse-mode gradient. Under jax.vmap the stations run as one filter on a batch of $N_\Omega$ three-dimensional states, so the sequential scan over the $N$ steps is shared. Below we time one jitted log likelihood and its gradient for a single station at the padded length $N$ and for the whole network, and we list the wall-clock times of the fits and the predictions.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• Ragged station records go into one model through pad_sites, which pads every record after its last day and returns the mask. The masked padding changes no station's log marginal, so the gaps stay in the days and the padding stays out of the likelihood.
  • A hierarchical Markov-GP model is a plain NumPyro function: global sample sites, a numpyro.plate over stations, a non-centred draw of each station's kernel hyperparameters around the population, and MarkovGPPrior.log_marginal(..., mask=...) vmapped over the stations into one factor site.
  • The latent paths and the station offsets stay integrated out, so NUTS runs on $7 + 2 N_\Omega$ values for any record length. The network fit took 97.5 s of NUTS on CPU, and one gradient over six stations costs 1.5 times one station.
  • The two short stations borrow strength from the network: the 90 % intervals of their kernel hyperparameters are 1.7 to 3.7 times narrower than when each is fitted on its own. With six stations the population spread is poorly known (posterior mean 0.16 against a true 0.3), so the model also pulls unusual stations towards the population, and four of the twelve per-station intervals miss the truth on that side.
  • MarkovGPPrior.condition(..., mask=...).predict(...), vmapped over posterior draws and stations, predicts every station through its gaps and beyond its record, and 96.2 % of the 130 withheld days fall inside the $\pm 2\sigma$ band for a new observation. Away from their records, the short stations' bands in the network have a mean half-width of 4.07 to 4.27 °C against 4.81 to 7.52 °C on their own, because the seasonal cycle comes from the whole network.

The next example keeps the stations but adds a regional anomaly that all of them share, on top of each station's own anomaly. For the single-station model and its predictions see Example 1.

def occurrence_prior(times):
    # Shapes: n days; D_θ = 3 parameters

    # today (numpyro): the three sample sites of θ
    # c ~ 𝒩(−1, 1.5²)
    offset = numpyro.sample("offset", dist.Normal(-1.0, 1.5))
    # σ_f² ~ LogNormal(0, 1)
    variance = numpyro.sample("variance", dist.LogNormal(0.0, 1.0))
    # ℓ ~ LogNormal(log 7, 1)
    lengthscale = numpyro.sample("lengthscale", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(7.0), 1.0))

    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_f², ℓ) as a linear SDE
    sde = MaternSDE(variance, lengthscale, order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # μ + f ~ 𝒢𝒫(μ, k_Matérn-3/2) on the given days
    return MarkovGPPrior(sde, times, mean_fn=lambda t: climatology(t, offset))


# today (pyrox_gp)
# p(y_k ∣ f) = Bernoulli(σ(μ(t_k) + f(t_k)))
likelihood = BernoulliLikelihood()
# today (pyrox_ssm)
# damped Newton steps on the sites, s ← (1 − α) s + α 𝒯(s) with α = 0.5
laplace = LaplaceMarkovInference(damping=0.5, max_iter=50)


def collapsed_model(times, wet, mask, strategy=laplace):
    # Shapes: N record days; D_θ = 3 parameters

    # user
    prior = occurrence_prior(times)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # log p(y ∣ θ) ≈ log p(y ∣ f̂) + log 𝒩(f̂; μ, K_tt) − ½ log det(I + Λ_site K_tt)
    markov_laplace_factor(
        "y",
        prior,
        likelihood,
        wet,
        strategy=strategy,
        mask=mask,
        reject_unconverged=True,
    )


def site_kind(site):
    """A short label for a trace site: factor, deterministic or its family."""
    if site["type"] != "sample":
        return site["type"]
    fn = site["fn"]
    if isinstance(fn, dist.Unit):
        return "factor"
    while isinstance(fn, (dist.ExpandedDistribution, dist.Independent)):
        fn = fn.base_dist
    if isinstance(fn, dist.MaskedDistribution):
        fn = fn.base_dist
    return type(fn).__name__


def print_trace(model, *args):
    """Every site of one seeded run of the model, and the values NUTS samples."""
    # today (numpyro)
    trace = handlers.trace(handlers.seed(model, rng_seed=0)).get_trace(*args)
    for name, site in trace.items():
        shape = tuple(jnp.shape(site["value"]))
        print(f"site {name!r:16} {site_kind(site):<14} value shape={shape}")
    n_latent = sum(
        int(np.prod(jnp.shape(site["value"])))
        for site in trace.values()
        if site["type"] == "sample"
        and not site["is_observed"]
        and not isinstance(site["fn"], dist.Unit)
    )
    print(f"unconstrained values for NUTS: {n_latent}")

So Route A's trace looks like Example 1's: three scalar sample sites and one factor, and no latent path.

We do not use the strategy's defaults (a full Newton step, damping=1.0, and max_iter=20). Without a line search a full Newton step can overshoot and oscillate when the prior variance is large, and then the fit stops at max_iter without converging. Under reject_unconverged=True that region of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ becomes a wall of $-\infty$, which NUTS reports as divergences, and without it the factor there is an evidence and a gradient taken away from the fixed point. Below we fit both settings at four values of $\sigma_f^2$, with $c$ and $\ell$ at their true values, and print whether each fit converged and in how many iterations. Damping does not move the fixed point, so where both converge they give the same evidence, the damped one in more iterations.

def fit_converged(variance, strategy):
    """Convergence and iterations at σ_f², with c and ℓ at the truth."""
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    sde = MaternSDE(variance, truth["lengthscale"], order=1)

        record_days,

    cond = prior.condition_nongauss(
        likelihood, record_wet, strategy=strategy, mask=record_mask

N_DRAWS = 100

def evenly_spaced(samples, n_draws=N_DRAWS):
    """n_draws draws evenly spaced through the chains."""
    num_samples = samples["variance"].shape[0]
    idx = jnp.linspace(0, num_samples - 1, n_draws).astype(int)  # → (N_E,)
    return {k: samples[k][idx] for k in hyper_names}


def conditioned_one(theta, strategy):
    """Fit the sites for one θ⁽ᵉ⁾ and predict the log odds at every grid day."""
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    sde = MaternSDE(theta["variance"], theta["lengthscale"], order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    prior = MarkovGPPrior(
        sde,
        record_days,
        mean_fn=lambda t: climatology(t, theta["offset"]),
    )
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # q(f ∣ y; θ⁽ᵉ⁾) from the sites fitted by the strategy
    cond = prior.condition_nongauss(
        likelihood, record_wet, strategy=strategy, mask=record_mask
    )
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # μ_k⁽ᵉ⁾, (σ_k⁽ᵉ⁾)² of μ(t_k) + f(t_k) at all T days
    mean, var = cond.predict(days)  # (T,) → (T,), (T,)
    return mean, var, cond.converged, cond.n_iter


def conditioned_draws(theta_draws, strategy):
    """conditioned_one for every draw, vectorised and jitted."""
    # today (jax)
    one = jax.vmap(lambda theta: conditioned_one(theta, strategy))
    # today (jax)
    return jax.jit(one)(theta_draws)  # → (N_E, T), (N_E, T), (N_E,), (N_E,)


def prob_summary(prob_draws):
    """Mean and 95 % band of p_k over the pooled draw axis."""
    # p̄_k = (1/N_draws) ∑ p_k⁽ᵉ⁾, also ℙ(y_k = 1 ∣ y)
    mean = einx.mean("draw k -> k", prob_draws)  # → (T,)
    # the 2.5 % and 97.5 % quantiles over the draws
    lo, hi = np.percentile(np.asarray(prob_draws), [2.5, 97.5], axis=0)
    return {"mean": np.asarray(mean), "lo": lo, "hi": hi}


def collapsed_probabilities(theta_draws, strategy, key):
    """Pooled draws of p_k from the Gaussian q of every θ⁽ᵉ⁾."""
    means, variances, converged, n_iter = conditioned_draws(theta_draws, strategy)
    # ε ~ 𝒩(0, 1), N_MC per draw and day
    noise = jr.normal(key, (N_MC, *means.shape))  # → (N_MC, N_E, T)
    # μ_k⁽ᵉ⁾ + σ_k⁽ᵉ⁾ ε
    logit_draws = einx.add(  # → (N_MC, N_E, T)
        "e k, m e k -> m e k",
        means,
        einx.multiply("e k, m e k -> m e k", jnp.sqrt(variances), noise),
    )
    # p_k = σ(μ(t_k) + f(t_k)), pooled over the draws and the N_MC values
    prob_draws = einx.id("m e k -> (m e) k", jax.nn.sigmoid(logit_draws))
    return prob_draws, means, variances, converged, n_iter
