The two routes give almost the same picture. Both posterior means smooth the wet and dry days into a wet spell in April, a dry May and a smaller wet spell in June, and both bands hold the true $p_k$ on nearly every day. Through the outage and in the forecast the bands widen, and in the forecast they relax towards the seasonal mean and the stationary spread of the anomaly, as the Gaussian bands did in Example 1. The visible difference is in May. On the log-odds scale Route A's band sits a little above Route B's through the run of dry days after the outage, and section 7 shows where that comes from.

Because the record is simulated, we know $p_k$ on every day and whether each withheld day was wet. A 95 % predictive interval for a single 0 or 1 is not a useful check, since it holds both outcomes unless $\mathbb{P}(y_k = 1 \mid \mathbf{y})$ is below 2.5 % or above 97.5 %. So we score each route in two ways. The first is the fraction of days on which the true $p_k$ is inside the 95 % band (the coverage of the latent probability). The second, on the withheld days and the forecast, is the mean log predictive density, $\frac{1}{N_\text{sel}} \sum_k \log \mathbb{P}(y_k \mid \mathbf{y})$ over the $N_\text{sel}$ selected days (higher is better), and the Brier score, $\frac{1}{N_\text{sel}} \sum_k (\mathbb{P}(y_k = 1 \mid \mathbf{y}) - y_k)^2$ (lower is better). The scores of the true $p_k$ are the best that any model of these days can do on average.

def scores(prob, sel):
    """Mean log predictive density and Brier score of ℙ(y_k = 1) on sel."""
    # log ℙ(y_k ∣ y) = y_k log p̄_k + (1 − y_k) log(1 − p̄_k)
    log_pred = wet_np * np.log(prob) + (1.0 - wet_np) * np.log1p(-prob)  # → (T,)
    # (p̄_k − y_k)²
    brier = (prob - wet_np) ** 2  # → (T,)
    return float(np.mean(log_pred[sel])), float(np.mean(brier[sel]))

def mixture(means, variances):
    """Mean and sd of the equal-weight Gaussian mixture over the draw axis."""
    # μ̄_k = (1/N_E) ∑ₑ μ_k⁽ᵉ⁾
    mean = einx.mean("member k -> k", means)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (μ_k⁽ᵉ⁾ − μ̄_k)²
    spread = einx.var("member k -> k", means)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_k⁽ᵉ⁾)²
    variance_mean = einx.mean("member k -> k", variances)
    # 𝕍 ≈ (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_k⁽ᵉ⁾)² + spread
    return np.asarray(mean), np.asarray(jnp.sqrt(variance_mean + spread))

With Route B's own hyperparameters, the Laplace posterior of the log odds matches Route B's in April (a mean difference of −0.002 and a standard deviation ratio of 0.95) and in June (0.063 and 0.98). In May it does not. There the record holds 1 wet day in 17 observed days, and the Laplace mean sits on average 0.152 above Route B's, most of all in the run of dry days after the outage (top panel). EP at the same hyperparameters stays within 0.036 of Route B in May and within 0.026 in the other months. This is the sparse binary case. A run of dry days skews the posterior of the log odds, with a long tail towards very negative values (a dry day says little about how dry the day was). A Gaussian centred at the mode then sits above the mean of such a distribution. EP matches the mean and variance of the tilted distribution at each site, rather than the curvature at the mode, so it follows the skew.

Route A's own posterior (dotted) also carries its trimmed $\sigma_f^2$. Its bands are narrower than Route B's in every month (standard deviation ratios of 0.89, 0.87 and 0.93), whereas the Laplace bands at Route B's hyperparameters are not (0.95 to 0.98). So in this example the Laplace approximation costs Route A a shift of about 0.14 in the log odds where the data are sparse, and somewhat narrower bands through the hyperparameters. Both are small next to the width of the bands, which is why the coverage and the scores of section 6 barely differ.

def time_grad(model, args, values, repeats=3):
    """One jitted log joint density and its gradient, in ms."""

    def log_joint(v):
        # today (numpyro)
        # log p(θ, ·, y) at the given unconstrained sample values
        log_p, _ = log_density(model, args, {}, v)
        return log_p

    # today (jax)
    loss_and_grad = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(log_joint))
    jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(values))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(values))
    return 1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / repeats

One log density and its gradient cost 32.3 ms for Route A and 0.62 ms for Route B, about fifty times more. Route A runs the damped fixed-point iteration to convergence (about 25 smoother passes here, from section 6) and then solves the implicit adjoint with GMRES, each step of which is another pass. Route B runs one scan over the 105 days and its reverse pass. Route A makes up some of this in the number of steps, 6.8 leapfrog steps per draw against 24.6, because it samples three values rather than 213. Per draw that is still about fourteen times the work of Route B, and per effective sample of the hyperparameters Route B is ahead by a similar factor, 6.21 against 0.44 per second (both including JIT compilation). So on a CPU and at this record length the sampled path is the cheaper route to the hyperparameters. Route A gives the smaller posterior: three values, few steps per draw, and no mass matrix to adapt over the path.

docs.title: Wet and dry days: a non-Gaussian likelihood with the path integrated out or sampled¶
docs.text:
In Examples 1, 2 and 3 the observations were Gaussian, so the Kalman filter integrated the latent path out exactly and NUTS only saw the hyperparameters. In Example 3b the observations were counts, and NUTS had to sample every latent value. Here we take one station's record of wet and dry days, a Bernoulli observation of a latent log odds, and fit it both ways. Route A integrates the path out approximately with a Laplace approximation, so NUTS again samples only the hyperparameters. Route B samples the path through whitened innovations, as Example 3b did, so its posterior is exact up to the Monte Carlo error of the chains. Since we simulate the record, we know the truth, and Route B gives us the reference to check Route A against: its hyperparameters, its latent wet-day probability through the gaps and the forecast, and what it costs.

pyrox-ssm capability shown: markov_laplace_factor, which fits the latent path with a site-based strategy (LaplaceMarkovInference here, ExpectationPropagationMarkov for comparison) and adds its approximate log evidence as a NumPyro factor, with reject_unconverged=True so NUTS rejects any $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ whose fit did not converge; MarkovGPPrior.condition_nongauss(...).predict(...), the conditioned non-Gaussian posterior at arbitrary days; and markov_gp_innovations_sample for Route B. The strategies iterate to a fixed point with optimistix.fixed_point, and their gradient comes from the implicit function theorem at that fixed point, so the factor jits and differentiates inside NUTS. Cost: every Route A log-density evaluation is a few Kalman filter and smoother passes, $\mathcal{O}(I N D_x^3)$ for $I$ fixed-point iterations, plus the implicit gradient; every Route B evaluation is one scan, $\mathcal{O}(T D_x^3)$, but NUTS has to move $T D_x$ more values. We measure both, per gradient, per draw and per effective sample, in section 8.

What you'll learn:

  1. How to write a Bernoulli model on a Markov GP as a plain NumPyro function in two ways: with the path collapsed by markov_laplace_factor, and with the path sampled by markov_gp_innovations_sample.
  2. How the hyperparameter posteriors of the two routes compare with each other and with the truth.
  3. How to predict the latent wet-day probability through withheld days and a forecast from Route A's conditioned posterior, averaged over its NUTS draws, and how it compares with Route B's.
  4. Where the Laplace approximation is close to the exact posterior and where it is biased, and what each route costs.

The Matérn-3/2 SDE and the Kalman filter are explained in Example 1, and the whitened innovations in Example 3b. For the four site-based strategies (Laplace, Gauss-Newton, posterior linearisation and EP) at fixed hyperparameters, see Non-Gaussian Markov GP inference. We reuse all three here without deriving them again.

docs.title: Why pyrox_gp and pyrox_ssm appear together¶
docs.text: The Bernoulli observation model is pyrox_gp.BernoulliLikelihood. pyrox_ssm never imports pyrox_gp (its import-guard test forbids it, see AGENTS.md), and its strategies take any pyrox.likelihoods.Likelihood, the protocol that lives in the shared pyrox core. So, as in Example 3b, we import both and compose them in one model: the packages do not depend on each other, the user does.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
The days $t_k$, $k = 1, \ldots, T$, form the grid $\mathcal{T}_x$ of $T \equiv N_{\mathcal{T}_x}$ days, counted from 1 January. The first $N$ of them are the record and the last $T - N$ are a forecast. On day $t_k$ the station reports $y_k \in \{0, 1\}$, 1 for a wet day, when the mask $o_k \in \{0, 1\}$ is 1, and $o_k = 0$ on the forecast days and on the days the station missed. The wet-day probability $p_k \in (0, 1)$ is the logistic function $\sigma(\cdot)$ of a seasonal mean of the log odds plus a Matérn-3/2 anomaly,

$$y_k \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_k)$$

$$\log \frac{p_k}{1 - p_k} = \mu(t_k) + f(t_k)$$

$$\mu(t) = c + a \cos(\omega t) + b \sin(\omega t)$$

$$f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(t, t'; \sigma_f^2, \ell))$$

where $\omega = 2\pi / 365.25 \text{ days}^{-1}$ as in Example 1, $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ set the shape of the seasonal cycle of the log odds, $c \in \mathbb{R}$ is the station's offset from it, and the anomaly $f$ (in log-odds units) has the kernel variance $\sigma_f^2 \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ and the lengthscale $\ell \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ (days). A record of a few months cannot pin down an annual cycle, so we take $a$ and $b$ as known, from the station's long-term climatology, and infer $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (c, \sigma_f^2, \ell) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$. With $\mathbf{f} = \mu(t_{1:N}) + f(t_{1:N}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ the log odds on the record days, the log likelihood keeps only the observed days,

$$\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{f}) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} o_k (y_k \log p_k + (1 - y_k) \log(1 - p_k))$$

with $\mathbf{y} \in \{0, 1\}^{N}$ the record. There is no Kalman marginal for it, so the two routes deal with $\mathbf{f}$ differently.

Route A, collapsed. We integrate $\mathbf{f}$ out with a Laplace approximation and give NUTS the three values of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ only. With $\hat{\mathbf{f}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ the mode of $p(\mathbf{f} \mid \mathbf{y}, \boldsymbol{\theta})$, $\hat{p}_k = \sigma(\hat{f}_k)$ and $\mathbf{K}_{tt} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$ the Matérn-3/2 kernel matrix over the record days, the approximate log evidence is

$$\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \approx \log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \hat{\mathbf{f}}) + \log \mathcal{N}(\hat{\mathbf{f}}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{K}_{tt}) - \frac{1}{2} \log \det(\mathbf{I}_N + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_\text{site} \mathbf{K}_{tt})$$

where $\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mu(t_{1:N}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_\text{site} = \mathrm{diag}(o_k \hat{p}_k (1 - \hat{p}_k)) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$ holds the curvature of the log likelihood at the mode, zero on a missed day. pyrox-ssm never forms $\mathbf{K}_{tt}$. It replaces each observed day by a Gaussian site, a pseudo-observation of $f(t_k)$ with precision $\Lambda_{\text{site},k} = \hat{p}_k (1 - \hat{p}_k)$, and gets $\hat{\mathbf{f}}$ and all three terms from Kalman filter and RTS smoother passes over the sites. Finding $\hat{\mathbf{f}}$ is a Newton iteration on the site natural parameters $\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{2N}$, a fixed point $\mathbf{s}^\star = \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{s}^\star; \boldsymbol{\theta})$ of the update $\mathcal{T}$. The gradient that NUTS needs comes from the implicit function theorem at that fixed point,

$$\frac{\partial \mathbf{s}^\star}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}} = \left(\mathbf{I}_{2N} - \frac{\partial \mathcal{T}}{\partial \mathbf{s}}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial \mathcal{T}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}}$$

which pyrox-ssm solves matrix-free with GMRES, whatever the number of iterations. It is the gradient of the evidence only when the iteration converged, which is why we pass reject_unconverged=True. Then we predict with the conditioned posterior $q(f(t_*) \mid \mathbf{y}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_*, \sigma_*^2)$ at any day $t_*$, which the smoother gives from the same sites.

Route B, latent. We sample the log odds on the whole grid of $T$ days through the whitened innovations of Example 3b, $\mathbf{z}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$, $\mathbf{z}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_{D_x})$, with $D_x = 2$, and the Bernoulli likelihood is an ordinary NumPyro observation. NUTS samples $p(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{z}_{1:T} \mid \mathbf{y})$, that is $3 + T D_x$ values, and every draw carries the path on the withheld days and the forecast. This posterior is exact, so we use Route B as the reference.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: We detect Colab and install pyrox, pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm only when the notebook runs there.

docs.title: 1. A record of wet and dry days¶
docs.text: We simulate one station from the model itself, so that we know every true value: a Mediterranean-like climate whose wet season ends in spring. The record runs for $N = 90$ days, from 1 April to 29 June, and we keep the $T - N = 15$ days after it, to 14 July, for a forecast. On the seasonal mean alone the wet-day probability falls from about 0.4 on 1 April to about 0.03 on 29 June. The anomaly, with $\sigma_f^2 = 1$ and $\ell = 8$ days, adds wet and dry spells of a week or two on top. Then we take days out as in Example 1: a 10-day logger outage in May, and each day missing at random with probability 0.1. A missed day is NaN in the station file, and we keep its true value to score the predictions. So the record runs from a wet regime into the sparse binary one, a few wet days among many dry ones, which is where a Gaussian approximation of the latent log odds is least comfortable.

docs.title: 2. Route A: the path integrated out¶
docs.text:
Both routes share the priors, which we put in one function. The offset gets $c \sim \mathcal{N}(-1, 1.5^2)$, so a station anywhere between much drier and much wetter than its climatology is plausible. The anomaly gets $\sigma_f^2 \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(0, 1)$ and Example 1's prior for the lengthscale, $\ell \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 7, 1)$. The function returns the MarkovGPPrior with the seasonal mean as its mean_fn.

Route A then passes that prior, BernoulliLikelihood() and the record to markov_laplace_factor, which fits the sites with the strategy we give it and adds the approximate log evidence as a factor site named "y". The masked days, stored as NaN, get a zero site and never reach the arithmetic. With reject_unconverged=True the factor is $-\infty$ whenever the fit stops at max_iter without meeting its tolerance, so NUTS rejects that $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ rather than move on an evidence and a gradient taken away from the fixed point.

docs.title: 3. Route B: the path sampled¶
docs.text: Route B builds the same prior on the whole grid of $T$ days, the record and the forecast, and draws the log odds with markov_gp_innovations_sample("logit", prior), which registers the innovations as "logit_eps" and the path (mean included) as the deterministic site "logit". The observation is a plain NumPyro Bernoulli site, masked with .mask(mask) and with the days as its event dimension. NumPyro's masked distribution still evaluates the log density on a masked day before it zeroes it, and a NaN there would turn the gradient into NaN, so Route B gets the record with 0 on the missed and forecast days, which are never read.

docs.title: 4. NUTS on both routes¶
docs.text: Route A has three values to sample, so, as in Example 1, we give it a dense mass matrix (dense_mass=True). Its log density is the expensive one (a damped Laplace fit and its implicit gradient), so we keep its run short, with 50 warm-up steps and 50 draws per chain. We also cap the tree depth at 4 (at most 15 leapfrog steps per draw), which is plenty for three values once the mass matrix is adapted. Route B has 213 values, so, as in Example 3b, only the three hyperparameters share a dense block of the mass matrix, and the innovations stay on the diagonal. Its log density is one scan, so it gets 150 warm-up steps and 150 draws per chain. Both routes run their chains one after the other with chain_method="sequential". We avoid "parallel", under which markov_gp_innovations_sample with its default Cholesky square root fails (issue #420). Both start at the prior medians, and the wall-clock times include JIT compilation.

docs.title: 5. The hyperparameters against the truth¶
docs.text: For each hyperparameter we print the posterior mean, standard deviation and 90 % interval of each route, next to the value we simulated the record with.

docs.title: 6. The wet-day probability through the gaps and the forecast¶
docs.text: Route B's draws $e \in \mathcal{E}$ carry the log odds on every day of the grid, so its wet-day probability is $p_k^{(e)} = \sigma(\mu^{(e)}(t_k) + f^{(e)}(t_k))$, with no extra step, as in Example 3b. Route A's draws carry only $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}$. For each of $N_{\mathcal{E}} = 100$ of them we refit the Laplace sites with condition_nongauss and call predict at all $T$ days of the grid, which gives the Gaussian $q(\mu(t_k) + f(t_k) \mid \mathbf{y}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_k^{(e)}, (\sigma_k^{(e)})^2)$, also on the withheld days and the forecast, where the smoother runs its predict step only. The wet-day probability is a nonlinear function of the log odds, so we draw $N_\text{MC} = 20$ log odds from each Gaussian, push them through $\sigma(\cdot)$ and pool the $N_{\mathcal{E}} N_\text{MC}$ values. For both routes we then summarise $p_k$ by its posterior mean, which is also the predictive probability of a wet day, $\mathbb{P}(y_k = 1 \mid \mathbf{y})$, and by the 2.5 % and 97.5 % quantiles, the 95 % band.

docs.title: 7. Where the Laplace approximation is biased¶
docs.text: Route A approximates in two places. Its hyperparameter posterior comes from the approximate evidence, and for each $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ its latent posterior is a Gaussian $q(\mathbf{f} \mid \mathbf{y}, \boldsymbol{\theta})$ centred at the mode. To separate the two, we condition on Route B's own hyperparameter draws: for $N_{\mathcal{E}} = 100$ of them we fit the Laplace sites and, for comparison, the EP sites of ExpectationPropagationMarkov, and compare the resulting latent posteriors with Route B's, which is exact for the same draws. Any difference is then the error of the Gaussian approximation alone. We compare the posterior mean and standard deviation of the log odds $\mu(t_k) + f(t_k)$, mixed over the draws as in Example 1, in each month of the record: the wet start in April, May with the outage and a long dry run, and the dry June.

docs.title: 8. Cost¶
docs.text: We compare the two routes in three ways. First, the time of one jitted log density and its gradient, at the prior medians and with Route B's innovations at zero. Second, the NUTS wall-clock time and the leapfrog steps per draw from section 4. Third, the smallest effective sample size over the three hyperparameters per second of NUTS, which is the number that decides which route is cheaper for $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• A Bernoulli model on a Markov GP is a plain NumPyro function either way. Route A calls markov_laplace_factor(..., strategy=LaplaceMarkovInference(damping=0.5, max_iter=50), mask=mask, reject_unconverged=True), so its trace holds three sample sites and one factor. Route B calls markov_gp_innovations_sample and adds a masked Bernoulli site, so NUTS moves 213 values.
  • The strategy's defaults (a full Newton step, 20 iterations) stop without converging at $\sigma_f^2 = 8$ and 16 on this record. A damping of 0.5 converged at all four values we checked, in 24 to 27 iterations.
  • The two routes agree on the offset and the lengthscale, and both hold all three true values in their 90 % intervals. The Laplace evidence trims the upper tail of $\sigma_f^2$ (a 90 % interval up to 3.36, against 4.57 for Route B).
  • Route A's prediction, condition_nongauss(...).predict(...) averaged over 100 NUTS draws, follows Route B's through the outage and the forecast. Both bands hold the true $p_k$ on every outage and forecast day, and the log predictive densities differ by at most 0.016.
  • The Laplace latent posterior is close to exact where the data are informative (April, June) and 0.152 too high in the log odds in May, the sparse month with 1 wet day in 17, where EP stays within 0.036.
  • Route A costs 32.3 ms per gradient against 0.62 ms and needs 6.8 leapfrog steps per draw against 24.6, so here Route B gives 6.21 effective samples per second against 0.44.

For the four site-based strategies at fixed hyperparameters see Non-Gaussian Markov GP inference, for whitened paths in a spatial model Example 3b, and for the Gaussian case with the Kalman filter Example 1.

# Shapes: D_x = 3 state components; D_y = 1; T = 120 steps; T_f = 20 forecast steps

DT = 0.05  # Δt [MTU]
BETA = 8.0 / 3.0  # β, fixed
N_STEPS = 120
N_FORECAST = 20


def lorenz_rhs(x, sigma, rho):
    """The Lorenz-63 vector field f_c(x; θ)."""
    # dx₁/dt = σ (x₂ − x₁)
    rate_1 = sigma * (x[1] - x[0])
    # dx₂/dt = x₁ (ρ − x₃) − x₂
    rate_2 = x[0] * (rho - x[2]) - x[1]
    # dx₃/dt = x₁ x₂ − β x₃
    rate_3 = x[0] * x[1] - BETA * x[2]
    return jnp.stack([rate_1, rate_2, rate_3])  # → (D_x,)


def lorenz_step(x, sigma, rho):
    """f(x; θ): one RK4 step of f_c over Δt."""
    # ẋ⁽¹⁾ = f_c(x)
    slope_1 = lorenz_rhs(x, sigma, rho)  # (D_x,) → (D_x,)
    # ẋ⁽²⁾ = f_c(x + ½ Δt ẋ⁽¹⁾)
    slope_2 = lorenz_rhs(x + 0.5 * DT * slope_1, sigma, rho)  # → (D_x,)
    # ẋ⁽³⁾ = f_c(x + ½ Δt ẋ⁽²⁾)
    slope_3 = lorenz_rhs(x + 0.5 * DT * slope_2, sigma, rho)  # → (D_x,)
    # ẋ⁽⁴⁾ = f_c(x + Δt ẋ⁽³⁾)
    slope_4 = lorenz_rhs(x + DT * slope_3, sigma, rho)  # → (D_x,)
    # f(x; θ) = x + Δt/6 (ẋ⁽¹⁾ + 2 ẋ⁽²⁾ + 2 ẋ⁽³⁾ + ẋ⁽⁴⁾)
    increment = slope_1 + 2.0 * slope_2 + 2.0 * slope_3 + slope_4  # → (D_x,)
    return x + DT / 6.0 * increment  # → (D_x,)


def observe(x):
    """h(x) = x₁, the first component."""
    return x[:1]  # (D_x,) → (D_y,)


truth = {"sigma": 10.0, "rho": 28.0, "noise_var": 1.0}
# Σ_η = 0.01 I
PROCESS_NOISE = 0.01 * jnp.eye(3)  # → (D_x, D_x)
key_eta, key_eps, key_gap = jr.split(jr.PRNGKey(0), 3)

x_start = jnp.array([1.0, 1.0, 25.0])  # → (D_x,)
for _ in range(300):
    x_start = lorenz_step(x_start, truth["sigma"], truth["rho"])
# η_k ~ 𝒩(0, Σ_η)
eta = 0.1 * jr.normal(key_eta, (N_STEPS + N_FORECAST, 3))  # → (T + T_f, D_x)


def true_step(x, noise):
    # x_k = f(x_k−1; θ) + η_k
    x_next = lorenz_step(x, truth["sigma"], truth["rho"]) + noise  # → (D_x,)
    return x_next, x_next


# today (jax)
_, x_true = jax.lax.scan(true_step, x_start, eta)  # → (T + T_f, D_x)
# t_k = k Δt, k = 1, …, T + T_f
times = DT * jnp.arange(1, N_STEPS + N_FORECAST + 1)  # → (T + T_f,)
# ε_k ~ 𝒩(0, Σ_ε)
eps = jnp.sqrt(truth["noise_var"]) * jr.normal(key_eps, (N_STEPS + N_FORECAST, 1))
# y_k = h(x_k) + ε_k
y_full = jax.vmap(observe)(x_true) + eps  # (T + T_f, D_x) → (T + T_f, D_y)

outage = (times > 3.0) & (times <= 4.0)  # → (T + T_f,) bool
dropout = jr.uniform(key_gap, (N_STEPS + N_FORECAST,)) < 0.15  # → (T + T_f,) bool
forecast = jnp.arange(N_STEPS + N_FORECAST) >= N_STEPS  # → (T + T_f,) bool
# o_k = 1 on an observed step
mask_all = ~(outage | dropout | forecast)  # → (T + T_f,) bool
keep = einx.id("time -> time 1", mask_all)  # → (T + T_f, 1) bool
# what the record holds, forecast steps included as missing
y_all = jnp.where(keep, y_full, jnp.nan)  # → (T + T_f, D_y)
# the record that NUTS sees
y, mask = y_all[:N_STEPS], mask_all[:N_STEPS]  # → (T, D_y), (T,)
n_obs, n_miss = int(mask.sum()), int((~mask).sum())
print(f"T = {N_STEPS} steps, observed = {n_obs}, missing = {n_miss}")
print(
    f"  outage: {int(outage.sum())} steps, "
    f"random dropouts: {int((dropout & ~outage & ~forecast).sum())} steps"
)

def time_ms(fn, theta, repeats=20):
    """Wall-clock time of one jitted call of ``fn`` at ``theta``, in ms."""

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        jax.block_until_ready(jitted(theta))

The forward-mode Jacobian (4.34 ms) costs half as much as the reverse-mode gradient (8.86 ms), or about three evaluations of the log likelihood (1.38 ms each). So we pass forward_mode_differentiation=True to NUTS. We run two chains of 200 draws after 100 warm-up steps, with a dense mass matrix, started at the prior medians and run one after the other (chain_method="sequential"). We cap the trajectories at $2^5$ leapfrog steps (max_tree_depth=5), which bounds the cost of the long early warm-up trajectories. The wall-clock time includes JIT compilation.

def smoothed_moments(theta, integrator=UNSCENTED):
    """μ_x,k∣T and the diagonal of Σ_x,k∣T over the record and the forecast."""
    dynamics = lambda x: lorenz_step(x, theta["sigma"], theta["rho"])
    # today (pyrox_ssm), outside a model, for the returned FilterState
    state = nonlinear_ssm_factor(
        "y",
        dynamics,
        observe,
        PROCESS_NOISE,
        theta["noise_var"] * jnp.eye(1),
        y_all,
        INIT_MEAN,
        INIT_COV,
        integrator=integrator,
        mask=mask_all,
    )
    # today (gaussx)
    # μ_x,k∣T, Σ_x,k∣T by the moment-matched RTS smoother
    smoothed = gaussx.nonlinear_rts_smoother(state, dynamics, integrator=integrator)
    means, covs = smoothed  # → (T + T_f, D_x), (T + T_f, D_x, D_x)
    # the per-component variances, diag Σ_x,k∣T
    variances = einx.id("time d d -> time d", covs)  # → (T + T_f, D_x)

The posterior mean follows the truth in all three components, also in $x_2$ and $x_3$, which never reach the data: the dynamics couple them to $x_1$, so the filter infers them from how $x_1$ moves. On the observed steps the $\pm 2\sigma$ band covers 95.6 %, 92.2 % and 100 % of the true values of $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$, with RMSEs of 0.25, 0.47 and 0.56. The band hardly widens through the outage, where every true value is inside it and the RMSEs (0.24, 0.24 and 0.30) are no worse than on the observed steps. The smoother has the record on both sides of the gap, and with model noise as small as $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\eta$ only a narrow set of paths joins the two ends. The forecast has data on one side only, and there the band opens within 1 MTU to a good part of the range of the attractor. The RMSEs grow to 2.09, 2.65 and 4.28, and the band still covers every true value. This is the predictability limit of a chaotic system, seen from the filter: the record pins the state down tightly, and the forecast loses that within about one MTU.

At $\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ the two log likelihoods are close, −139.24 for the unscented filter and −140.22 for the EKF. The profiles in $\rho$ tell them apart. Below the true $\rho = 28$ they nearly coincide, but above it the EKF profile falls off much faster. Its maximum on the grid is at $\rho = 27.70$ against 28.20 for the unscented one. That shift is about one posterior standard deviation of $\rho$ (0.460), so the choice of rule alone would move the inferred Rayleigh number by that much. Neither surrogate is the exact likelihood, and this comparison does not say which one is closer to it.

The smoothed states agree on the record, where the means differ by at most 1.03. They also agree in the outage, where they differ by at most 0.40 and the EKF is even slightly closer to the truth (RMSEs of 0.18, 0.21 and 0.24 against 0.24, 0.24 and 0.30). In the forecast they part ways. There the means differ by up to 9.58, and the EKF's RMSEs grow to 3.70, 5.38 and 5.55 against 2.24, 2.85 and 4.20. Its band covers only 55 % and 65 % of the true $x_1$ and $x_2$ (95 % of $x_3$), while the unscented band covers all of them. On the record the belief is narrow, so $f$ is close to linear across it and both rules give the same moments. In the forecast the belief is wide, and the linearisation at the mean misses the spread that the sigma points pick up, so the EKF is overconfident exactly where the uncertainty matters.

One evaluation costs 1.42 ms with the unscented rule and 1.23 ms with the EKF, so the seven sigma points cost little more than one Jacobian. The forward-mode gradient goes the other way, 4.49 ms against 7.55 ms, because the EKF's gradient differentiates through $\mathbf{J}_f$, a second derivative of the RK4 step. So on this model the unscented default is both the cheaper filter for NUTS and the better-calibrated one.

docs.title: Nonlinear dynamics: Lorenz-63 seen through one noisy component, with a moment-matched Kalman likelihood¶
docs.text:
In Examples 1 to 5 the dynamics were linear, so a Kalman filter (exact, or with an ensemble standing in for the covariance) gave the log likelihood. Here the dynamics are nonlinear. We take the Lorenz-63 system, the three-variable model of convection that Lorenz used to show sensitive dependence on initial conditions, and observe only its first component, with noise and with gaps. From that one noisy record we infer two of its parameters and the noise variance with NUTS, and we reconstruct all three components through the gaps and a short forecast. The likelihood comes from a moment-matched nonlinear Kalman filter: it pushes a Gaussian belief through the dynamics with a quadrature rule (the unscented transform by default), so it is a surrogate and not the exact marginal. We compare it with the extended Kalman filter at the end.

pyrox-ssm capability shown: nonlinear_ssm_factor with mask=, which runs gaussx.nonlinear_kalman_filter with any gaussx integrator, adds its log likelihood as a NumPyro factor and returns the gaussx FilterState. We pass that state to gaussx.nonlinear_rts_smoother for the smoothed states. Cost: every log-density evaluation is one filter pass; per step the unscented rule runs the dynamics and the observation map on $2 D_x + 1$ sigma points and factorises a $D_x \times D_x$ covariance. We measure the value and gradient times in section 3 and compare them with the extended filter in section 6.

What you'll learn:

  1. How to write a nonlinear state-space model as a plain NumPyro function with nonlinear_ssm_factor, and why forward-mode gradients pay off for NUTS here.
  2. How the NUTS posterior of the Lorenz parameters compares with the truth.
  3. How to get the smoothed state, observed and unobserved components, through the gaps and a forecast from the returned FilterState, averaged over posterior draws.
  4. Where the unscented and the extended Kalman filter differ, in the likelihood and in the state.

The NUTS workflow and the average over posterior draws are explained in Example 1, and the linear Kalman recursions in Kalman filtering and RTS smoothing. We reuse them here without deriving them again.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
The physical symbols of this page are below. Everything else follows the notation of the earlier examples, with the state $\mathbf{x}$, the observations $\mathbf{y}$ and the parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. The classic Lorenz variables $(x, y, z)$ would collide with the state and the observations, so we write them as the components $x_1, x_2, x_3$ of the state.

Symbol Meaning Shape, units $x_1, x_2, x_3$ convection intensity, horizontal and vertical temperature differences $\mathbb{R}$, dimensionless $\sigma$ Prandtl number $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ $\rho$ Rayleigh number, scaled by its critical value $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ $\beta$ aspect-ratio factor of the convection cell $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ $t$ model time $\mathbb{R}$, model time units (MTU)

The state $\mathbf{x}(t) = (x_1(t), x_2(t), x_3(t)) \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$, $D_x = 3$, follows the vector field $f_\text{c}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}): \mathbb{R}^{D_x} \to \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$,

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}x_1}{\mathrm{d}t} = \sigma (x_2 - x_1)$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}x_2}{\mathrm{d}t} = x_1 (\rho - x_3) - x_2$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}x_3}{\mathrm{d}t} = x_1 x_2 - \beta x_3$$

With Lorenz's values $\sigma = 10$, $\rho = 28$ and $\beta = 8/3$ the solutions are chaotic: nearby states separate exponentially, and the trajectory jumps between two lobes at irregular times. We step it on the grid $t_k = k \Delta t$, $k = 0, 1, \ldots, T$, with $\Delta t = 0.05$ MTU, and write $\mathbf{x}_k = \mathbf{x}(t_k)$. The dynamics $f(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}): \mathbb{R}^{D_x} \to \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ are one classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) step of $f_\text{c}$ over $\Delta t$. The state-space model is then in its standard form,

$$\mathbf{x}_k = f(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) + \boldsymbol{\eta}_k, \quad \boldsymbol{\eta}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\eta)$$

$$\mathbf{y}_k = h(\mathbf{x}_k; \boldsymbol{\theta}) + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_k, \quad \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon)$$

for $k = 1, \ldots, T$, with $\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,0})$. The model noise $\boldsymbol{\eta}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$, with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\eta = 0.01 \mathbf{I}_{D_x}$, stands for everything RK4 and the three equations leave out. The observation map $h(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) = x_1$ picks the first component, so $\mathbf{y}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}$ with $D_y = 1$, and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_y}$ is a single variance. We fix $\beta = 8/3$ and infer $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\sigma, \rho, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$. Here $h$ is linear, so all the nonlinearity is in $f$.

The moment-matched filter. For linear $f$ and $h$ the Kalman filter gives $\log p(\mathbf{y}_{1:T} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})$ exactly. For a nonlinear $f$ the belief about $\mathbf{x}_k$ is no longer Gaussian, and gaussx.nonlinear_kalman_filter keeps it Gaussian by matching moments. With $q(\mathbf{x}_{k-1} \mid \mathbf{y}_{1:k-1}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}; \boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k-1 \mid k-1}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k-1 \mid k-1})$ the filtered belief, the predict step is

$$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid k-1} = \mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{x}_{k-1} \mid \mathbf{y}_{1:k-1})}[f(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta})]$$

$$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid k-1} = \mathbb{V}_{q(\mathbf{x}_{k-1} \mid \mathbf{y}_{1:k-1})}[f(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta})] + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\eta$$

where $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$. The update matches $h$ in the same way at the predicted belief, which gives $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{y,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_y}$ (with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon$ added) and the gain. With $o_k \in \{0, 1\}$ the observation mask, the factor is the sum of the one-step-ahead log densities,

$$\log p(\mathbf{y}_{1:T} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{T} o_k \log \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y}_k; \boldsymbol{\mu}_{y,k}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{y,k})$$

The integrator decides how the expectations are computed. The unscented rule (gaussx.UnscentedIntegrator(alpha=1.0), the factor's default) evaluates $f$ at $2 D_x + 1 = 7$ sigma points spread along the columns of a square root of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k-1 \mid k-1}$ and needs no derivatives. The Taylor rule (gaussx.TaylorIntegrator()) is the extended Kalman filter (EKF): it takes $f(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k-1 \mid k-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta})$ for the mean and $\mathbf{F}_k \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k-1 \mid k-1} \mathbf{F}_k^\top$ in place of the variance of $f$, with $\mathbf{F}_k = \mathbf{J}_f(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k-1 \mid k-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ the Jacobian. Both are exact for affine maps, where the factor equals the Kalman log marginal (the package's tests check this for every deterministic integrator). For a nonlinear $f$ the sum above is a surrogate, and NUTS samples the posterior under that surrogate. The RTS smoother runs backwards over the same moments, with the cross-covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{xf,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ between $\mathbf{x}_k$ and $f(\mathbf{x}_k; \boldsymbol{\theta})$ from the same rule in its gain, and gives $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid T}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid T}$.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: We detect Colab and install pyrox, pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm only when the notebook runs there.

docs.title: 1. Lorenz-63 seen through its first component, with gaps¶
docs.text: We simulate one record from the model itself, so that we know the truth: Lorenz's $\sigma = 10$ and $\rho = 28$, and an observation noise variance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon = 1$. The record has $T = 120$ steps (6 MTU), and we add $T_\text{f} = 20$ steps (1 MTU) after it that we keep for the forecast. We start from a point on the attractor (300 noise-free steps from $(1, 1, 25)$). Then we punch two kinds of gap into the record: a 20-step outage from $t = 3$ to $t = 4$ MTU, and each step missing at random with probability 0.15. The missing steps are NaN, and the mask $o_k$ says which steps are observed.

docs.title: 2. The model as a plain NumPyro function¶
docs.text: The priors say what we would know before seeing the record: a Prandtl number of order 10, a Rayleigh number in the twenties and a noise variance below a few units, all positive. So we take $\sigma \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 8, 0.5^2)$, $\rho \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 25, 0.3^2)$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 0.5, 1^2)$. We take a wide initial state, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,0} = (0, 0, 25)$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,0} = 64 \mathbf{I}_{D_x}$, about the spread of the attractor. Then nonlinear_ssm_factor takes $f$ built from the two sample sites, $h$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\eta$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon$, the record, the initial moments and the mask, and registers the factor "y". The first row of y is $\mathbf{y}_1$, scored after one step from $\mathbf{x}_0$.

docs.title: 3. NUTS, with forward-mode gradients¶
docs.text: NUTS needs the gradient of the log density at every leapfrog step. The filter is a jax.lax.scan over 120 small steps, each with seven RK4 evaluations, so a reverse-mode gradient has to store and replay every one of them. With only three parameters, forward mode (three tangent passes alongside the filter) can be cheaper. We time the log likelihood, its reverse-mode gradient and its forward-mode Jacobian at the truth before choosing.

docs.title: 5. The smoothed state through the gaps, and a forecast¶
docs.text: nonlinear_ssm_factor returns the gaussx FilterState, which holds the filtered and the predicted moments at every step. We pass it to gaussx.nonlinear_rts_smoother with the same $f$ and the same integrator, which gives $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid T}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid T}$. For the forecast we run the filter on all $T + T_\text{f}$ rows of the record, with the last $T_\text{f}$ masked. A masked step only predicts, and the smoother has no data after the record to correct with, so on the forecast steps the smoothed moments are the filter's predictions. We do this at $N_{\mathcal{E}} = 50$ NUTS draws $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}$, $e \in \mathcal{E}$, with jax.vmap. We combine them per component as in Example 1, with the mean over the draws of $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid T}^{(e)}$, and the mean of the variances plus the variance of the means. So the bands carry the uncertainty of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ as well as that of the path. Since we simulated the record, we score them against the true state on the observed steps, the random dropouts, the outage and the forecast.

docs.title: 6. The unscented against the extended Kalman filter¶
docs.text: We now swap the integrator for gaussx.TaylorIntegrator(), the EKF, and keep everything else. We compare the two at the NUTS posterior mean $\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ in three ways. We look at the log likelihood and its cost per evaluation, at the profile of the log likelihood in $\rho$ with $\sigma$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon$ held at their posterior means (81 values, one filter pass each), and at the smoothed state on the outage and the forecast. A second NUTS run under the EKF would answer the same question more fully, but it costs as much as section 3 again.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• A nonlinear state-space model is a plain NumPyro function: priors on $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, the dynamics $f$ built from the sample sites, and nonlinear_ssm_factor("y", f, h, Σ_η, Σ_ε, y, μ_x0, Σ_x0, mask=mask). The default integrator is the unscented rule with alpha=1.0, which needs no derivatives of $f$.
  • NUTS on $(\sigma, \rho, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\varepsilon)$ from 90 noisy observations of $x_1$ took 51.2 s with forward-mode gradients, with no divergences and 5.0 leapfrog steps per draw. All three 90 % intervals contain the truth, and $\rho$ comes out at 28.124 ± 0.460.
  • The FilterState that the factor returns, passed to gaussx.nonlinear_rts_smoother, gives the smoothed state, including the two components that are never observed. Averaged over 50 NUTS draws, the band bridges the 1 MTU outage tightly and opens in the forecast, and it covers every true value in both.
  • The integrator is a modelling choice. The unscented filter and the EKF agree on the record, but their likelihood profiles peak at $\rho = 28.20$ and 27.70, and in the forecast the EKF band covers only 55 % of the true $x_1$.
  • One log likelihood costs 1.38 ms and one forward-mode gradient 4.34 ms at $T = 120$ (the reverse-mode gradient 8.86 ms), so NUTS is the expensive step here.

For linear dynamics, where the Kalman filter is exact, see Example 1. For a state too large to carry a $D_x \times D_x$ covariance, see the ensemble filter of Example 5.

# Shapes: N = 730 days; D_x = 2 (the Matérn-3/2 state)

# ω = 2π / 365.25 days⁻¹, the annual angular frequency
OMEGA = 2.0 * jnp.pi / 365.25


def climatology(t, c, a, b):
    """Seasonal mean μ(t) = c + a cos(ωt) + b sin(ωt)."""
    return c + a * jnp.cos(OMEGA * t) + b * jnp.sin(OMEGA * t)


truth = {
    "mean_temp": 10.0,
    "cos_amp": -8.0,  # coldest near day 0 (1 January)
    "sin_amp": -1.5,
    "variance": 4.0,  # (2 °C)^2
    "lengthscale": 4.0,  # days
    "noise_var": 0.25,  # (0.5 °C)^2
}

N = 2 * 365
# t_k, days since 1 January of year 1
times = jnp.arange(N, dtype=jnp.float64)  # → (N,)

key_f, key_eps, key_gap = jr.split(jr.PRNGKey(2024), 3)
# today (pyrox_ssm)
# k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_f², ℓ) as a linear SDE
sde_true = MaternSDE(truth["variance"], truth["lengthscale"], order=1)
# today (pyrox_ssm)
prior_true = MarkovGPPrior(sde_true, times)
innovations = jr.normal(key_f, (N, prior_true.state_dim))  # → (N, D_x)
# today (pyrox_ssm)
# f(t_k), the SDE run forward from the innovations
f_true = markov_gp_from_innovations(prior_true, innovations)  # (N, D_x) → (N,)
# μ(t_k) = c + a cos(ω t_k) + b sin(ω t_k)
mu_true = climatology(  # (N,) → (N,)
    times, truth["mean_temp"], truth["cos_amp"], truth["sin_amp"]
)
noise_std = jnp.sqrt(truth["noise_var"])  # → ()
# ε_k ~ 𝒩(0, σ_ε²)
obs_noise = noise_std * jr.normal(key_eps, (N,))  # → (N,)
# y_k = μ(t_k) + f(t_k) + ε_k
y_full = mu_true + f_true + obs_noise  # (N,) → (N,)

# late January to early March, year 2
outage = (times >= 395) & (times < 440)  # → (N,) bool
dropout = jr.uniform(key_gap, (N,)) < 0.12  # → (N,) bool
# o_k = 1 on an observed day
mask = ~(outage | dropout)  # → (N,) bool
# what the station file holds
y = jnp.where(mask, y_full, jnp.nan)  # → (N,)

print(f"N = {N} days, observed = {int(mask.sum())}, missing = {int((~mask).sum())}")
print(
    f"  outage: {int(outage.sum())} days, "
    f"random dropouts: {int((dropout & ~outage).sum())} days"
)

def station_model(times, y, mask):
    # Shapes: N = 730 days; D_θ = 6 parameters

    # today (numpyro): the six sample sites of θ
    # c ~ 𝒩(10, 10²)
    c = numpyro.sample("mean_temp", dist.Normal(10.0, 10.0))
    # a ~ 𝒩(0, 10²)
    a = numpyro.sample("cos_amp", dist.Normal(0.0, 10.0))
    # b ~ 𝒩(0, 10²)
    b = numpyro.sample("sin_amp", dist.Normal(0.0, 10.0))
    # σ_f² ~ LogNormal(log 2, 1)
    variance = numpyro.sample("variance", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(2.0), 1.0))
    # ℓ ~ LogNormal(log 7, 1)
    lengthscale = numpyro.sample("lengthscale", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(7.0), 1.0))
    # σ_ε² ~ LogNormal(log 0.1, 1)
    noise_var = numpyro.sample("noise_var", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.1), 1.0))

    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_f², ℓ) as a linear SDE
    sde = MaternSDE(variance=variance, lengthscale=lengthscale, order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # μ + f ~ 𝒢𝒫(μ, k_Matérn-3/2) on the N days
    prior = MarkovGPPrior(sde, times, mean_fn=lambda t: climatology(t, c, a, b))
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # log p(y ∣ θ) = ∑ₖ oₖ log 𝒩(yₖ; μ(tₖ) + H μ_x,k∣k−1, H Σ_x,k∣k−1 Hᵀ + σ_ε²)
    markov_gp_factor("y", prior, y, noise_var, mask=mask)


# today (numpyro)
seeded_model = handlers.seed(station_model, rng_seed=0)
# today (numpyro)
trace = handlers.trace(seeded_model).get_trace(times, y, mask)
for name, site in trace.items():
    kind = "factor" if isinstance(site["fn"], dist.Unit) else type(site["fn"]).__name__
    print(f"site {name!r:14} {kind:<10} value shape={tuple(jnp.shape(site['value']))}")
def station_model(times, y, mask): # Shapes: N = 730 days; D_θ = 6 parameters # today (numpyro): the six sample sites of θ # c ~ 𝒩(10, 10²) c = numpyro.sample("mean_temp", dist.Normal(10.0, 10.0)) # a ~ 𝒩(0, 10²) a = numpyro.sample("cos_amp", dist.Normal(0.0, 10.0)) # b ~ 𝒩(0, 10²) b = numpyro.sample("sin_amp", dist.Normal(0.0, 10.0)) # σ_f² ~ LogNormal(log 2, 1) variance = numpyro.sample("variance", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(2.0), 1.0)) # ℓ ~ LogNormal(log 7, 1) lengthscale = numpyro.sample("lengthscale", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(7.0), 1.0)) # σ_ε² ~ LogNormal(log 0.1, 1) noise_var = numpyro.sample("noise_var", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.1), 1.0)) # today (pyrox_ssm) # k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_f², ℓ) as a linear SDE sde = MaternSDE(variance=variance, lengthscale=lengthscale, order=1) # today (pyrox_ssm) # μ + f ~ 𝒢𝒫(μ, k_Matérn-3/2) on the N days prior = MarkovGPPrior(sde, times, mean_fn=lambda t: climatology(t, c, a, b)) # today (pyrox_ssm) # log p(y ∣ θ) = ∑ₖ oₖ log 𝒩(yₖ; μ(tₖ) + H μ_x,k∣k−1, H Σ_x,k∣k−1 Hᵀ + σ_ε²) markov_gp_factor("y", prior, y, noise_var, mask=mask) # today (numpyro) seeded_model = handlers.seed(station_model, rng_seed=0) # today (numpyro) trace = handlers.trace(seeded_model).get_trace(times, y, mask) for name, site in trace.items(): kind = "factor" if isinstance(site["fn"], dist.Unit) else type(site["fn"]).__name__ print(f"site {name!r:14} {kind:<10} value shape={tuple(jnp.shape(site['value']))}") 
site 'mean_temp'    Normal     value shape=()
site 'cos_amp'      Normal     value shape=()
site 'sin_amp'      Normal     value shape=()
site 'variance'     LogNormal  value shape=()
site 'lengthscale'  LogNormal  value shape=()
site 'noise_var'    LogNormal  value shape=()
site 'y'            factor     value shape=(0,)

So the trace holds six scalar sample sites and one factor. The 730-day latent path is not in the trace at all, because the Kalman filter has integrated it out. This is what makes NUTS cheap on this model, as there is no high-dimensional latent and no funnel between the path and its hyperparameters.

# Shapes: D_θ = 6 parameters; 1,000 guide draws

# today (numpyro)
# q(θ; ν), a full-covariance Gaussian over the unconstrained θ
guide = AutoMultivariateNormal(station_model, init_loc_fn=init_to_median)
# today (optax)
optimizer = optax.adam(0.02)
# today (numpyro)
# ℒ_ELBO(ν) = −ELBO, a Monte Carlo estimate from 2 particles
elbo = Trace_ELBO(num_particles=2)
# today (numpyro)
svi = SVI(station_model, guide, optimizer, elbo)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
# today (numpyro)
# ν⋆ = argmin_ν ℒ_ELBO(ν), 1000 Adam steps
svi_result = svi.run(jr.PRNGKey(3), 1000, times, y, mask, progress_bar=False)
jax.block_until_ready(svi_result.params)
svi_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0
# today (numpyro)
# 1,000 draws θ ~ q(θ; ν⋆)
svi_samples = guide.sample_posterior(  # → {name: (1000,)}
    jr.PRNGKey(4), svi_result.params, sample_shape=(1000,)
)
final_loss = float(svi_result.losses[-100:].mean())  # → ()
print(f"SVI wall-clock: {svi_seconds:.1f} s for 1000 steps x 2 particles")
print(f"final negative ELBO (mean of last 100 steps): {final_loss:.1f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3))
ax.plot(np.asarray(svi_result.losses), "C0", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylim(np.percentile(np.asarray(svi_result.losses), [0, 95]))
ax.set_xlabel("SVI step")
ax.set_ylabel("negative ELBO")
ax.set_title("SVI convergence")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The NUTS and SVI marginals overlap for every parameter, and their posterior means differ by at most 0.12 (the lengthscale, 3.77 against 3.89 days). With the path integrated out, the six-parameter posterior is close enough to Gaussian in the unconstrained space for a full-rank guide to match it. The NUTS 90 % intervals contain four of the six true values and the SVI ones contain five. Both methods put the noise variance $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ low (posterior mean 0.19 against 0.25), and the NUTS interval for the mean temperature stops at 10.05 °C, just above the true 10 °C; both misses are about two posterior standard deviations. Since the two methods agree, these misses belong to this one realisation of the record and not to either fitting method.

def predict_one(theta, t_star):
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    sde = MaternSDE(theta["variance"], theta["lengthscale"], order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    prior = MarkovGPPrior(
        sde,
        times,
        mean_fn=lambda t: climatology(
            t, theta["mean_temp"], theta["cos_amp"], theta["sin_amp"]
        ),
    )
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # p(x_1:N ∣ y; θ⁽ᵉ⁾) by the Kalman filter and RTS smoother
    cond = prior.condition(y, theta["noise_var"], mask=mask)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # μ_*⁽ᵉ⁾, (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)² of μ(t_*) + f(t_*)
    mean, var = cond.predict(t_star)  # (M,) → (M,), (M,)
    # (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + (σ_ε⁽ᵉ⁾)² for a new observation y_*
    obs_var = var + theta["noise_var"]  # → (M,)
    return mean, var, obs_var


def posterior_predict(samples, t_star, n_draws=200):
    num_samples = samples["variance"].shape[0]
    # N_E draws θ⁽ᵉ⁾, evenly spaced through the chain
    idx = jnp.linspace(0, num_samples - 1, n_draws).astype(int)  # → (N_E,)
    draws = {k: v[idx] for k, v in samples.items()}
    # today (jax)
    predict_draws = jax.vmap(predict_one, in_axes=(0, None))
    # today (jax)
    predict_draws = jax.jit(predict_draws)
    # μ_*⁽ᵉ⁾, (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)², (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + (σ_ε⁽ᵉ⁾)²
    means, f_vars, y_vars = predict_draws(draws, t_star)  # → 3 × (N_E, M)
    # μ̄_* = (1/N_E) ∑ₑ μ_*⁽ᵉ⁾
    mean = einx.mean("member test -> test", means)  # (N_E, M) → (M,)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (μ_*⁽ᵉ⁾ − μ̄_*)²
    spread = einx.var("member test -> test", means)  # (N_E, M) → (M,)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)²
    f_var_mean = einx.mean("member test -> test", f_vars)  # (N_E, M) → (M,)
    # 𝕍[μ(t_*) + f(t_*) ∣ y] ≈ (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + spread
    f_var = f_var_mean + spread  # → (M,)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ ((σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + (σ_ε⁽ᵉ⁾)²)
    y_var_mean = einx.mean("member test -> test", y_vars)  # (N_E, M) → (M,)
    # the same for a new observation y_*
    y_var = y_var_mean + spread  # → (M,)
    return mean, f_var, y_var

Inside the outage, the band widens to the climatology plus the stationary anomaly spread within a few lengthscales of its edges. The posterior mean relaxes to the seasonal cycle, and the same happens in the forecast after the last day. Short random gaps barely widen the band, because the neighbouring days pin the anomaly down. The SVI band lies on top of the NUTS one.

def time_grad(n, repeats=10):
    # Shapes: n days (N, 4N or 16N); D_θ = 3 log parameters (σ_f², ℓ, σ_ε²)
    t = jnp.arange(n, dtype=jnp.float64)  # → (n,)
    noise = jr.normal(jr.PRNGKey(0), (n,))  # → (n,)
    obs = jnp.sin(OMEGA * t) + noise  # → (n,)
    all_observed = jnp.ones(n, dtype=bool)  # → (n,) bool

    def neg_log_marginal(log_params):
        params = jnp.exp(log_params)  # → (3,)
        # today (pyrox_ssm)
        sde = MaternSDE(params[0], params[1], order=1)
        # today (pyrox_ssm)
        prior = MarkovGPPrior(sde, t)
        # today (pyrox_ssm)
        # ℒ_NLL(θ) = −log p(y; θ), one Kalman filter pass
        log_marginal = prior.log_marginal(obs, params[2], mask=all_observed)
        return -log_marginal

    # today (jax)
    # ℒ_NLL(θ) and ∇_θ ℒ_NLL, jitted once
    loss_and_grad = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(neg_log_marginal))
    log_params = jnp.log(jnp.array([4.0, 4.0, 0.25]))  # → (3,)
    jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(log_params))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(log_params))
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / repeats

The time per day stays flat while the record grows sixteen-fold, so one log density and its gradient scale linearly in $N$. A dense GP would pay an $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ Cholesky on every one of them. NUTS is the expensive step because it evaluates the gradient thousands of times (the leapfrog count above, plus warm-up). SVI needs about a thousand evaluations per particle, and the posterior predictive is a few filter-and-smoother passes per draw, vectorised over the draws.

docs.title: One site, end to end: a station record with NUTS, SVI and prediction through the gaps¶
docs.text:
This is the shortest complete pyrox-ssm workflow. We take one station with one daily series that has gaps, write one NumPyro model, fit it with two inference methods and draw a posterior predictive through the missing days. The later examples (many sites, a shared regional signal, non-Gaussian counts, ensembles, nonlinear dynamics) all start from this model and change one piece of it.

pyrox-ssm capability shown: markov_gp_factor with mask=, which adds the Kalman-filter marginal likelihood of a Markov GP as a NumPyro factor and leaves the missing observations out, and MarkovGPPrior.condition(...).predict(...), which gives the smoothed posterior at arbitrary times. Cost: every log-density evaluation is one Kalman filter pass, $\mathcal{O}(N D_x^3)$ in the record length $N$ and the state dimension $D_x$. We measure the wall-clock times for NUTS, SVI and one gradient in section 7.

What you'll learn:

  1. How to write a Markov-GP regression as a plain NumPyro function, with a mean function and a mask for missing days.
  2. How to fit it with NUTS and with SVI, and how their hyperparameter posteriors compare with the truth.
  3. How to predict the latent signal and new observations at dense times, through the gaps, averaged over the posterior.

For the Kalman recursions themselves see Kalman filtering and RTS smoothing. For maximum likelihood, mean-field versus full-rank guides and what a record can identify, see Training a Markov GP.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
Our toy record is the daily mean air temperature $y_k$ (°C) at one station, where $t_k$ is the $k$-th day of the record, $k = 1, \ldots, N$. We model it as a seasonal climatology plus a weather anomaly plus sensor noise,

$$y_k = \mu(t_k) + f(t_k) + \varepsilon_k$$

$$\mu(t) = c + a \cos(\omega t) + b \sin(\omega t)$$

where $c, a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ (°C) set the climatology and $\omega = 2\pi / 365.25 \text{ days}^{-1}$. The anomaly is a Matérn-3/2 GP and the noise is independent and Gaussian,

$$f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(t, t'; \sigma_f^2, \ell))$$

$$\varepsilon_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$$

with the kernel variance $\sigma_f^2$, the lengthscale $\ell$ (days) and the noise variance $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ all in $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$. The Matérn-3/2 kernel has an exact state-space form with a two-dimensional state $\mathbf{x}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$, $D_x = 2$. So the Kalman filter gives us the marginal likelihood with $f$ integrated out. A day without an observation runs only the filter's predict step. So with $o_k \in \{0, 1\}$ the observation mask,

$$\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} o_k \log \mathcal{N}(y_k; \mu(t_k) + \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid k-1}, \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid k-1} \mathbf{H}^\top + \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$$

where $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ is the record, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ are the one-step-ahead mean and covariance of the state, $\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times D_x}$ is the measurement row, and $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (c, a, b, \sigma_f^2, \ell, \sigma_\varepsilon^2) \in \mathbb{R}^{6}$ are the six parameters that NUTS and SVI infer.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: We detect Colab and install pyrox, pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm only when the notebook runs there.

docs.title: 1. A station record with gaps¶
docs.text: We use two years of daily values, drawn from the model itself so that we know the true parameters: a 10 °C mean with an 8 °C annual cycle, a 2 °C weather anomaly that decorrelates over about four days, and 0.5 °C sensor noise. We simulate the anomaly path with markov_gp_from_innovations, which runs the SDE forward from standard normal innovations in linear time. Then we punch two kinds of gap into it: a 45-day logger outage in the second winter, and each day missing at random with probability 0.12. We store the missing days as NaN, as they would be in a real file, and the mask $o_k$ says which days are observed.

docs.title: 2. The model as a plain NumPyro function¶
docs.text: Every parameter is an ordinary numpyro.sample site. We choose priors that say what a climatologist would say before seeing this station: a mean somewhere within $\pm 20$ °C of 10 °C, a seasonal amplitude of up to about 10 °C, an anomaly of a couple of degrees that lasts about a week, and sensor noise well below a degree. We pass the mean function to MarkovGPPrior as mean_fn. Then markov_gp_factor adds the masked Kalman log marginal as a factor site named "y". The NaNs in y are safe, because masked entries are zeroed before any arithmetic, so they reach neither the value nor the gradient.

docs.title: 3. NUTS¶
docs.text: We run two chains of 300 draws after 200 warm-up steps with a dense mass matrix (dense_mass=True). So warm-up adapts to the correlations between the six unconstrained parameters and not only to their scales. With six parameters the $6 \times 6$ matrix costs nothing next to the filter. The wall-clock time includes JIT compilation.

docs.title: 4. SVI with a full-rank Gaussian guide¶
docs.text: AutoMultivariateNormal fits a Gaussian over the six unconstrained parameters with a full covariance, so it can represent the correlations between them (Training a Markov GP shows what a mean-field guide loses). We keep the same model as for NUTS. Its guide is $q( oldsymbol{ heta}; oldsymbol{ u})$, with the variational parameters $ oldsymbol{ u}$ (the Gaussian's mean and covariance), and SVI minimises the negative ELBO, $\mathcal{L}_ ext{ELBO}( oldsymbol{ u}) = -\mathrm{ELBO}$. We start the guide at the prior medians (init_to_median) rather than at the autoguide default of random points in $[-2, 2]$ in the unconstrained space. From a random start the climatology mean $c$ begins far from 10 °C, and the optimiser can settle in a poor local optimum where a long-lengthscale anomaly and a large noise variance absorb the misfit.

docs.title: 5. The two posteriors against the truth¶
docs.text: For each parameter we print the posterior mean, standard deviation and 90 % interval from NUTS and from SVI, next to the value we simulated the data with.

docs.title: 6. Prediction through the gaps¶
docs.text:
For one parameter draw, MarkovGPPrior.condition(y, noise_var, mask=mask) runs the filter and RTS smoother and returns a ConditionedMarkovGP. Its predict(t_star) gives the posterior mean and variance of the latent $\mu(t_*) + f(t_*)$ at any test times $t_*$. It re-runs the smoother over the merged grid with the test times masked out of the update. The conditioned GP keeps the mask, so the missing days stay unobserved. We do this for $N_{\mathcal{E}} = 200$ NUTS draws $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}$, $e \in \mathcal{E}$, at once with jax.vmap and average them, so the bands carry the hyperparameter uncertainty as well as the uncertainty of the path. With $\mu_*^{(e)} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $(\sigma_*^{(e)})^2 \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ the posterior mean and variance under draw $e$,

$$\mathbb{E}[\mu(t_*) + f(t_*) \mid \mathbf{y}] \approx \bar{\mu}_* = \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} \mu_*^{(e)}$$

$$\mathbb{V}[\mu(t_*) + f(t_*) \mid \mathbf{y}] \approx \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} (\sigma_*^{(e)})^2 + \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} (\mu_*^{(e)} - \bar{\mu}_*)^2$$

and a new observation $y_*$ adds $(\sigma_\varepsilon^{(e)})^2$ to each $(\sigma_*^{(e)})^2$. The dense grid has a test time every six hours over the record and for 30 days beyond its end.

docs.title: 7. Cost¶
docs.text: Each NUTS leapfrog step and each SVI particle costs one Kalman filter pass over the $N$ days plus its reverse-mode gradient, which is $\mathcal{O}(N D_x^3)$ with $D_x = 2$ for Matérn-3/2. In the cell below we time one jitted log density and gradient at this record's length and at records of the same daily station that are 4 and 16 times longer. So we measure the linear scaling rather than assert it. For the crossover against the dense $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ Cholesky path, see section 4 of Kalman filtering and RTS smoothing.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• A Markov-GP regression for one station is a plain NumPyro function: priors on the SDE kernel, the mean function and the noise, then markov_gp_factor(..., mask=mask). Missing days are a mask, not a reindexing, and NaN placeholders are safe.
  • The trace holds only the six parameters, as the Kalman filter integrates the latent path out. So NUTS and SVI both run on a six-dimensional posterior. Here they agree with each other, and their 90 % intervals contain four (NUTS) and five (SVI) of the six true values.
  • MarkovGPPrior.condition(..., mask=mask).predict(t_star) gives the smoothed posterior at any times, inside gaps and beyond the record. Averaging it over posterior draws gives bands that include the hyperparameter uncertainty.
  • Every step is linear in the record length.

The next examples change one piece of this model at a time: many sites with pooled hyperparameters, a regional signal shared between sites, and non-Gaussian observations. For the kernels in state-space form see Matérn kernels in state-space form.

    "regional_variance": 4.0,  # (2 °C)^2

    "local_variance": 1.0,  # (1 °C)^2
    "local_lengthscale": 2.0,  # days
    "noise_var": 0.25,  # (0.5 °C)^2
}
N_DAYS = 135
LAST_REPORT = 120  # stations report on days 0, …, 119; the rest is a forecast

# (first day, last day + 1, outage or None, extra dropout rate, reading interval)
schedule = [
    (0, 120, None, 0.0, 1),
    (0, 120, (80, 100), 0.0, 1),
    (10, 111, None, 0.0, 2),
    (30, 120, None, 0.3, 1),
    (0, 81, None, 0.0, 1),
]
n_stations = len(schedule)

# every simulated day, t = 0, …, 134
days = jnp.arange(N_DAYS, dtype=jnp.float64)  # → (N_days,)
key_g, key_h, key_eps, key_gap = jr.split(jr.PRNGKey(2026), 4)

# today (pyrox_ssm)
# k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_g², ℓ_g) as a linear SDE
regional_sde_true = MaternSDE(
    truth["regional_variance"], truth["regional_lengthscale"], order=1
)
# today (pyrox_ssm)
regional_prior = MarkovGPPrior(regional_sde_true, days)
innovations_g = jr.normal(key_g, (N_DAYS, regional_prior.state_dim))
# today (pyrox_ssm)
# g(t), the SDE run forward from the innovations
g_true = markov_gp_from_innovations(regional_prior, innovations_g)  # → (N_days,)

# today (pyrox_ssm)
# k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_h², ℓ_h) as a linear SDE
local_sde_true = MaternSDE(truth["local_variance"], truth["local_lengthscale"], order=1)
# today (pyrox_ssm)
local_prior = MarkovGPPrior(local_sde_true, days)
innovations_h = jr.normal(key_h, (n_stations, N_DAYS, local_prior.state_dim))
# today (jax)
local_paths = jax.vmap(markov_gp_from_innovations, in_axes=(None, 0))
# today (pyrox_ssm)
# h_n(t) for every station, from independent innovations
h_true = local_paths(local_prior, innovations_h)  # (N_Ω, N_days, D_h) → (N_Ω, N_days)

# g(t) + h_n(t), the anomaly each station would see
signal_true = einx.add("d, n d -> n d", g_true, h_true)  # → (N_Ω, N_days)
noise_std = jnp.sqrt(truth["noise_var"])  # → ()
# ε_n(t) ~ 𝒩(0, σ_ε²)
obs_noise = noise_std * jr.normal(key_eps, (n_stations, N_DAYS))  # → (N_Ω, N_days)
# y_n(t) = g(t) + h_n(t) + ε_n(t), on every day
y_true = signal_true + obs_noise  # → (N_Ω, N_days)

gap_keys = jr.split(key_gap, n_stations)
times_per_station, y_per_station, reported_per_station = [], [], []
for n, (first, end, outage, extra, interval) in enumerate(schedule):
    # the days the station was due to report
    due = (days >= first) & (days < end) & ((days - first) % interval == 0)
    # a due day is reported unless it drops out or falls in the outage
    kept = jr.uniform(gap_keys[n], (N_DAYS,)) >= 0.08 + extra  # → (N_days,) bool
    in_outage = jnp.zeros(N_DAYS, dtype=bool)  # → (N_days,) bool
    if outage is not None:
        in_outage = (days >= outage[0]) & (days < outage[1])  # → (N_days,) bool
    reported = due & kept & ~in_outage  # → (N_days,) bool
    reported_per_station.append(reported)
    times_per_station.append(days[reported])
    y_per_station.append(y_true[n][reported])
reported_true = jnp.stack(reported_per_station)  # → (N_Ω, N_days) bool

record_lengths = [int(t_n.shape[0]) for t_n in times_per_station]
print(f"{'station':<9}{'first day':>10}{'last day':>10}{'N_n':>6}")

Unlike Example 2's padded rows, every column of the mask is the same day at every station, which is what lets the regional block of the state link the stations day by day. A day with three stations reporting is one Kalman update with three rows of $\mathbf{H}$.

As a check of the exactness claim, we compare log_marginal at the true parameters with the dense Gaussian over all the observed (day, station) pairs, whose covariance is $k_g(t, t') + [n = n'] k_h(t, t') + [n = n', t = t'] \sigma_\varepsilon^2$ for the pairs $(t, n)$ and $(t', n')$. The dense one builds the Matérn-3/2 kernel matrices with kernellib and evaluates the Gaussian with gaussx, on a matrix with one row per observation.

def network_model(times, mask, y_grid):
    # Shapes: T merged days; N_Ω = 5 stations; D_θ = 5 parameters

    # today (numpyro): the five sample sites of θ
    # σ_g² ~ LogNormal(log 2, 1)
    regional_variance = numpyro.sample(
        "regional_variance", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(2.0), 1.0)
    )
    # ℓ_g ~ LogNormal(log 7, 1)
    regional_lengthscale = numpyro.sample(
        "regional_lengthscale", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(7.0), 1.0)
    )
    # σ_h² ~ LogNormal(log 2, 1)
    local_variance = numpyro.sample("local_variance", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(2.0), 1.0))
    # ℓ_h ~ LogNormal(log 7, 1)
    local_lengthscale = numpyro.sample(
        "local_lengthscale", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(7.0), 1.0)
    )
    # σ_ε² ~ LogNormal(log 0.1, 1)
    noise_var = numpyro.sample("noise_var", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.1), 1.0))

    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_g², ℓ_g) as a linear SDE
    regional_sde = MaternSDE(regional_variance, regional_lengthscale, order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_h², ℓ_h), pooled over the stations
    local_sde = MaternSDE(local_variance, local_lengthscale, order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # x_k = (x_g,k, x_h,1,k, …, x_h,N_Ω,k) on the merged grid
    network = SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP(regional_sde, local_sde, times, mask)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # log p(Y ∣ θ) = ∑ₖ log 𝒩(y_𝒪ₖ; H_𝒪ₖ μ_x,k∣k−1, H_𝒪ₖ Σ_x,k∣k−1 H_𝒪ₖᵀ + σ_ε² I)
    log_marginal = network.log_marginal(y_grid, noise_var)  # (T, N_Ω) → ()
    # today (numpyro)
    numpyro.factor("y", log_marginal)

Four of the five 90 % intervals contain the true value. The local kernel is the best determined, with $\sigma_h^2$ at 1.12 ± 0.17 (true 1) and $\ell_h$ at 1.69 ± 0.24 days (true 2), because every station contributes its own local path to it. The regional kernel is much less certain, $\sigma_g^2$ at 3.81 ± 1.38 (true 4) and $\ell_g$ at 6.92 ± 1.46 days (true 8). There is only one regional path, and 120 days of it span only 15 of its lengthscales. The miss is the noise variance, at 0.14 ± 0.06 against 0.25, with an interval that stops at 0.233. The local anomaly and the noise are both fast and both private to a station, so the posterior trades a little of the noise for a slightly shorter and larger local anomaly, as we see in the two local rows.

def decompose_one(theta):
    # Shapes: M test times; N_Ω stations; D_x = D_g + N_Ω D_h
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    regional_sde = MaternSDE(
        theta["regional_variance"], theta["regional_lengthscale"], order=1
    )
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    local_sde = MaternSDE(theta["local_variance"], theta["local_lengthscale"], order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # the model on 𝒯_y ∪ 𝒯_*, test times masked out of the update
    network = SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP(regional_sde, local_sde, t_dense, dense_mask)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # 𝔼[g(t_*) ∣ Y; θ⁽ᵉ⁾], 𝔼[h_n(t_*) ∣ Y; θ⁽ᵉ⁾]
    g_mean, h_mean = network.decompose(y_dense, theta["noise_var"])  # → (M,), (M, N_Ω)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    lgssm = network.as_lgssm(theta["noise_var"])
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # Σ_x,*∣T, the smoothed covariance of the joint state
    _, state_cov, _ = lgssm.smooth(y_dense, mask=network.mask)  # → (M, D_x, D_x)
    obs_rows = lgssm.obs_model  # → (N_Ω, D_x)
    # 1 on the regional block of the state, 0 on the local blocks
    in_regional = jnp.arange(network.state_dim) < network.shared.state_dim
    # h_g, the regional block of any row of H
    regional_row = obs_rows[0] * in_regional  # → (D_x,)
    # h_h,n = h_n − h_g, station n's local block
    local_rows = obs_rows - regional_row  # → (N_Ω, D_x)
    # h_gᵀ Σ_x,*∣T h_g
    g_var = einx.dot(  # → (M,)
        "m d e, d, e -> m", state_cov, regional_row, regional_row
    )
    # h_h,nᵀ Σ_x,*∣T h_h,n
    h_var = einx.dot(  # → (M, N_Ω)
        "m d e, n d, n e -> m n", state_cov, local_rows, local_rows
    )
    # h_nᵀ Σ_x,*∣T h_n, the variance of g + h_n
    total_var = einx.dot(  # → (M, N_Ω)
        "m d e, n d, n e -> m n", state_cov, obs_rows, obs_rows
    )
    # 𝔼[g + h_n ∣ Y; θ⁽ᵉ⁾]
    total_mean = einx.add("m, m n -> m n", g_mean, h_mean)  # → (M, N_Ω)
    return {
        "g_mean": g_mean,
        "g_var": g_var,
        "h_mean": h_mean,
        "h_var": h_var,
        "total_mean": total_mean,
        "total_var": total_var,
        "noise_var": theta["noise_var"],
    }


def mixture(means, variances):
    """Mean and variance of the equal-weight mixture over the draw axis."""
    # μ̄_* = (1/N_E) ∑ₑ μ_*⁽ᵉ⁾
    mean = einx.mean("member ... -> ...", means)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (μ_*⁽ᵉ⁾ − μ̄_*)²
    spread = einx.var("member ... -> ...", means)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)²
    variance_mean = einx.mean("member ... -> ...", variances)
    # 𝕍 ≈ (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + spread
    return mean, variance_mean + spread


def draws_from(samples):
    """N_E draws evenly spaced through the chains."""
    num_samples = samples["noise_var"].shape[0]
    idx = jnp.linspace(0, num_samples - 1, N_DRAWS).astype(int)  # → (N_E,)
    return {name: values[idx] for name, values in samples.items()}

Inside each record the band is narrow and follows the observations. The interesting part is where a station has no data. During station 2's outage (days 80 to 99) the posterior mean follows the cold spell that stations 1, 3 and 4 saw, and the right-hand panel shows why: the regional part stays as narrow as elsewhere, while the station's local part falls back to zero with its prior band of $\pm 2 \sigma_h$. The same happens before station 4 starts and after station 5 stops. Station 3 is read every second day, and between two readings its band barely widens. In the forecast after day 119 the regional and the local parts both relax to zero.

The regional signal on its own, with every station's anomalies behind it, is the same green band as in the right-hand panels. No station measures $g$ directly, and yet the posterior mean follows the true path through every regional swing of the reporting days, including the cold spell around day 90, because the local parts of different stations average out. In the forecast it relaxes towards zero and its band widens to the prior spread.

Because the data are simulated, we know the regional and the local paths on every day and the value each station would have reported on every day it missed. The local part of a station is scored over the days from its first to its last report.

def score(mean, sd, target, sel):
    """RMSE of the mean and the fraction of the target inside ±2σ, on sel."""
    # r = target − mean
    residual = np.asarray(target)[sel] - np.asarray(mean)[sel]
    # RMSE = √(mean of r²)
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(residual**2)))
    # fraction of days with |r| < 2σ
    cover = float(np.mean(np.abs(residual) < 2.0 * np.asarray(sd)[sel]))
    return rmse, cover

Over the reporting days the posterior mean of the regional signal is 0.47 °C RMSE from the truth, and the truth is inside its $\pm 2\sigma$ band on 97.5 % of the days. The local parts are harder to recover, with RMSEs of 0.52 to 0.74 °C and coverage between 93.8 and 98.3 %, because each of them is a 1 °C signal that decorrelates over two days and that only one station sees. The largest local error is at station 2, whose local part is unconstrained during its 20-day outage. In the forecast the regional RMSE grows to 1.18 °C, and its band contains the truth on all 15 days.

For the predictions we score every day a station did not report, against the value it would have reported, $y_{n,*} = g + h_n + \varepsilon_n$. We split these days into four kinds: station 2's outage, the isolated gaps inside a record (random dropouts and station 3's days between readings), the reporting days outside a station's own record (before station 3 or 4 started, after station 3 or 5 stopped), when the other stations were still reporting, and the 15-day forecast after day 119.

def station_log_marginal(t_n, y_n, o_n, variance, lengthscale, noise_var):
    # Shapes: N padded steps; D_h = 2
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_f², ℓ) as a linear SDE
    sde = MaternSDE(variance, lengthscale, order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    prior = MarkovGPPrior(sde, t_n)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # log p(y_n ∣ σ_f², ℓ, σ_ε²) by station n's own Kalman filter
    return prior.log_marginal(y_n, noise_var, mask=o_n)  # (N,) → ()


def independent_model(times, y, mask):
    # Shapes: N_Ω = 5 stations; N padded steps; D_θ = 3 parameters

    # today (numpyro): Example 1's priors, pooled over the stations
    # σ_f² ~ LogNormal(log 2, 1)
    variance = numpyro.sample("variance", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(2.0), 1.0))
    # ℓ ~ LogNormal(log 7, 1)
    lengthscale = numpyro.sample("lengthscale", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(7.0), 1.0))
    # σ_ε² ~ LogNormal(log 0.1, 1)
    noise_var = numpyro.sample("noise_var", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.1), 1.0))
    # today (jax)
    per_station = jax.vmap(station_log_marginal, in_axes=(0, 0, 0, None, None, None))
    # log p(y_n ∣ ·) for n = 1, …, N_Ω
    log_marginals = per_station(  # (N_Ω, N) → (N_Ω,)
        times, y, mask, variance, lengthscale, noise_var
    )
    # log p(Y ∣ ·) = ∑ₙ log p(y_n ∣ ·)
    log_likelihood = einx.sum("n ->", log_marginals)  # (N_Ω,) → ()
    # today (numpyro)
    numpyro.factor("y", log_likelihood)

def predict_station(theta, t_n, y_n, o_n, t_star):
    # Shapes: N padded steps; M test times
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    sde = MaternSDE(theta["variance"], theta["lengthscale"], order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    prior = MarkovGPPrior(sde, t_n)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # p(x_n,1:N ∣ y_n; θ⁽ᵉ⁾) by the Kalman filter and RTS smoother
    cond = prior.condition(y_n, theta["noise_var"], mask=o_n)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # μ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾, (σ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾)² of f_n(t_*)
    mean, var = cond.predict(t_star)  # (M,) → (M,), (M,)
    # (σ_n,*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + (σ_ε⁽ᵉ⁾)² for a new observation y_n,*
    obs_var = var + theta["noise_var"]  # → (M,)
    return mean, var, obs_var

Inside the records the two models agree, with an RMSE of 0.77 and 0.79 °C on the isolated gaps, because a station's own neighbouring days pin its value down in either model. Away from a station's own data they differ a lot. During station 2's outage the independent model relaxes to zero within a few days, while the station's true anomaly goes down to −6 °C, so its RMSE is 2.63 °C against 1.11 °C for the joint model, and its band holds only 90 % of the withheld values. On the days outside a station's own record the RMSE is 2.74 against 1.08 °C, and the coverage of the independent band drops to 84.3 %. Its band has the right width for one day, but the days outside a record are not independent, and in a cold spell most of them miss on the same side. In the forecast neither model has data, and the two are close (1.48 against 1.61 °C).

def time_grad(n_rows, repeats=10):
    # Shapes: n_rows stations; T merged days; D_x = 2 + 2 n_rows; 5 log parameters
    copies = -(-n_rows // n_stations)
    # the network's mask and records, repeated to n_rows stations
    mask_rows = jnp.tile(grid_mask, (1, copies))[:, :n_rows]  # → (T, n_rows)
    y_rows = jnp.tile(y_grid, (1, copies))[:, :n_rows]  # → (T, n_rows)

    def neg_log_marginal(log_params):
        params = jnp.exp(log_params)  # → (5,)
        # today (pyrox_ssm)
        regional_sde = MaternSDE(params[0], params[1], order=1)
        # today (pyrox_ssm)
        local_sde = MaternSDE(params[2], params[3], order=1)
        # today (pyrox_ssm)
        network = SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP(regional_sde, local_sde, grid_times, mask_rows)
        # ℒ_NLL(θ) = −log p(Y ∣ θ)
        return -network.log_marginal(y_rows, params[4])

    # today (jax)
    # ℒ_NLL(θ) and ∇_θ ℒ_NLL, jitted once
    loss_and_grad = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(neg_log_marginal))
    log_params = jnp.log(jnp.array(list(truth.values())))  # → (5,)
    jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(log_params))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(log_params))
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / repeats


def time_grad_independent(n_rows, repeats=10):
    # Shapes: n_rows stations; N padded steps; 3 log parameters
    copies = -(-n_rows // n_stations)
    t_rows = jnp.tile(padded_times, (copies, 1))[:n_rows]  # → (n_rows, N)
    y_rows = jnp.tile(padded_y, (copies, 1))[:n_rows]  # → (n_rows, N)
    o_rows = jnp.tile(padded_mask, (copies, 1))[:n_rows]  # → (n_rows, N)
