        params = jnp.exp(log_params)  # → (3,)
        # today (jax)
        per_station = jax.vmap(
            station_log_marginal, in_axes=(0, 0, 0, None, None, None)
        )
        log_marginals = per_station(  # (n_rows, N) → (n_rows,)
            t_rows, y_rows, o_rows, params[0], params[1], params[2]
        )
        # ℒ_NLL = −∑ₙ log p(y_n ∣ ·)
        return -einx.sum("n ->", log_marginals)

    # today (jax)
    loss_and_grad = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(neg_log_likelihood))
    log_params = jnp.log(jnp.array([5.0, 4.0, 0.25]))  # → (3,)
    jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(log_params))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(log_params))
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / repeats

One log density and its gradient cost 12.07 ms for this network of five stations ($D_x = 12$), against 3.96 ms for Example 2's five independent filters, so the joint model costs 3.0 times as much per gradient. It also needs more gradients, 10.2 leapfrog steps per draw against 4.9, as its posterior has five parameters instead of three, and the joint fit took 58.4 s against 18.3 s. The decomposition of 100 draws on the 270-point grid took 3.9 s, including JIT compilation.

With growing networks the joint gradient went from 4.03 ms for one station ($D_x = 4$) to 45.62 ms for 20 stations ($D_x = 42$), while the independent filters went from 2.40 to 10.85 ms. Between 10 and 20 stations the joint time grew by a factor of 2.3, whereas $D_x^3$ grew by $(42/22)^3 \approx 7$, so at these sizes the fixed cost of each filter step still outweighs the $D_x^3$ term. We did not time networks beyond 20 stations. The docstring of SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP points to gaussx's mean-field Kalman filter, which ignores the posterior correlation between the regional and the local parts, and to an ensemble Kalman filter for the point where $D_x^3$ does dominate.

docs.title: Regional plus local: one signal shared by every station and one signal per station¶
docs.text:
Example 2 gave every station its own weather anomaly and let the stations share only their hyperparameters. However, stations a few tens of kilometres apart see the same weather systems pass over them, so a large part of their anomalies is one regional signal. Here we split each station's anomaly into a slow regional part that every station shares and a faster local part of its own. The regional part couples the stations, so they can no longer be fitted one at a time. We put all of them into one state-space model on the merged grid of the days that any station reported, with SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP, and the Kalman filter integrates out the regional path and every local path at once. A station's gaps are then filled by its neighbours, and the posterior splits each record into its regional and local parts.

pyrox-ssm capability shown: SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP.from_sites, which merges ragged station records onto one grid with a (T, N_Ω) mask, log_marginal, which is the exact Kalman log marginal of the observed (day, station) pairs under one block-diagonal linear-Gaussian SSM, and decompose together with as_lgssm(...).smooth(...), which give the posterior of the regional and the local parts. Cost: every log-density evaluation is one Kalman filter pass over the $T$ merged days with a state of dimension $D_x = D_g + N_\Omega D_h$, so $\mathcal{O}(T D_x^3)$, cubic in the number of stations $N_\Omega$. We measure the wall-clock times of the fits, of the predictions and of one gradient for growing networks in section 8.

What you'll learn:

  1. How to write a regional-plus-local model for a station network as a plain NumPyro function, with from_sites for the merged grid and log_marginal as one factor.
  2. How to recover the regional signal and each station's local signal, with their uncertainty, from the posterior averaged over the NUTS draws.
  3. How the regional signal lets the network predict a station through its outages and after it stops, compared with Example 2's model, in which the stations do not share their anomalies.

The single-station model, its priors and the Kalman marginal likelihood are explained in Example 1, and the ragged records and pad_sites in Example 2. We reuse both here without deriving them again.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
The network is again a set $\Omega_y$ of $N_\Omega \equiv N_{\Omega_y}$ stations, indexed by $n = 1, \ldots, N_\Omega$, and station $n$ reported on the days $\mathcal{T}_{y,n}$. We work with daily mean temperature anomalies (°C), each station's record minus its climatology, which we take as known (it is Example 2's $c_n + \mu(t)$). The anomaly that Example 2 modelled as one independent GP $f_n$ per station is now a regional anomaly $g$, shared by every station, plus a local anomaly $h_n$,

$$y_n(t) = g(t) + h_n(t) + \varepsilon_n(t)$$

$$g \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(t, t'; \sigma_g^2, \ell_g))$$

$$h_n \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(t, t'; \sigma_h^2, \ell_h))$$

$$\varepsilon_n(t) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$$

with $g$, $h_1, \ldots, h_{N_\Omega}$ and the noise all independent. The kernel variances $\sigma_g^2$ and $\sigma_h^2$ (°C²), the lengthscales $\ell_g$ and $\ell_h$ (days) and the noise variance $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ (°C²) are all in $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, and the local kernel is pooled over the stations, so $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\sigma_g^2, \ell_g, \sigma_h^2, \ell_h, \sigma_\varepsilon^2) \in \mathbb{R}^{5}$ are the five parameters that NUTS infers. We expect the regional signal to be the slower and the larger of the two, but the model does not impose it.

Because $g$ is shared, the stations are no longer independent given $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, and Example 2's one filter per station does not apply. Instead we merge the station days into one grid, $\mathcal{T}_y = \bigcup_n \mathcal{T}_{y,n} = \{t_1 < \ldots < t_T\}$ with $T \equiv N_{\mathcal{T}_y}$, on which the day index $k$ is the same for every station. So station $n$'s anomaly on day $t_k$ is $y_{n,k}$, observed when the mask $o_{n,k} \in \{0, 1\}$ is 1. The state stacks the Matérn-3/2 states of $g$ and of every $h_n$,

$$\mathbf{x}_k = (\mathbf{x}_{g,k}, \mathbf{x}_{h,1,k}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{h,N_\Omega,k}) \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{g,k}, \mathbf{x}_{h,n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$, so $D_g = D_h = 2$ and $D_x = D_g + N_\Omega D_h$. The independent processes give block-diagonal transitions and model noise covariances,

$$\mathbf{F}_k = \mathrm{blockdiag}(\mathbf{F}_{g,k}, \mathbf{F}_{h,1,k}, \ldots, \mathbf{F}_{h,N_\Omega,k})$$

with $\mathbf{F}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\eta,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ and each block the discretisation of its SDE over $\Delta t_k = t_k - t_{k-1}$ (Example 1), and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\eta,k}$ built in the same way. Station $n$ observes the sum of the regional block and its own block, so row $n$ of the measurement matrix $\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\Omega \times D_x}$ is $(\mathbf{H}_g, \mathbf{0}, \ldots, \mathbf{H}_h, \ldots, \mathbf{0})$, with $\mathbf{H}_g, \mathbf{H}_h \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 2}$ the Matérn-3/2 measurement rows and $\mathbf{H}_h$ in block $n$. On day $t_k$ only the stations $\mathcal{O}_k = \{n : o_{n,k} = 1\}$ reported, and the Kalman filter updates with those rows only. With $\mathbf{y}_{\mathcal{O}_k} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathcal{O}_k}}$ their anomalies and $\mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{O}_k} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathcal{O}_k} \times D_x}$ their rows of $\mathbf{H}$,

$$\log p(\mathbf{Y} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{k=1}^{T} \log \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathcal{O}_k}; \mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{O}_k} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid k-1}, \mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{O}_k} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid k-1} \mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{O}_k}^\top + \sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I}_{N_{\mathcal{O}_k}})$$

where $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times N_\Omega}$ holds the anomalies with one row per merged day and one column per station, and $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,k \mid k-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ are the one-step-ahead moments of the joint state. This is the dense Gaussian of all the observed (day, station) pairs, computed in $\mathcal{O}(T D_x^3)$ instead of $\mathcal{O}((\sum_n N_n)^3)$, where $N_n \equiv \vert \mathcal{T}_{y,n} \vert$.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: We detect Colab and install pyrox, pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm only when the notebook runs there.

docs.title: 1. A network that shares its weather¶
docs.text:
We simulate 135 days of a five-station network from the model itself, so that we know every true value. The regional anomaly has Example 1's 2 °C spread but decorrelates over about eight days, as a passing weather system would. Each station adds a local anomaly of 1 °C that decorrelates over about two days, and the sensor noise is again 0.5 °C. We simulate all the paths on every day, including days that no station reported, so that we can score the predictions later.

The stations report on their own schedules over the first 120 days, and days 120 to 134 are left for a forecast. Stations 1 and 2 cover the whole window, and station 2 has a 20-day logger outage from day 80, which falls in the coldest regional spell of the record. Station 3 is read by hand every second day from day 10 to day 110, station 4 starts on day 30 and misses another 30 % of its days, and station 5 stops after day 80. As in Example 2, every station also misses each day with probability 0.08, and we keep only the days a station reported.

docs.title: 2. The merged grid with from_sites¶
docs.text: SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP.from_sites takes the regional kernel, the local kernel and one array of days and one array of values per station, as pad_sites did. It returns the model on the merged grid $\mathcal{T}_y$ and the $(T, N_\Omega)$ array $\mathbf{Y}$, which is NaN wherever a station did not report. The model keeps the merged days and the mask. Here we build it with the true kernels, and inside the NumPyro model we rebuild it on the same grid with the sampled ones. Every entry that a station did not report is masked, so it enters neither the value of the log marginal nor its gradient.

docs.title: 3. The model as a plain NumPyro function¶
docs.text: We give the regional and the local kernel the same priors, Example 1's priors for $\sigma_f^2$ and $\ell$: $\sigma_g^2, \sigma_h^2 \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 2, 1)$ and $\ell_g, \ell_h \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 7, 1)$. So nothing in the priors says which part is slow or large, and only the data separate the regional signal from the local ones. The noise variance keeps Example 1's prior too, $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 0.1, 1)$. The model rebuilds SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP on the merged days and mask of network_true with the sampled kernels, and numpyro.factor adds its log_marginal as one site named "y". The local kernel has scalar hyperparameters, which SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP pools over the stations. A local kernel whose leaves have a leading axis of length $N_\Omega$ would give each station its own, which is how Example 2's hierarchy would go on top of this model.

docs.title: 4. NUTS¶
docs.text: We run two chains of 200 draws after 200 warm-up steps with a dense mass matrix, started at the prior medians (init_to_median), and run the chains in parallel on two CPU devices as in Example 2. The wall-clock time includes JIT compilation.

docs.title: 5. The hyperparameters against the truth¶
docs.text: For each parameter we print the posterior mean, standard deviation and 90 % interval, next to the value we simulated the data with.

docs.title: 6. Decomposition and prediction at every station¶
docs.text:
A posterior draw $e \in \mathcal{E}$ gives $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}$. For one draw we build the model on an extended grid, the merged days together with the test times $t_*$, every 12 hours from day 0 to day 134.5. A test time that is not a station day is a row of the mask with no station reporting, so the filter only predicts there. decompose runs the Kalman filter and RTS smoother on that model and returns the smoothed means of the regional part, $\mathbb{E}[g(t_*) \mid \mathbf{Y}; \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}]$, and of every local part, $\mathbb{E}[h_n(t_*) \mid \mathbf{Y}; \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}]$. decompose returns no variances, so we take them from the smoothed state covariances $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,* \mid T} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ of as_lgssm(noise_var).smooth(...), which its docstring points to. With $\mathbf{h}_n \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ row $n$ of $\mathbf{H}$, and $\mathbf{h}_g, \mathbf{h}_{h,n} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ the same row with only its regional or only its local block kept, so that $\mathbf{h}_n = \mathbf{h}_g + \mathbf{h}_{h,n}$,

$$\mathbb{V}[g(t_*) \mid \mathbf{Y}; \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}] = \mathbf{h}_g^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,* \mid T} \mathbf{h}_g$$

$$\mathbb{V}[h_n(t_*) \mid \mathbf{Y}; \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}] = \mathbf{h}_{h,n}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,* \mid T} \mathbf{h}_{h,n}$$

$$\mathbb{V}[g(t_*) + h_n(t_*) \mid \mathbf{Y}; \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(e)}] = \mathbf{h}_n^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,* \mid T} \mathbf{h}_n$$

The last one is not the sum of the first two, because given the data the regional and the local part of a station are correlated: a warm reading can be either. A new observation $y_{n,*}$ adds $(\sigma_\varepsilon^{(e)})^2$. We do this for $N_{\mathcal{E}} = 100$ NUTS draws with jax.vmap and average each mean and variance over the draws as in Example 1, so every band carries the hyperparameter uncertainty as well as the uncertainty of the paths.

docs.title: 7. What the regional signal buys¶
docs.text: To see what the joint model buys, we fit the network with Example 2's structure instead, in which each station has one anomaly $f_n \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(t, t'; \sigma_f^2, \ell))$ of its own and the anomalies of different stations are independent. We pool $\sigma_f^2$, $\ell$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ over the stations (Example 1's priors), so this model has three parameters and shares only them. As in Example 2, pad_sites pads the records, and one vmapped MarkovGPPrior.log_marginal per station goes into one factor. Both models see the same data, and we score their predictions on the same withheld days.

docs.title: 8. Cost¶
docs.text: Each NUTS leapfrog step costs one Kalman filter pass over the $T$ merged days with the $D_x$-dimensional joint state, plus its reverse-mode gradient, so $\mathcal{O}(T D_x^3)$ with $D_x = 2 + 2 N_\Omega$. Below we time one jitted log density and its gradient for networks of 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 stations on the same merged grid, which we build by repeating this network's mask and records, and compare with Example 2's vmapped independent filters on the same number of stations.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• A regional signal plus one local signal per station is a plain NumPyro function: priors on two SDE kernels and the noise, SharedPlusSiteMarkovGP rebuilt on the merged grid that from_sites returns, and its log_marginal as one factor site. The log marginal equals the dense Gaussian over all 391 observed (day, station) pairs to a relative difference of 2.2e-16.
  • The Kalman filter integrates out the regional path and every local path, so NUTS runs on five parameters. It recovered four of them within their 90 % intervals, and the local kernel much more tightly than the regional one, since every station sees its own local path but there is only one regional path.
  • decompose, with the variances read from as_lgssm(...).smooth(...) and averaged over 100 NUTS draws, splits every station into its regional and local parts. The regional signal comes back with an RMSE of 0.47 °C and 97.5 % coverage over the reporting days.
  • The shared signal is what fills a station's outage and the days outside its record. There the joint model's RMSE is 1.11 and 1.08 °C, against 2.63 and 2.74 °C for Example 2's independent stations, and its bands keep their coverage.
  • Each gradient costs 12.07 ms for five stations ($D_x = 12$), 3.0 times Example 2's independent filters, and it grows with the number of stations because the joint state does. The fit took 58.4 s of NUTS on CPU.

The next example moves from a handful of stations to a spatial field, where the regional signal varies in space as well as in time. For the stations on their own see Example 2, and for one station Example 1.

# Shapes: N_Ω = 8 facilities; T = 80 days; M = 1,600 map cells; D_x = 2

truth = {
    "intercept": float(jnp.log(2.0)),  # two events per day at a typical facility
    "spatial.variance": 0.5,
    "spatial.lengthscale": 30.0,  # km
    "temporal_variance": 0.4,
    "temporal_lengthscale": 7.0,  # days
}
N_FACILITIES = 8
N_DAYS = 80
LAST_REPORT = 65  # facilities report on days 0, …, 64; the rest is a forecast
BASIN_KM = 100.0
N_SIDE = 40

key_s, key_g, key_f, key_y, key_gap = jr.split(jr.PRNGKey(2027), 5)
# s_n, uniform over the basin
coords = BASIN_KM * jr.uniform(key_s, (N_FACILITIES, 2))  # → (N_Ω, 2)
# t_k, days since the start of the record
days = jnp.arange(N_DAYS, dtype=jnp.float64)  # → (T,)

# the map cells, east varying fastest
axis_km = jnp.linspace(0.0, BASIN_KM, N_SIDE)  # → (N_SIDE,)
east = einx.id("i -> (j i)", axis_km, j=N_SIDE)  # → (M,)
north = einx.id("j -> (j i)", axis_km, i=N_SIDE)  # → (M,)
map_coords = einx.id("m, m -> m (1 + 1)", east, north)  # → (M, 2)
n_cells = map_coords.shape[0]

# today (pyrox_gp)
# k_Matérn-3/2(s, s'; σ_g², ℓ_g) with the true hyperparameters
spatial_kernel_true = Matern(
    nu=1.5,
    init_variance=truth["spatial.variance"],
    init_lengthscale=truth["spatial.lengthscale"],
    pyrox_name="spatial",
)
# map cells first, then the facilities
field_points = jnp.concatenate([map_coords, coords])  # → (M + N_Ω, 2)
# today (pyrox_gp)
# g(s) on the map cells and at the facilities, one joint draw
field_true = GPPrior(spatial_kernel_true, field_points).sample(key_g)  # → (M + N_Ω,)
g_map_true = field_true[:n_cells]  # → (M,)
g_true = field_true[n_cells:]  # → (N_Ω,)

# today (pyrox_ssm)

temporal_sde_true = MaternSDE(
    truth["temporal_variance"], truth["temporal_lengthscale"], order=1
)
# today (pyrox_ssm)
temporal_prior_true = MarkovGPPrior(temporal_sde_true, days)
# z_n,k ~ 𝒩(0, I_D_x)
innovations = jr.normal(key_f, (N_FACILITIES, N_DAYS, 2))  # → (N_Ω, T, D_x)
# today (pyrox_ssm)
# f_n(t_k), one path per facility from its own innovations
f_true = markov_gp_from_innovations(temporal_prior_true, innovations)  # → (N_Ω, T)

# c + g(s_n), the baseline log rate of each facility
baseline_true = truth["intercept"] + g_true  # → (N_Ω,)

log_rate_true = einx.add("n, n k -> n k", baseline_true, f_true)  # → (N_Ω, T)
rate_true = jnp.exp(log_rate_true)  # → (N_Ω, T)

mask = einx.logical_and("k, n k -> n k", reporting, ~downtime & ~outage)

def emissions_model(
    coords, days, counts, mask, sample_path=markov_gp_innovations_sample
):
    # Shapes: N_Ω facilities; T days; D_x = 2

    # today (numpyro)
    # c ~ 𝒩(0, 1)
    intercept = numpyro.sample("intercept", dist.Normal(0.0, 1.0))

    # today (pyrox_gp)
    # k_Matérn-3/2(s, s'; σ_g², ℓ_g), whose hyperparameters are sample sites
    spatial_kernel = Matern(nu=1.5, pyrox_name="spatial")
    # today (pyrox)
    # σ_g² ~ LogNormal(log 0.5, 1)
    spatial_kernel.set_prior("variance", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.5), 1.0))
    # today (pyrox)
    # ℓ_g ~ LogNormal(log 30, 0.5)
    spatial_kernel.set_prior("lengthscale", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(30.0), 0.5))
    # today (pyrox_gp)
    # g ~ 𝒩(0, K_SS) at the facility coordinates S_y
    spatial_prior = GPPrior(spatial_kernel, coords)
    # today (pyrox_gp)
    # g = L_SS z_g, z_g ~ 𝒩(0, I)
    effect = gp_sample("facility_effect", spatial_prior, whitened=True)  # → (N_Ω,)

    # today (numpyro)
    # σ_f² ~ LogNormal(log 0.5, 1)
    temporal_variance = numpyro.sample(
        "temporal_variance", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(0.5), 1.0)
    )
    # today (numpyro)
    # ℓ ~ LogNormal(log 7, 1)
    temporal_lengthscale = numpyro.sample(
        "temporal_lengthscale", dist.LogNormal(jnp.log(7.0), 1.0)
    )
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    # k_Matérn-3/2(t, t'; σ_f², ℓ) as a linear SDE, pooled over the facilities
    temporal_sde = MaternSDE(temporal_variance, temporal_lengthscale, order=1)
    # today (pyrox_ssm)
    temporal_prior = MarkovGPPrior(temporal_sde, days)

    # c + g(s_n)
    baseline = intercept + effect  # → (N_Ω,)
    # today (numpyro): one path and one row of counts per facility
    with numpyro.plate("facility", coords.shape[0]):
        # today (pyrox_ssm)
        # f_n(t_k) = H x_n,k with x_n,k = F_k x_n,k−1 + L_η,k z_n,k
        path = sample_path("path", temporal_prior)  # → (N_Ω, T)
        # log ρ_n,k = c + g(s_n) + f_n(t_k)
        log_rate = einx.add("n, n k -> n k", baseline, path)  # → (N_Ω, T)
        # today (numpyro)
        # ρ_n,k, recorded on every day
        rate = numpyro.deterministic("rate", jnp.exp(log_rate))  # → (N_Ω, T)
        # today (numpyro)
        # y_n,k ~ Poisson(ρ_n,k) where o_n,k = 1
        numpyro.sample("y", dist.Poisson(rate).mask(mask).to_event(1), obs=counts)


def site_kind(site):
    """A short label for a trace site: plate, deterministic or its family."""
    if site["type"] != "sample":
        return site["type"]
    fn = site["fn"]
    while isinstance(fn, (dist.ExpandedDistribution, dist.Independent)):
        fn = fn.base_dist
    if isinstance(fn, dist.MaskedDistribution):
        fn = fn.base_dist
    return type(fn).__name__

seeded_model = handlers.seed(emissions_model, rng_seed=0)
# today (numpyro)

for name, site in trace.items():
    shape = tuple(jnp.shape(site["value"]))
    print(f"site {name!r:24} {site_kind(site):<14} value shape={shape}")
n_latent = sum(
    int(np.prod(jnp.shape(site["value"])))
    for site in trace.values()
    if site["type"] == "sample" and not site["is_observed"]
)

NUTS has all five true values inside its 90 % intervals. The temporal kernel is the best determined, with $\sigma_f^2$ at 0.394 ± 0.104 (true 0.4) and $\ell$ at 6.55 ± 1.77 days (true 7), because each of the eight facilities contributes its own path to it. The spatial kernel rests on only eight points. So $\sigma_g^2$ is uncertain (0.56 ± 0.38, true 0.5) and the 90 % interval of $\ell_g$ runs from 13.5 to 71.4 km, which is mostly the prior. The intercept, 0.30 ± 0.40 against $\log 2 = 0.69$, is wide because it trades off against the mean of the eight facility effects, which section 7 shows.

SVI does much worse on the hyperparameters. Only $\sigma_g^2$ falls inside its 90 % interval. The temporal kernel comes out at under a third of the true variance ($\sigma_f^2$ = 0.123 ± 0.018) and less than half the true lengthscale ($\ell$ = 2.94 ± 0.27 days), with standard deviations about six times smaller than those of NUTS. The mean-field guide makes every value independent of every other, whereas in the posterior the temporal hyperparameters and the 1,280 innovations depend strongly on each other (the same path can come from a larger $\sigma_f^2$ with smaller innovations, or the other way round). So we take the NUTS posterior as the reference here, and SVI as a fast approximation of the latent rates, which we check next.

def rate_summary(rate_draws, key):
    """Mean and 95 % bands of ρ and of a new count y, over the draw axis."""
    # ρ̄_n,k = (1/N_E) ∑ₑ ρ_n,k⁽ᵉ⁾
    mean = einx.mean("member n k -> n k", rate_draws)  # → (N_Ω, T)
    # the 2.5 % and 97.5 % quantiles of ρ_n,k⁽ᵉ⁾ over the draws
    lo, hi = np.percentile(np.asarray(rate_draws), [2.5, 97.5], axis=0)
    # y_n,k⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ Poisson(ρ_n,k⁽ᵉ⁾), one new count per draw
    new_counts = jr.poisson(key, rate_draws)  # → (N_E, N_Ω, T)
    # the same quantiles of the new counts
    y_lo, y_hi = np.percentile(np.asarray(new_counts), [2.5, 97.5], axis=0)
    return {"mean": mean, "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "y_lo": y_lo, "y_hi": y_hi}

Where a facility reports, the NUTS band follows the true rate and its mean smooths the noisy counts. Over facility 3's outage the band widens and still holds the true rate, as the days on either side of the outage pin the path down at its ends. In the forecast after day 64 the NUTS band widens towards the stationary spread of the path, whereas the SVI band stays narrow. Its temporal kernel is too small and too short (section 5), so its forecast relaxes to the baseline quickly and with too little spread. It misses the late rise at facility 4, which the NUTS band holds, and neither band reaches the rise at facility 7 in the last days of the forecast.

Because the data are simulated, we know the true rate on every day and the count each facility would have reported on the days its monitoring was down. Below we score both methods: the fraction of facility days on which the true rate is inside the 95 % band, and the fraction of withheld counts inside the 95 % predictive interval, split into the isolated downtime days, facility 3's outage and the forecast.

def coverage(lower, upper, target, sel):
    """Fraction of target inside [lower, upper] on the entries in sel."""
    # lower ≤ target ≤ upper
    inside = (np.asarray(target) >= np.asarray(lower)) & (
        np.asarray(target) <= np.asarray(upper)
    )
    return float(np.mean(inside[sel]))

def draws_from(samples):
    """N_E draws evenly spaced through the chains."""
    num_samples = samples["intercept"].shape[0]
    idx = jnp.linspace(0, num_samples - 1, N_DRAWS).astype(int)  # → (N_E,)

def mixture(means, variances):
    """Mean and variance of the equal-weight mixture over the draw axis."""
    # μ̄_* = (1/N_E) ∑ₑ μ_*⁽ᵉ⁾
    mean = einx.mean("member ... -> ...", means)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (μ_*⁽ᵉ⁾ − μ̄_*)²
    spread = einx.var("member ... -> ...", means)
    # (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)²
    variance_mean = einx.mean("member ... -> ...", variances)
    # 𝕍 ≈ (1/N_E) ∑ₑ (σ_*⁽ᵉ⁾)² + spread
    return mean, variance_mean + spread

    counts_n = jr.poisson(jr.PRNGKey(0), 2.0, (N_FACILITIES, n_days))  # → (N_Ω, n_days)
    mask_n = jnp.ones((N_FACILITIES, n_days), dtype=bool)  # → (N_Ω, n_days)
    model = partial(emissions_model, sample_path=sample_path)
    # every sample site at its prior median, the paths at zero
    params = {
        "intercept": jnp.asarray(0.0),
        "spatial.variance": jnp.asarray(0.5),
        "spatial.lengthscale": jnp.asarray(30.0),
        "facility_effect_u": jnp.zeros(N_FACILITIES),
        "temporal_variance": jnp.asarray(0.5),
        "temporal_lengthscale": jnp.asarray(7.0),
        path_site: jnp.zeros((N_FACILITIES, n_days, *path_shape)),
    }

    def log_joint(values):
        # today (numpyro)
        # log p(θ, z_g, Z, Y) at the given sample values
        log_p, _ = log_density(model, (coords, days_n, counts_n, mask_n), {}, values)
        return log_p

    # today (jax)
    # the log joint and its gradient, jitted once
    loss_and_grad = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(log_joint))
    jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(params))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        jax.block_until_ready(loss_and_grad(params))
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / repeats

docs.title: A spatial field and one path per facility: Poisson counts of emission events with NUTS and SVI¶
docs.text:
Examples 1, 2 and 3 all had Gaussian observations, so the Kalman filter integrated every latent path out and NUTS only ever saw a handful of hyperparameters. Here the observations are counts. We take a set of oil and gas facilities at known locations in one basin, and for each facility the daily number of methane emission events that its monitoring flagged. The log of a facility's event rate is a spatial facility effect, a GP over the facility locations (facilities close to each other share operators, equipment and gas composition), plus a temporal path of its own, a Markov GP over the days (maintenance, liquids unloading and other episodes that last days to weeks). With a Poisson likelihood there is no Kalman marginal, so the paths have to be sampled. We sample them through whitened innovations with markov_gp_innovations_sample, inside a numpyro.plate over the facilities, and fit the same model with NUTS and with SVI.

pyrox-ssm capability shown: markov_gp_innovations_sample, which registers standard normal innovations as one sample site f"{name}_eps" and the Markov-GP path built from them as a deterministic site name, with one independent path per index of an enclosing numpyro.plate. The path is the SDE run forward by a lax.scan, so the latent paths are sampled in a whitened (non-centred) form, which is the geometry NUTS needs. Cost: every log-density evaluation is one scan over the $T$ days per facility, $\mathcal{O}(N_\Omega T D_x^3)$, against the $\mathcal{O}(T^3)$ Cholesky factor (and the $T \times T$ kernel matrix) of the dense markov_gp_sample. We measure both, per gradient and per NUTS draw, in section 8.

What you'll learn:

  1. How to write a spatio-temporal Poisson model as a plain NumPyro function that composes a pyrox_gp kernel over the facility locations with a pyrox_ssm path over the days.
  2. How to fit it with NUTS and with SVI, and how their posteriors of the five hyperparameters compare with the truth.
  3. How to read the latent rates, the predictions on withheld days and a short forecast, and a map of the spatial facility effect, off the posterior draws.
  4. What the whitened path costs against the dense one, per gradient and per NUTS draw.

The Matérn-3/2 SDE and its state-space form are explained in Example 1, and the plate over sites and the non-centred draws in Example 2. We reuse both here without deriving them again.

docs.title: Why pyrox_gp and pyrox_ssm appear together¶
docs.text: The spatial effect is an ordinary GP over a few points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, which is what pyrox_gp provides: a Matérn kernel whose hyperparameters carry priors (Matern with set_prior), a GPPrior over the facility coordinates and the whitened gp_sample. The temporal paths are Markov GPs, which are pyrox_ssm. Neither package imports the other. Both depend only on pyrox (the bridge), and pyrox-ssm is forbidden from importing pyrox-gp by its import-guard test (AGENTS.md). That rule is about the dependencies between the packages, not about the models people build with them. So a user who imports both and composes them in one NumPyro function, as we do below, is the intended use, and the two packages meet only through NumPyro's sample sites.

docs.title: Background¶
docs.text:
The basin holds a set $\Omega_y$ of $N_\Omega \equiv N_{\Omega_y} = 8$ facilities. We index them by $n = 1, \ldots, N_\Omega$, as we indexed the stations in Examples 2 and 3, and keep $\mathbf{s}$ for coordinates: facility $n$ sits at $\mathbf{s}_n \in \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^{2}$ (km), and $\mathbf{S}_y \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\Omega \times 2}$ stacks the $\mathbf{s}_n$ as rows. The days $t_k$, $k = 1, \ldots, T$, form the grid $\mathcal{T}_x$ of $T \equiv N_{\mathcal{T}_x}$ days on which the latent paths live, and $y_{n,k} \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$ is the number of events at facility $n$ on day $t_k$, observed when the mask $o_{n,k} \in \{0, 1\}$ is 1. The counts are Poisson with a log-linear rate,

$$y_{n,k} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\rho_{n,k})$$

$$\log \rho_{n,k} = c + g(\mathbf{s}_n) + f_n(t_k)$$

$$g \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}'; \sigma_g^2, \ell_g))$$

$$f_n \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(t, t'; \sigma_f^2, \ell))$$

where $\rho_{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ is the event rate (events per day), $c \in \mathbb{R}$ is the intercept (the log rate of a typical facility), $g$ is the spatial facility effect and $f_n$ is facility $n$'s temporal path. The paths $f_1, \ldots, f_{N_\Omega}$ are independent of each other and of $g$, and they share one kernel, as the local paths of Example 3 did. The kernel variances $\sigma_g^2$ and $\sigma_f^2$ (in log-rate units squared), the spatial lengthscale $\ell_g$ (km) and the temporal lengthscale $\ell$ (days) are all in $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, so $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (c, \sigma_g^2, \ell_g, \sigma_f^2, \ell) \in \mathbb{R}^{5}$. With $\mathbf{Y} \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}^{N_\Omega \times T}$ the counts and $\boldsymbol{\rho} \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}^{N_\Omega \times T}$ the rates, the log likelihood keeps only the observed entries,

$$\log p(\mathbf{Y} \mid \boldsymbol{\rho}) = \sum_{n=1}^{N_\Omega} \sum_{k=1}^{T} o_{n,k} (y_{n,k} \log \rho_{n,k} - \rho_{n,k} - \log y_{n,k}!)$$

The Poisson likelihood is not Gaussian, so we cannot integrate the latent values out with a Kalman filter as in Examples 1 to 3, and NUTS has to sample them. Sampled directly, the latent values and their hyperparameters form a funnel, as $\boldsymbol{\tau}_\theta$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}_n$ did in Example 2. So we sample both in a whitened form, with standard normal values that are a priori independent of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. For the spatial effect at the facilities, $\mathbf{g} = g(\mathbf{S}_y) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\Omega}$,

$$\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{L}_{SS} \mathbf{z}_g$$

$$\mathbf{z}_g \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_{N_\Omega})$$

where $\mathbf{L}_{SS} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\Omega \times N_\Omega}$ is the lower Cholesky factor of the kernel matrix $\mathbf{K}_{SS} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\Omega \times N_\Omega}$, $[\mathbf{K}_{SS}]_{nn'} = k_\text{Matérn-3/2}(\mathbf{s}_n, \mathbf{s}_{n'}; \sigma_g^2, \ell_g)$. This is what pyrox_gp.gp_sample(..., whitened=True) registers. For the temporal paths we run the Matérn-3/2 SDE of Example 1 forward from standard normal innovations $\mathbf{z}_{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$, with the state $\mathbf{x}_{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}$ and $D_x = 2$,

$$\mathbf{x}_{n,1} = \mathbf{L}_{x,\infty} \mathbf{z}_{n,1}$$

$$\mathbf{x}_{n,k} = \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{x}_{n,k-1} + \mathbf{L}_{\eta,k} \mathbf{z}_{n,k}$$

$$f_n(t_k) = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{x}_{n,k}$$

$$\mathbf{z}_{n,k} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_{D_x})$$

where $\mathbf{F}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ is the transition over $\Delta t_k = t_k - t_{k-1}$, $\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times D_x}$ the measurement row, and $\mathbf{L}_{x,\infty}, \mathbf{L}_{\eta,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}$ the Cholesky factors of the stationary covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,\infty}$ and of the model noise covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\eta,k} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,\infty} - \mathbf{F}_k \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x,\infty} \mathbf{F}_k^\top$. The map from the innovations to the path is linear, so the path $\mathbf{f}_n = f_n(t_{1:T}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathcal{T}_x}}$ has exactly the prior $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{K}_{tt})$, with $\mathbf{K}_{tt} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times T}$ the Matérn-3/2 kernel matrix over the days, but it costs $\mathcal{O}(T D_x^3)$ and never forms $\mathbf{K}_{tt}$. This is markov_gp_innovations_sample; markov_gp_sample instead samples $\mathbf{f}_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{K}_{tt})$ directly, which is centred and needs $\mathbf{K}_{tt}$ and its Cholesky factor on every evaluation. The API calls the $\mathbf{z}_{n,k}$ innovations, which are not the Kalman residuals of the same name. NUTS then samples $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, $\mathbf{z}_g$ and the $N_\Omega T$ innovations $\mathbf{z}_{n,k}$, that is $5 + N_\Omega + N_\Omega T D_x$ unconstrained values.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: We detect Colab and install pyrox, pyrox-gp[colab] (which pulls in matplotlib and watermark) and pyrox-ssm only when the notebook runs there.

docs.title: 1. Eight facilities in one basin¶
docs.text:
We simulate the model itself, so that we know every true value. The basin is 100 km by 100 km and the eight facilities sit at random locations in it. A typical facility has two events per day ($c = \log 2$). The spatial effect has a variance of 0.5, so the baseline rates of different facilities differ by a factor of about two either way, and it decorrelates over about 30 km. Each facility's path has a variance of 0.4 and decorrelates over about a week. We draw the spatial effect jointly on a 40 by 40 grid of map cells and at the facilities, so that we can score the map in section 7.

The record runs for $T = 80$ days. The facilities report on days 0 to 64, and days 65 to 79 are left for a forecast. On each reporting day a facility's monitoring is down with probability 0.1, and facility 3 has a 15-day outage from day 40. A day without monitoring is a count we never see, so its mask entry is 0, and we keep its true count to score the predictions.

docs.title: 2. The model as a plain NumPyro function¶
docs.text:
The intercept gets $c \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, so a typical facility has between about 0.14 and 7 events per day (two standard deviations either way). The spatial kernel is pyrox_gp.Matern(nu=1.5), and its hyperparameters get their priors with set_prior, so the kernel itself registers them as the sample sites "spatial.variance" and "spatial.lengthscale": $\sigma_g^2 \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 0.5, 1)$ and $\ell_g \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 30, 0.5)$. Eight facilities say very little about a spatial lengthscale, so its prior states the scale of the basin (between about 10 and 80 km). The temporal kernel gets $\sigma_f^2 \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 0.5, 1)$ and Example 1's prior for the lengthscale, $\ell \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\log 7, 1)$.

Then gp_sample(..., whitened=True) draws $\mathbf{z}_g$ as the site "facility_effect_u" and records $\mathbf{g}$ as the deterministic "facility_effect". Inside numpyro.plate("facility", N_Ω), markov_gp_innovations_sample("path", ...) draws one $(T, D_x)$ block of innovations per facility as the site "path_eps" and records the paths as the deterministic "path". The Poisson site "y" is masked with .mask(mask), so an unobserved day adds nothing to the log density, and its count, stored as 0, is never read. Its last dimension, the days, is an event dimension (.to_event(1)), so the facility plate owns the first one. We also record the rates as a deterministic site "rate", so the posterior samples carry $\rho_{n,k}$ on every day, observed or not.

sample_path defaults to markov_gp_innovations_sample; section 8 passes markov_gp_sample instead, which has the same signature, to fit the dense, centred version of the same model.

docs.title: 3. NUTS¶
docs.text: We run two chains of 150 draws after 150 warm-up steps, started at the prior medians with init_to_median, which puts every whitened value at 0. A dense mass matrix over all 1,293 values would have about 1.7 million entries to adapt. However, only a few of them are strongly correlated in the posterior: the intercept trades off against the mean of the facility effects (a higher $c$ with lower $g(\mathbf{s}_n)$ gives the same rates), and $\sigma_g^2$ against the scale of $\mathbf{z}_g$. So we give the 13 values outside the paths ($\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and $\mathbf{z}_g$) one dense $13 \times 13$ block of the mass matrix, with dense_mass=[(...)], and keep the 1,280 innovations on the diagonal, where their unit prior scale suits it. The chains run one after the other with chain_method="sequential", as in Example 1. The wall-clock time includes JIT compilation. We print the summary for the five hyperparameters, and for the spatial effects and the rates on the observed facility days only the worst $\hat{R}$ and the smallest effective sample size.

docs.title: 4. SVI with a mean-field guide¶
docs.text: With 1,293 latent values a full-rank Gaussian guide, as in Example 1, would have about a million covariance parameters. In the whitened coordinates, however, the prior is a standard normal with no correlations at all, which is what makes a mean-field guide workable for the latent values, and the reason gp_sample has its whitened=True mode. Whether it is good enough for the hyperparameters we check against NUTS in section 5. AutoNormal puts an independent Gaussian on every unconstrained value, the five hyperparameters included, and we start it at the prior medians. The guide is $q( oldsymbol{ heta}, \mathbf{z}_g, \mathbf{Z}; oldsymbol{ u})$ with $ oldsymbol{ u}$ its means and scales, and SVI minimises $\mathcal{L}_ ext{ELBO}( oldsymbol{ u}) = -\mathrm{ELBO}$. Predictive with the guide then gives the deterministic sites, the paths and the rates, for 1,000 guide draws.

docs.title: 5. The hyperparameters against the truth¶
docs.text: For each hyperparameter we print the posterior mean, standard deviation and 90 % interval from NUTS and from SVI, next to the value we simulated the data with.

docs.title: 6. Latent rates and predictions at every facility¶
docs.text: Every posterior draw $e \in \mathcal{E}$ carries the whole rate field, $\rho_{n,k}^{(e)} = \exp(c^{(e)} + g^{(e)}(\mathbf{s}_n) + f_n^{(e)}(t_k))$, on every day of the grid. The paths were sampled on all $T$ days, and the mask only kept the unobserved days out of the likelihood, so the withheld days and the forecast need no extra step: they are the days on which the posterior of the path is informed by its neighbours (or, in the forecast, by nothing but the prior after the last observation). The rate is a nonlinear function of the latent values, so we summarise it with the posterior mean $\bar{\rho}_{n,k} = \frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{E}}} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} \rho_{n,k}^{(e)}$ and the 2.5 % and 97.5 % quantiles over the draws, the 95 % band. For a new count we draw $y_{n,k}^{(e)} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\rho_{n,k}^{(e)})$ once per draw and take the same quantiles, which gives the 95 % predictive interval of the count.

docs.title: 7. The spatial facility effect on a map¶
docs.text: The posterior draws give the spatial effect only at the eight facilities, $\mathbf{g}^{(e)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\Omega}$. To map it, we condition the spatial GP of each draw on its own values at the facilities and predict at the map cells, which pyrox_gp does with GPPrior(...).condition(g, 0).predict(...), noise-free apart from the prior's $10^{-6}$ jitter. For a map cell $\mathbf{s}_* \in \Omega$, with $\mathbf{K}_{*S} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times N_\Omega}$ the kernel row between the cell and the facilities under draw $e$, this gives the mean $\mu_*^{(e)} = \mathbf{K}_{*S} \mathbf{K}_{SS}^{-1} \mathbf{g}^{(e)} \in \mathbb{R}$ and the variance $(\sigma_*^{(e)})^2 = (\sigma_g^{(e)})^2 - \mathbf{K}_{*S} \mathbf{K}_{SS}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{*S}^\top \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, and we average them over $N_{\mathcal{E}} = 100$ NUTS draws as in Example 1. The posterior of the whole field then carries the uncertainty of the hyperparameters, of $\mathbf{g}$ and of the field between the facilities.

docs.title: 8. Cost: the whitened path against the dense one¶
docs.text: markov_gp_innovations_sample and markov_gp_sample give the paths the same prior. The dense one registers $\mathbf{f}_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{K}_{tt})$ as one MultivariateNormal site, batched over the facility plate. So every log-density evaluation builds the $T \times T$ kernel matrix $\mathbf{K}_{tt}$ (one matrix exponential per pair of days, $\mathcal{O}(T^2 D_x^3)$) and its Cholesky factor ($\mathcal{O}(T^3)$), and NUTS samples the paths in the centred form. The whitened one runs one scan of $T$ steps per facility. We compare them in two ways. First, we time one jitted log joint density and its gradient for the full model (all eight facilities, the same priors), with every sample site at its prior median, for records of 30 to 240 days. Then we run NUTS on both versions of the model for the first 20 days of the record, one chain of 60 draws after 60 warm-up steps each, and count the leapfrog steps per draw. We use only 20 days because the dense gradient grows so quickly with $T$ (the first table below) that a dense fit of the full record does not fit in this notebook's time budget.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• A spatio-temporal Poisson model is a plain NumPyro function that composes a pyrox_gp Matérn kernel over the facility coordinates (its priors set with set_prior, its values drawn with the whitened gp_sample) with one pyrox_ssm Markov-GP path per facility, drawn by markov_gp_innovations_sample under a numpyro.plate. The two packages never import each other; the user composes them through NumPyro's sites.
  • The trace holds the five hyperparameters, the whitened spatial values "facility_effect_u", the innovations "path_eps" with one $(T, D_x)$ block per facility, and the deterministic "facility_effect", "path" and "rate". So the posterior draws, from NUTS or from Predictive with a guide, carry the rates on every day, and the withheld days and the forecast need no extra step.
  • NUTS recovers all five hyperparameters within their 90 % intervals, in 83.4 s with 63 leapfrog steps per draw. Mean-field SVI took 14.7 s and gets the rates on the observed days right (97.1 % coverage), but not the hyperparameters: its temporal kernel is far too small and short, and in the forecast its band holds the true rate on only 63.3 % of the facility days, against 85.0 % for NUTS.
  • Conditioning the spatial GP of each draw on its values at the facilities maps the facility effect, with bands that say how little eight facilities tell about the field away from themselves (98.6 % of the map cells inside $\pm 2\sigma$ for NUTS).
  • Per gradient, the whitened path cost 0.67 to 3.33 ms for records of 30 to 240 days and the dense markov_gp_sample 2.91 to 306.83 ms. On the first 20 days NUTS needed 49.6 leapfrog steps per draw with the whitened paths against 151.5 with the dense, centred ones.

For the plate over sites and the non-centred draws see Example 2, for a shared signal that couples the sites Example 3, and for the Matérn SDE and the Kalman filter Example 1.
